articles.title: Western F-16s promised safe skies over Kiev: Why could they all go MIA soon?
articles.body:
Western F-16s promised safe skies over Kiev: Why could they all go MIA soon?
Ukraine’s NATO-donated F-16 fleet is out of commission more often than it engages Russian drones, The Wall Street Journal has claimed.
The American-produced fighter jets were touted as the latest “gamechanger” weapon in Kiev’s conflict with Russia, a tool that will help “achieve goals outside of Ukraine,” as Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said when the first batch was set to arrive in the summer of 2024.
However, a key EU member in the European-led scheme cannot keep up with necessary maintenance of the fleet, according to the newspaper.
What is the F-16 initiative?
The plan was launched in 2023, as Ukraine’s fleet of Soviet-built military aircraft was dwindling. Pro-Kiev propaganda implied that the US-made multirole jets would help Ukrainian forces challenge Russia’s air dominance over the front line. But it was hardly a secret that they would be kept far away from Russian SAMs and fighter jets and only engage long-range drones and cruise missiles.
Donor nations announced they were prepared to spend years training Ukrainian pilots, refurbishing the aircraft they were willing to spare, and happily signing deals for modern replacements to bolster their own militaries – the F-16 initiative was effectively a NATO-backed pyramid scheme allowing everyone to spend big and upgrade their air forces.
Ukraine has since received about 40 jets, roughly half of what the donors pledged, and lost several of them during combat missions, reportedly after corners were cut for expediency during training courses. It is now facing winter with an acute shortage of air defense systems.
What’s the problem?
Belgium’s Sabena Aerospace Engineering, awarded a $235.5 million contract for maintenance of Ukraine’s F-16 fleet, is not keeping up with the demand, according to the Wall Street Journal editorial board.
An inspection that normally takes two to six weeks lasts “as long as 40 weeks in Belgium,” retired US Navy Rear Admiral Mark Montgomery said. Another Western source said more than half of Ukrainian jets are now in maintenance limbo, with the rest set to become grounded by the end of the year.
Was the issue unexpected?
Media reports saying that the Ukrainian F-16 fleet is being overworked surfaced as early as July, as Kiev’s shortage of ground-launched interceptor missiles became more acute. There were also indicators pointing to a bottleneck in Belgium.
In April, the Norwegian Broadcasting Corporation reported that not one of the six F-16s that Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store pledged to Ukraine in 2023 had been delivered. Four of them were not airworthy to begin with, but the two others were previously used to train Ukrainian pilots in Denmark.
The six jets were stuck at a Sabena workshop in Belgium due to “significant capacity problems,” the report said.
Is Ukraine getting more jets?
There were delays in deliveries as well.
Belgium promised in 2024 to transfer 30 aircraft set to be phased out by its air force, which was expecting F-35 replacements. Then-Defense Minister Ludivine Dedonder said Ukraine would start receiving the old jets “as soon as the F-35s arrive on Belgian soil,” but no transfers have been reported since.
Most of the aircraft that Kiev did get reportedly came from the Netherlands and Denmark, the co-leaders of the F-16 initiative.
Why does Ukraine have air defense problems?
A shortage of Western weapons partially caused Ukraine’s current situation.
When this summer Vladimir Zelensky announced a 40-day “pressure campaign” of long-rage strikes on refineries, civilian ships, and commercial warehouses, his team reportedly hoped that images of smoke-plumes stretching over big Russian cities would support his bid to receive more Patriot missile interceptors from the limited US stockpile.
If true, the plan backfired. NATO nations are scrambling to provide what Kiev wants, while the economic damage caused by Russian retaliation is mounting. And Ukraine already has a $27 billion military budget hole that European donors are struggling to fill.
Ukrainian forces previously learned that Western arms gifts come with caveats. Donated NATO artillery systems lacked interoperability and were described as a “zoo” by troops. Much-hyped NATO battle tanks turned out to be mostly useless in drone-driven warfare and had to be kept away from the front line.
Can Ukraine come up with alternatives?
Zelensky puts on a brave face talking about the dire situation. Last week he claimed Ukraine had successfully tested four new interceptor drones designed to shoot down faster-moving jet UAVs – the kind of targets the WSJ claimed F-16s are well-suited to take down.
But an earlier Reuters report said trials in July “did not go to plan” as the prototypes lost control and “crashed into nearby fields and forests.”
Ukrainian opposition lawmaker Sergey Rakhmanin, who sits on the national defense committee, has said Kiev missed Russia’s rapid development of jet kamikaze drones. He said Ukrainian interceptors cost up to $100,000 apiece and that scaling up production would require too much time, even if funding becomes available.

articles.title: "Droneports": inside Russian UAV bases and why they are so difficult to destroy
articles.body:
"Droneports": inside Russian UAV bases and why they are so difficult to destroy
When the Russian forces began stepping up their use of jet-powered drones, perhaps the most common question among Ukrainians was: "Why haven't we destroyed the launch sites yet?"
Although Ukraine's defence forces regularly attack Russian drone launch sites, the strikes have not produced an effect on the scale of Operation Spider's Web, in which a dozen Tu-95MS and Tu-22M3 bombers were destroyed.
The reason is that, over the past two years, Russia has built an extensive network of specialised drone launch facilities, capable of handling dozens of jet-powered and conventional drones every hour. In Ukrainian and Russian discourse, these facilities are dubbed "droneports" – a catch-all term for dedicated sites used to operate drones.
Ukrainska Pravda and CyberBoroshno, a Ukrainian open-source intelligence (OSINT) community, have looked into Russian drone launch sites and attacks on them. Read on to find out where Russian forces launch their UAVs from and why it is highly unlikely that these droneports will ever be destroyed.
Where does Russia launch its Shaheds from?
When the first Iranian-made Shahed loitering munitions arrived in Russia in autumn 2022, little preparation was needed before they could be put to use. The drones could be launched straight out of the box.
The only thing they needed was a site from which they could be launched.
Military airfields were among the first – and perhaps the most obvious – choices for launching the drones. They already had everything needed: secure perimeters, security personnel, ground staff, air defence systems and established logistics for receiving new drones. The airfields were also located away from civilian infrastructure and prying eyes.
Long runways also made it possible to use pick-ups and lorries as mobile launch platforms for Shaheds. Lightweight launchers were also deployed at the airfields. The UAVs took off from these launchers with the help of solid-fuel rocket boosters before switching to their piston engines for the rest of the flight. For the Russians, the existing airfield infrastructure was more than enough.
The first airfields used by Russian forces to launch Shaheds were in occupied Crimea and the border regions of Bryansk and Kursk oblasts. As the number of drones Russia received grew, so did the geographical scope of their deployment. Known launch sites included Cape Chauda, Yeysk, Primorsko-Akhtarsk, Kursk and Seshcha.
The Russians later began using sites other than airfields to launch Shahed drones, including positions around Balaklava on Crimea's southern coast.
This enabled Russian forces to launch dozens of drones every week. The locations were also far enough from the combat zone to keep the launch sites relatively safe, yet close enough to Ukraine for the drones to reach Ukrainian territory within a few hours.
The droneports
When Russia acquired the technology to produce Shahed loitering munitions, another problem emerged: there was a shortage of existing airfield infrastructure.
Unlike the Shaheds supplied by Iran, Russia's domestically produced versions, known as Geran drones, had to be not only launched but also maintained. They had to be assembled, stored, inspected and prepared for launch somewhere. Although the existing infrastructure could support an increase in the number of launch sites, it was still not enough.
Therefore, as Geran production got underway, the Russians began preparing new launch sites in parallel.
Garages for assembling and storing drones began appearing at airfields already used as launch sites. Russia also built underground storage facilities large enough to accommodate both the drones and their warheads. Launchers were also being installed in revetments – protected bays surrounded by earth banks or blast walls.
Alongside the expansion of existing sites, new ones have begun to appear across Russia. In just a few months, large drone bases capable of launching hundreds of drones a day have sprung up on land that was previously covered by fields or forests.
Perhaps the best-known of these is Tsimbulova in Oryol Oblast, about 180 km from the Ukrainian border. Russian sources describe it as "the world's largest droneport". And with good reason: the site covers 5 sq km.
OSINT analyst Dnipro Osint ⟨Harbuz⟩ told Ukrainska Pravda: "The Alabuga began building the site in August 2024, and by February 2025, the main facilities had been completed. Its construction was directly linked to the expansion of drone production at Alabuga. This droneport has, in essence, become the first facility whose infrastructure was designed entirely for storing, maintaining and launching drones."
Tsimbulova has been equipped with runways and fixed catapult launchers for drones. The site also includes hundreds of garages and dozens of underground shelters.
The base's facilities are spread out across the site, with each one separated from the others and surrounded by earthworks. The droneports were built on the assumption that they would eventually be attacked. The Russians therefore sought to ensure that only a direct bombardment could destroy them.
The drones themselves can be stored not only inside buildings but also outdoors. Satellite imagery shows both Shahed attack drones and Gerbera decoy drones, which are also launched from these droneports.
The sites are supported by the infrastructure needed for day-to-day operations: solar panels, diesel generators, fuel depots and radio and navigation equipment for drone control. Each facility has its own access roads, parking areas and additional exit routes. It is also protected by air defence and electronic warfare systems intended to counter Ukrainian attacks.
Harbuz says: "The droneports were initially built much larger than 'necessary'. By the end of 2024, Defence Intelligence of Ukraine estimated the production rate of Shaheds at 2,000 units per month – roughly 64 UAVs a day – yet the droneport infrastructure at Tsimbulova could store up to 3,000 combat drones and 100 UAVs simultaneously. It was clearly built with capacity to spare."
In 2026, the infrastructure at Tsimbulova has continued to expand. New hangars and warehouses were built at the droneport, alongside larger specialised launchers for Geran-4/5 jet-powered drones. These drones can also be launched from mobile platforms mounted on vehicles.
An analysis of satellite images by Ukrainska Pravda estimates that Tsimbulova has 23 launchers for different types of drones, 387 garages and 26 underground storage facilities. The site is still expanding: the Russians are preparing to build four more launchers for jet-powered drones, plus 83 garages and underground shelters.
Another well-known droneport has been established at the site of the destroyed Donetsk airport (DAP). Despite being 50 km from the front line, the site now has hangars and drone launch pads used to launch drones towards frontline areas and targets in the rear.
Up to 95% of drone launches take place from bases in Russia's Bryansk, Rostov, Smolensk and Oryol oblasts, as well as in Krasnodar Krai and occupied Crimea. There are also research droneports where Russia tests UAVs in flight.
Although these sites are smaller than Tsimbulova, they have much the same basic infrastructure.
Ukrainska Pravda has identified at least 63 launchers at the main droneports, but the total could be higher. The sites can accommodate hundreds of drones and tens of thousands of combat components for them.
Can droneports be destroyed?
Ukraine's defence forces could not ignore the fact that Russians were launching Shaheds across Ukraine. Therefore, they gradually began targeting the drone launch sites, choosing their targets according to the capabilities and resources available to them.
Some of the first known strikes on Shahed launch sites were carried out in 2024. Ukrainian forces hit a Shahed depot near Balaklava and a storage facility for the drones near Yeysk.
After the strike, the area near Balaklava ceased to be used for Shahed launches. Yeysk was the first – and so far the only – case in which the impact of a strike could be seen in the launch figures. For the first time, Russia then went 48 days without launching Shaheds on Ukraine.
Russia's droneports have also been struck whilst under construction. On 26 December 2024, at least three Storm Shadow cruise missiles hit a facility between Tsimbulova and Rudnevo. Russian media outlet Astra said two Russian service members were killed and seven others were taken to hospital as a result of the strike.
A month later, the same complex was once again targeted by Storm Shadow/SCALP cruise missiles. Ukraine's General Staff reported that more than 200 Shaheds had been destroyed. The images show damage to one of the warehouses.
Donetsk airport is another well-known target that has come under repeated attacks by Ukraine's defence forces. In a separate article, Ukrainska Pravda details how Ukraine's drone forces have been destroying Shahed launchers at the airport.
Because the airport is so close to the front line, Ukraine's 1st Separate Centre of the Unmanned Systems Forces has been able to regularly destroy Russian weapons, mobile fire groups defending the airfield and infrastructure. Ukrainian forces have repeatedly used mid-range drones and even FPV drones to strike targets at the airfield.
(12) FP-2 drone strikes on the DAP. Video: Special Operations Forces
DAP itself is a good example of just how difficult droneports are to strike.
Harbuz says: "The Russians have built drone launch sites to make them as costly as possible for Ukraine's defence forces to destroy. Ammunition and fuel depots are concealed beneath concrete and earth. Conventional UAVs cannot penetrate these structures, and even if they do, the explosion is contained inside, preventing debris from reaching other depots and triggering a chain reaction.
If any facilities are destroyed, they can be rebuilt relatively quickly and cheaply. As the example of Donetsk airport shows, the Russians are adapting and expanding the drone launch site even there, despite constant Ukrainian strikes."
Therefore, the main objective of Ukraine's defence forces when striking drone launch sites is to disrupt Russia's ability to launch drones.
Falco, an officer with Ukraine's 1st Separate Drone Centre, tells Ukrainska Pravda: "The primary objective is to disrupt their ability to launch drones, so that they are unable to launch them for an extended period. This also affects the overall coordination of their actions and the cohesion of their units. It also makes it easier for our air defence units to engage aerial assets, because there are generally fewer of them."
There are several ways to disrupt drone launches: striking launchers and storage facilities, or creating an aerial threat over the droneport. The attacks can force launches to be postponed indefinitely, while the destruction of infrastructure can reduce the overall number of drones launched.
According to Falco, launch pads and storage garages are among the easiest targets to strike: they are stationary, and there may not always be personnel nearby. But the value of hitting static targets depends on the circumstances and the overall strategy. If a garage or warehouse is packed with explosives or drones, then it makes sense to strike it.
Over the past two years, Ukraine's defence forces have stepped up attacks on Russian droneports. Alongside DAP and Tsimbulova, they have repeatedly targeted sites at Navlya, Hvardiiske, Primorsko-Akhtarsk and elsewhere. The strikes have hit warehouses, launchers, garages and drones left out in the open.
In the latest attack on Tsimbulova, on 21 September, Ukrainian strikes hit a bunker used to store combat drones. One strike penetrated the bunker, and another caused an explosion on the surface. Separate strikes also hit drones near the launch sites.
The strategy behind the strikes has also evolved. Ukraine is no longer targeting only storage, preparation and launch sites, but has also begun striking relay stations used to control Geran and Gerbera drones. UAV ground control stations have reportedly been destroyed in Trubchevsk, Russia, and in the temporarily occupied settlements of Zaliznyi Port, Skadovsk, Chornomorsk and Olenivka.
These facilities are important too, but Ukraine's Unmanned Systems Forces have another target in their sights: the drone operators themselves.
"The most difficult target there is also the most valuable one: the operator," Falco says. "They don't stay near the launch sites for very long. So when you take out the people launching the drones, you're taking away a scarce resource. There aren't many operators to begin with, and the enemy then has to spend even more money training new crews."
Military personnel are not the only people involved in launching Russian drones. Staff from Alabuga take part in the process on a daily basis too. In its study of Russian drone launch sites, the Molfar Intelligence Institute released several classified Alabuga documents.
According to the documents, Alabuga employees complained about "unjustified risk" after a Ukrainian attack on a major droneport in Oryol Oblast in December 2024. They said they were expected to continue working even though Russian air defence systems could not prevent strikes on the launch sites. Many employees said they wanted to leave the sites – and Alabuga itself.
Employees were threatened that they would be shot in the knees if they did not come to work, and were forced to turn up. Apart from Alabuga staff, local residents are also enlisted to assemble drones. Staff at droneports, however, complain about the low efficiency of their work.
Meanwhile, keeping droneports out of operation requires constant pressure on Russian positions.
Falco concludes: "If we want to keep the pressure on, we need to increase the scale of our strikes. The more we can hit, the better. As a country, we are constantly moving towards the level we need. But it's not just about strikes. We also have to think about how the enemy may respond and plan our operations accordingly."
Another factor that could significantly disrupt the operation of Russian droneports would be the use of Ukraine's own ballistic missiles. Their speed and penetrating power could allow them to target drone operators during launches – as has already happened at Donetsk airport – and destroy underground depots.
Translated by Artem Yakymyshyn
Edited by Susan McDonald

articles.title: Russia’s state arms giant claims a new drone-missile class
articles.body:
- Russian state conglomerate Rostec said its S-71M, S-71K and Dan-T jet-powered strike drones perform the role of cruise missiles at lower cost.
- Rostec said the weapons are already used in Ukraine and should become standard weapons for Russian frontline aviation.
Russia’s state defense conglomerate Rostec says three of its newest jet-powered strike drones, the S-71M, S-71K and Dan-T, can now do the job of cruise missiles at a fraction of the cost, and that all three are already being used against Ukraine.
Rostec made the claims in comments to the Russian Defense Ministry newspaper Krasnaya Zvezda published on Sept. 30, describing the weapons as a new category that sits between attack drones and missiles. The company did not give prices, production numbers or performance figures for any of the three, and its claims about accuracy and combat results could not be independently verified.
“In fact, a classic cruise missile is already a fixed-wing unmanned aerial vehicle. However, not every UAV of this type is a cruise missile. Nevertheless, in the new S-71M, S-71K and Dan-T, this line is being erased,” Rostec said in its statement.
The company said the drones have the accuracy, maneuverability and range of cruise missiles while being significantly cheaper than conventional missiles, and that the gap between the two kinds of weapon will keep shrinking as drone production matures. Rostec said it expects the new jet-powered drones to become a standard weapon for Russian frontline aviation in the near future, alongside the glide-bomb kits that Russian jets have dropped on Ukrainian front lines in large numbers since 2023.
The S-71M and S-71K are designed to be launched from fifth-generation fighters, including the Su-57, Rostec told the state news agency TASS. Both are sized to fit inside the Su-57’s internal weapons bay, which lets the jet carry them without spoiling its radar-evading shape, and Russia’s arms exporter Rosoboronexport displayed them next to a Su-57E at the El Alamein International Airshow in Egypt in September.
Ukraine’s military intelligence has examined debris from both. It says the S-71K, known as Kovyor, carries a 250-kg (550-pound) OFAB-250-270 high-explosive bomb as its warhead and lacks terminal guidance, and that the S-71M, called Monokhrom, contains an NVIDIA Jetson Orin computing module, a small U.S.-made computer built to run artificial intelligence software on board, Militarnyi reported. Some published reports have swapped the two designations, so details tied to each name should be treated with caution.
Rostec told TASS that the smaller Dan-T has been confirmed in hundreds of launches against Ukrainian targets and can be fired from aircraft and helicopters, including foreign-made ones, which suggests the company is aiming it at export buyers. Accounts of where the Dan-T comes from differ: some analysts describe it as the export name for the S8000 Banderol, a small jet-powered cruise missile built by Russian drone maker Kronshtadt, while Ukrainian experts have described it as a strike version of the Dan-M jet target drone that Russia used for air defense training.
Ukrainian estimates put the Dan-T’s range at roughly 500 km (310 miles) with a 135-kg (298-pound) warhead, The New Voice of Ukraine reported, citing Ukrainian intelligence officials who said Moscow wants the weapon built entirely from Russian components.
That goal follows Ukrainian findings about the Banderol, which first appeared over Ukraine in spring 2025 and is launched mainly from Su-30/34 combat aircraft, Orion drones and Mi-28 attack helicopters, often from occupied Crimea toward the Odesa region. Ukraine’s military intelligence says the Banderol contains a Chinese-made jet engine, a Japanese battery and mostly U.S.-made electronics, Euronews reported.
Cheap jet-powered weapons that fly like missiles force Ukraine to spend scarce and expensive air defense interceptors on targets that cost Russia far less to build, the same logic behind Russia’s mass use of Shahed-type drones.
Rostec placed the new drones in a wider family of guided weapons that includes the Iskander ballistic missile system, Tornado-S rocket launchers with guided rockets, Krasnopol guided artillery shells and the Kalashnikov Group’s KUB loitering munitions.

articles.title: Japan wants to stand up to Russia. Can it stand on its own?
articles.body:
Japan wants to stand up to Russia. Can it stand on its own?
A 15-meter-high bronze memorial towers over the Amur River embankment: a Soviet soldier swings his rifle butt, smashing a Japanese border marker bearing the Imperial Chrysanthemum emblem – a symbol held sacred in Japan.
On September 4 – the day following Victory Day over Militaristic Japan and the End of WWII (as observed in Russia) – the Victory in the East memorial was unveiled at the highest point of the Amur River embankment in Khabarovsk. The monument was created at the initiative of Russian President Vladimir Putin, with the participation of the Russian Military Historical Society and the government of Khabarovsk Krai. The stone border post is an exact replica of a border stone erected by Japan on Sakhalin after the Russo-Japanese War.
The following day, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi demanded the removal of the monument. The depiction of the smashed chrysanthemum, she wrote on X, was absolutely unacceptable and was an affront to the national sentiments of the Japanese people. Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi called the monument “unacceptable” and deeply regrettable, and said that Tokyo would continue to press for its removal.
Moscow responded that it would not dismantle or alter the monument. Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova even stated that one might as well demand that the wind stop blowing or the sun stop shining.
Beijing seized the opportunity to remind its neighbor of past crimes: Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning advised Japan to learn from history, make a definitive break with militarism, and earn the trust of its neighbors through concrete actions.
At first glance, the situation appears unprecedented. In the span of a single month, the Russian president made a historic visit to Iturup; both sides summoned ambassadors; Japan, the US, and Australia held military exercises just 20 kilometers from the Russian border; and now, there’s the issue with the monument and the demand to tear it down. Media outlets speak of a “sharp chill” in relations, a new wave of confrontation in the Russian Far East, and even a potential “second front” of the Cold War.
However, Russian experts who spoke to RT view the situation differently.
A series of coincidences
The situation was triggered not by Russia’s actions, but by the Japanese Ministry of Defense.
On August 4, the Cabinet of Japan approved its annual Defense of Japan White Paper – a record-breaking 598 pages featuring an anime-style cover showing a group of smiling young people against the backdrop of a futuristic city. This year’s theme was “Security for the Future.” The content of the whitepaper was quite pragmatic, however. China was identified as Japan’s greatest strategic challenge; on this list, China was followed by Russia and North Korea; for the first time, the buildup of military power was directly linked to economic prosperity (hence the peaceful cover design).
There is a section on Russian military activity in the Far East: the document notes Tu-95 flights, 214 interceptions of Russian aircraft over the course of the year, the expansion of joint naval patrols with China (in August 2025, a submarine participated in these patrols for the first time), as well as a flight by Russian and Chinese bombers to the area near Shikoku Island in December. There is also a chapter on new methods of warfare, such as the use of mass-produced, low-cost drones and AI in decision-making. For the second consecutive year, the document characterizes Russian military actions in the Southern Kuril Islands as “illegal occupation.”
Nine days later, on August 13, Vladimir Putin visited Iturup. Throughout his years in office, the Russian president had never visited the southern islands of the Kuril chain, which are also claimed by Japan.
Japan’s reaction was immediate. Takaichi called the visit “absolutely unacceptable,” Motegi repeated Tokyo’s position about the islands being an “inherent part of Japanese territory,” and the Japanese Foreign Ministry summoned Russian Ambassador to Japan Nikolay Nozdrev. Moscow responded firmly, dismissing the statements of Japanese officials as politically irrelevant, offensive, and legally null and void; it reiterated that Iturup, like the rest of the Kurils, is an integral part of Russia, and that Japanese officials have no right to tell Moscow which regions of the country the Russian president may visit.
On August 15, the anniversary of Japan’s surrender in WWII, Takaichi sent a ‘tamagushi’ (ritual offering) to the Yasukuni Shrine. However, she refrained from going there personally, and the ruling party clarified that the donation was made from personal funds and in Takaichi’s capacity as LDP leader, rather than as head of government. The gesture was calculated to satisfy the domestic audience, without triggering a diplomatic row with Beijing and Seoul.
On August 18, Japanese Ambassador to Russia Akira Muto was summoned to the Russian Ministry of Foreign Affairs. Deputy Foreign Minister Mikhail Galuzin lodged a strong protest regarding statements made by the Japanese prime minister and foreign minister, asserting that Russia’s sovereignty and jurisdiction over the Southern Kuril Islands are inviolable, and that any attempts to call this reality into question are unacceptable and illegitimate.
On August 31, another incident occurred, this time involving military exercises. From September 8-24, Japan, the US, and Australia conducted Exercises Orient Shield with some operations taking place on Hokkaido Island, near the Russian border. The Japanese side was informed that provocative military activity near Russia’s Far Eastern borders is absolutely unacceptable; Zakharova specifically noted plans to deploy US land-based Typhon missile systems – capable of firing medium-and shorter-range missiles – during the exercises and warned of compensatory countermeasures.
On September 4, the monument was unveiled in Khabarovsk. That same day, the UN General Assembly voted to adopt the Equal Earth Projection. Japan voted in favor. But a few days later, it demanded a correction: on the online version of the new map, the four Southern Kuril Islands were shaded the same color as the rest of Russia, which Japan found unacceptable.
So there we have it – six incidents in 30 days. Each incident compounds the previous one, and together they form a picture of rapidly deteriorating relations.
Below, Russian experts analyze the situation.
‘Relations have not cooled suddenly’
Vasily Shchepkin – a Japanologist with a PhD in History, senior researcher of the Far East Department at the Institute of Oriental Manuscripts of the Russian Academy of Sciences, and an associate professor at the Higher School of Economics in St. Petersburg – suggests reframing the question.
“In my view, relations between Russia and Japan have not cooled suddenly; they have been in this state for over four years, since the start of Russia’s military operation in Ukraine. Japan joined Western sanctions, and everything that has happened over the past four years is largely a consequence of that,” he said.
Therefore, the rift happened not in September 2026, but in March 2022 – when Tokyo backed the collective West’s sanctions regime, and Moscow responded by withdrawing from peace treaty negotiations, cancelling visa-free travel for Japanese citizens to the Kuril Islands, and halting dialogue on joint economic activity there. Everything that followed was the consequence of that single decision.
So, what happened in August? According to Shchepkin, the current chain of events was a direct result of Putin’s visit to Iturup. Tokyo’s reaction was inevitable. However, he draws attention to a neglected detail. “Aside from statements, no concrete measures have followed so far.”
No actions were undertaken by Japan in September. No new sanctions packages were adopted; diplomats were not expelled, and the remaining projects were not cancelled. As for démarches, the summoning of diplomats, and declarations of unacceptable behavior, all this is standard diplomatic procedure.
“Neither Tokyo nor Moscow seeks to aggravate relations further,” Shchepkin says. “In my view, [relations] are unlikely to deteriorate further, because, speaking of bilateral interaction, neither side wants to halt it or escalate tensions.”
Therefore, we may conclude that Russia-Japan relations, in their current form, are a dependent variable.
“The current state of relations is rather a consequence of other events, which are not directly tied to the Russian-Japanese agenda,” the expert says.
An independent bilateral agenda no longer exists; therefore, we may only speak of the global situation and how it relates to Russia’s Far East.
“We are currently in a sort of deadlock which we return to whenever the global situation gets worse – and particularly when relations between Russia and the US deteriorate,” the expert says. “The US has long been the ‘third force’ on which Russia-Japan relations largely depended.”
Who started it?
While it’s true that relations are frozen, there is no consensus among the parties on who is to blame for this. Russian experts, however, have a clear opinion.
Olga Bonch-Osmolovskaya, a Japanologist with a PhD in History, describes the reasons behind Tokyo’s decision. According to her, after 2022, Japan’s policy ceased to be truly independent. But that is only part of the story.
“It is one thing to politically condemn a distant war and state one’s position for the sake of appearances, given the existence of a sort of ‘suzerain’; it is quite another to actively integrate oneself into the corresponding policy,” she says. Japan chose the latter option. And it did so with particular zeal.
“Driven by what one might call the ‘straight-A student complex’ of the Japanese and their tendency to be highly conscientious, sometimes even fanatical in executing tasks, Japan closely aligned itself with this course, joining the full package of sanctions against Moscow and withdrawing from various forms of cooperation,” Bonch-Osmolovskaya says.
The former policy – one that allowed Tokyo to balance between allied obligations and its own interests in the north – was curtailed. Along with it, all the achievements of the previous decade came to naught.
“Russia did not initiate the deterioration of relations with Japan,” Bonch-Osmolovskaya says. “It responded and continues to respond to Japanese sanctions and to the increased US military presence.”
There is a fine line between words and capabilities, however. Take Exercises Orient Shield, for example. “During the exercises, all sorts of maneuvers are practiced – the landing of troops, the transfer of ammunition, the deployment of HIMARS systems, air defense systems, etc.”
This explains Russia’s strong reaction. “Of course, no one is saying that this is literally preparation for an attack on the Kuril Islands. But Russia is obliged to evaluate not only statements, but military capabilities,” Bonch-Osmolovskaya says.
Intentions change along with governments, but military infrastructure remains. And military officials all over the world take this into account.
The result is a vicious circle: Japan builds up its military potential jointly with the US; in response, Russia strengthens its position in the Far East; then, Tokyo presents this strengthening as an additional justification for further militarization. And the circle repeats itself.
This is confirmed by Japan’s military spending. Japan crossed the 2% defense spending threshold ahead of schedule, a year earlier than the mark outlined in the 2022 strategy. For the current fiscal year, defense spending amounted to a record 8.8 trillion yen, and the request for the next year is already a record 8.9 trillion yen (about $56 billion). In June, the parliament renamed the Air Self-Defense Force into the Air and Space Self-Defense Force; this was the first renaming of one of the three branches of the Self-Defense Forces since their creation in 1954. In August, Takaichi announced further changes: the creation of a Space Operations Group, a Space Domain Awareness (SDA) satellite, and the expansion of the Okinawa Ground Self-Defense Force’s 15th Brigade into a division.
These actions are mainly directed against Beijing. But considering the geography, they are also directed against Moscow.
Energy instead of diplomacy
Despite all this, there is something that balances the dramatic picture. While diplomats are exchanging demarches, gas carriers are departing from Sakhalin and transporting LNG to Japan.
The Sakhalin-2 project survived sanctions, frozen political dialogue, and demands to dismantle the monument. In June, the US Office of Foreign Assets Control once again extended the special license until December 18, 2026. Such an exception has been issued annually since 2022, and each time it was preceded by negotiations between Tokyo and Washington. Russian LNG, according to the Japanese Ministry of Economy, provided about 9% of Japanese liquefied gas imports in 2025; According to Bonch-Osmolovskaya, the inverse relationship is even stronger – Japan accounted for about 58% of the project’s exports.
Vladimir Nelidov – PhD in History, associate professor of the Department of Oriental Studies at MGIMO, Senior Researcher at the Center for Japanese Studies at the Institute of Oriental Studies of the Russian Academy of Sciences, and RIAC expert – considers this to be the main reason why the threats didn’t go beyond words.
“Severing diplomatic relations would be disproportionate,” he says. “The possibilities for introducing additional economic sanctions are also limited: Japan does not have much leverage. For example, it remains involved in Sakhalin oil and gas projects and, I believe, is not ready to sacrifice them.”
Notably, the US administration insisted on Japan’s withdrawal from the Sakhalin projects. However, Tokyo remained. “As far as we can judge, Takaichi either convinced the US or insisted [on doing things her way] and so, despite the position of its senior ally, Japan remained in the projects.”
The second possible lever is humanitarian. Tokyo tries to preserve it, too. “The Japanese side has invested a lot of effort in humanitarian cooperation with Russia. Before the current escalation, the Japanese even proudly said that, despite the lack of political dialogue, cultural festivals and other events continue between the countries.” And Nelidov adds, “in the long term, Japan has perhaps more need for such contacts than Russia.”
Shchepkin supports this idea, adding that even in the past four years, and thanks to the efforts of the pro-Russia lobby within the Japanese Foreign Ministry, cooperation has been preserved in areas like culture, education, and tourism. The current flow of Russian tourists to Japan, the expert adds, is largely a legacy of the Shinzo Abe administration, when the parties agreed to put the territorial issue aside and focus on the economy, culture, and visas.
The general picture is quite clear. Bonch-Osmolovskaya calls it “cold peace” and warns that a complete rupture of relations would not benefit either country: while Japan could technically replace Sakhalin gas, doing so would require time, money, and even greater dependence on US suppliers, whereas Russia would lose revenue from the project. “A definitive break, should it occur, would come at too high a price for both sides,” she says.
Therefore, the limit to how far relations can deteriorate is not determined by diplomacy. It is dictated by the energy balance, and this applies to both parties.
Why Takaichi could not remain silent
A pressing question remains: why did the Japanese Prime Minister issue all these loud statements if no concrete measures were to follow?
Nelidov suggests viewing the situation through the eyes of the Japanese leadership to better understand their logic. Sanae Takaichi rose to power as a nationalist politician and, among other things, a defender of national honor. Her policy is grounded in this.
“Had she failed to react to the Russian president’s visit to the territory claimed by Japan, to the installation of the monument – which [Russia] views as fine, necessary, and valuable, but which the Japanese see as a desecration of a state symbol – or to the military exercises, she would have been torn apart, figuratively speaking, by her own party,” the expert says.
For example, when the US administration imposed sanctions against the International Criminal Court – including its presiding judge, Japanese national Tomoko Akane – Takaichi faced criticism for not standing up for her compatriot firmly enough. “If public opinion and fellow party members demand decisive action from her even in dealings with the US, then what would they say about Russia?”
A scenario in which Tokyo would have remained silent to avoid damaging relations with Moscow is virtually impossible.
Valery Kistanov, head of the Center for Japanese Studies at the Institute of China and Contemporary Asia of the Russian Academy of Sciences, drew attention to the details of the protest against the monument in Khabarovsk. Takaichi posted her comment on social media but did not issue an official statement, and major Japanese media outlets (except for right-wing conservative publications) barely covered the story. It didn’t cause a nationwide outcry.
In other words, the statement was addressed not to Moscow, but to fellow party members and the segment of the Japanese electorate for whom the events of 1945 remain an enduring historical wound. The offering made at Yasukuni on August 15 followed the same logic: made from personal funds and without Takaichi herself present, it was intended as a signal to the domestic audience, but was carefully calibrated to avoid provoking a new crisis in relations with Beijing.
The fact that the series of incidents was not followed by any practical actions holds the key to understanding the events of September. This means that a large part of what happened did not concern bilateral relations but was intended for domestic audiences.
However, this does not render the situation entirely harmless. Symbolic commitments tend to become entrenched: a prime minister who has demanded the dismantling of a monument cannot refute their own statement, and a successor would have to start from the same position.
Who benefits?
Experts agree on who benefits from the conflict, though they differ on the implications. “It is clear that the US is the primary beneficiary,” says Bonch-Osmolovskaya. “The worse relations between Moscow and Tokyo become, the stronger Japan’s existing dependence on the US grows in all aspects: weaponry, intelligence, supplies, and security guarantees.” Washington gains a disciplined ally, additional bases for the deployment of forces, and another tool for exerting pressure on the Russian Far East.
However, she adds, “It is important not to reduce the situation to a scenario where the US is some sort of ‘dark empire’ and Japan is merely its puppet.”
In Japan, there are certain beneficiaries of this confrontation as well. Among the proponents of revising post-war restrictions is the defense establishment, which Bonch-Osmolovskaya characterizes as revanchist and nationalistic, and arms manufacturers, for whom expanded exports open up markets that had been closed for nearly 80 years. The image of an external threat serves as a mechanism for legitimization: the longer the list of threats, the easier it is for the parliament to increase military spending and lift export restrictions.
Bonch-Osmolovskaya gives a rather harsh assessment and makes a historical analogy. She believes that the current propaganda is reminiscent of the decades preceding WWII, when Japan designated China as its primary adversary and demonized it; today, a similar process is unfolding regarding Russia. At the root of this, she sees the unresolved trauma of 1945: while the cult of the emperor was formally dismantled and the atrocities of the military machine were acknowledged, the defeat was never truly accepted, and strategic sovereignty was lost.
Nelidov takes a more measured approach, offering a different view that does not suggest malicious intent. The problem, he believes, is the so-called ‘security dilemma’ – a long-standing concept in international relations theory. A state strengthens its defenses; its neighbors, unaware of its true intentions, interpret this as preparation for aggression and arm themselves in response; the first state observes these preparations and continues its military buildup. “The paradox of the security dilemma is that in seeking to protect itself, the state ultimately finds itself in an even more dangerous situation,” he explains.
Another factor also comes into play. “Most Japanese diplomats, politicians, and even military officials have no desire to develop an independent view of the global situation,” Nelidov says, describing Japanese political circles as highly compliant pupils of the West; the few who acknowledge that the situation in Ukraine might be more complex than the prevailing narrative risk becoming outcasts. These sentiments did not emerge in 2022; they were shaped throughout the post-war period by the media and the education system, initially as anti-Soviet views. In Japanese opinion polls, Russia consistently ranks low in terms of public favorability, alongside China and North Korea.
Freezing point
If the current situation resembles ‘freezing point’, it is logical to ask what might drive the relations between Japan and Russia below freezing.
Bonch-Osmolovskaya mentions a specific threshold. “The next stage of deterioration could be the deployment of US long-range systems in Japan,” she says. Russia’s reaction would be predictable: a further military buildup on the Kuril Islands and in Sakhalin. A further contraction of economic ties is also likely; she believes that the fishing industry would suffer first, followed by what remains of trade.
Bonch-Osmolovskaya does not predict a direct military conflict. According to her, if it were to occur at all, it would happen only as part of a larger clash between Russia and the US or a major crisis surrounding Taiwan that dragged in all the neighboring states. In other words, a Russo-Japanese war is impossible as a standalone event – it could only be an episode within someone else’s war.
Nelidov views the situation somewhat differently. He points out that Japan’s defense policy identifies China and North Korea as the primary threats, with Russia ranking third on the list. But even when it comes to China and North Korea, it’s not about direct confrontation but rather an arms race. While this is certainly a negative phenomenon, it is fundamentally different from a direct conflict.
The comparison the expert draws with Europe is interesting. He considers the rhetoric of Berlin, London, Helsinki, and Stockholm far more threatening than that of Tokyo, which demonstrates “virtually no real readiness for aggressive action against Russia.” He is convinced there are certain limits the Japanese side will not cross.
He attributes East Asia’s greater reluctance to engage in direct conflict to accumulated experience: territorial disputes and mutual historical grievances are common in the region, and the elites have learned to manage such crises. For example, following Takaichi’s November statement regarding potential intervention in Taiwan, Tokyo’s relations with Beijing plummeted to their lowest point in a decade, and China imposed economic restrictions; yet within a few months, the situation had stabilized.
“In East Asia, I don’t see the kind of crazy Russophobia and readiness to direct all resources into the conflict that we’re witnessing in Europe,” says Nelidov. “Japan doesn’t intend to go to war with Russia; and neither does Russia want war with Japan. Both sides realize it is not in their interests. There are no strategically vital or fundamental contradictions between them.”
Is there a way to achieve a thaw in relations? All three experts agree that there is no simple solution. Normalizing bilateral ties is impossible until relations between Russia and the West are normalized; the Japanese leadership lacks both the will and the capacity to adopt an independent stance. However, Shchepkin believes that once the conflict in Ukraine ends, Tokyo will be among the first to act: as soon as the sanctions regime is lifted or minimized, Japan will be ready to soften its position and resume dialogue.
However, the opinions of experts diverge when it comes to assessing the current pause in relations. For Nelidov, it is merely another fluctuation in a long history of regional squabbles. For Bonch-Osmolovskaya, it represents a deeper rift: Russia is asserting itself as an independent civilization, while Japan, in response, is becoming increasingly integrated into the US system of control over Eurasia. She advocates neither for reconciliation at any cost nor for territorial concessions, but rather for maintaining energy, economic, and cultural ties as a bridge – “not so much with the Japan of today, but with the Japan that might one day become more independent.”
As Bonch-Osmolovskaya concludes, “Japan cannot simultaneously be an independent civilization and America’s forward military outpost. It will have to make a choice.”

articles.title: Latvian Defense Minister Says Russia's Hybrid Attacks, Not Nuclear Rhetoric, Are The Main Concern
articles.body:
WASHINGTON -- Latvia’s defense minister has played down any immediate danger after Russia’s latest nuclear warning to NATO over Kaliningrad.
“I don’t see an imminent threat at this point,” Raivis Melnis told RFE/RL in an interview in Washington on September 30, echoing NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte, who said he did not take the Russian warning "that seriously."
Russia warned NATO this week that it was prepared to use its entire arsenal, including nuclear weapons, if the Western alliance attempted to cut off Kaliningrad, its heavily militarized Baltic exclave wedged between NATO members Poland and Lithuania.
In a diplomatic memo circulated to NATO member states, Moscow said it had information that the alliance was preparing an “air and naval blockade” of the territory.
The warning prompted Rutte to call on Russia to “stop the nuclear threats,” saying NATO is a defensive alliance and that “this is absolutely not called for and not helpful.” He added that Russian President Vladimir Putin knows that he cannot win in a direct confrontation with NATO.
Melnis said Russia had repeatedly resorted to nuclear threats since launching its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, arguing that Moscow uses such rhetoric to frighten Western populations, weaken support for Kyiv, and test the cohesion of the NATO alliance.
“Russia will use any means to threaten us, to bring fear to our people, to support Ukraine, and also to break our unity, cohesion, to support and just test where are those limits,” he said.
Escalation Risks?
The Russian warning has nevertheless raised concern among arms-control and security specialists, particularly because of Kaliningrad’s strategic position and Russia’s evolving nuclear doctrine.
Daryl Kimball, executive director of the Arms Control Association, a nonpartisan Washington based nonprofit, told RFE/RL that the Russian threat should be taken seriously and condemned as unacceptable. He said Moscow’s language reflected what he described as a careless approach to the dangers of nuclear weapons use.
Kimball noted that NATO does not appear to be preparing military action to isolate Kaliningrad. Even if such a confrontation were contemplated, he said, using nuclear weapons in a conflict involving another nuclear-armed state or alliance could trigger retaliation, escalation, and potentially catastrophic consequences.
He argued that Moscow should instead address its concerns with NATO through diplomatic channels, saying that “rather than threatening nuclear attack, the Kremlin should reach out to NATO capitals to clarify whatever concerns Russia might have and to address those concerns diplomatically and responsibly.”
Lynn Rusten, a senior fellow at the Center for European Policy Analysis and a former senior White House National Security Council official responsible for arms control and nonproliferation, told RFE/RL that Russia’s latest nuclear rhetoric appeared “unhinged and hyperbolic” from a Western perspective.
But Rusten also warned of a dangerous combination of factors: Russian threats and provocative hybrid warfare, NATO and Russian forces operating in close proximity, continued Western support for Ukraine, and a lack of meaningful dialogue.
She said those conditions could increase the risk of dangerous miscalculation, particularly as Russia and NATO assert competing red lines while channels for managing tensions remain limited.
“The lack of meaningful dialogue and the growing divide in security perceptions carries a grave risk of further and potentially unintended escalation and expansion of this conflict,” Rusten said.
Sylvia Mishra, nuclear policy director at the Institute for Security and Technology, said nuclear brinkmanship was not new for Moscow but should nonetheless be treated seriously.
Kaliningrad, she noted, is home to the headquarters of Russia’s Baltic Fleet and is strategically important but geographically vulnerable, surrounded by NATO members Poland and Lithuania and separated from mainland Russia.
Mishra said reported NATO air operations around the exclave in mid-August, which included aircraft with capabilities to disrupt communications, radar, and navigation systems, could have heightened Moscow’s sense of vulnerability.
She also pointed to Russia’s 2024 revised nuclear doctrine, which formally lowered the threshold described by Moscow for potential nuclear use.
Mishra said the latest warning appeared to be the first instance of Russia issuing a written diplomatic note explicitly warning that it was prepared to use nuclear weapons if the Western alliance attempted to isolate Kaliningrad.
Hybrid Attacks
For Melnis, however, the more immediate threat is neither nuclear nor a large-scale Russian conventional military assault on NATO, but an expanding campaign of hybrid activity -- hostile actions short of open warfare, including cyberattacks, sabotage, and the weaponization of migration.
He said Latvia and its allies are continuously reassessing the threat, monitoring Russia’s military capabilities, losses in Ukraine, force generation, and activities such as suspected attacks on military-industrial facilities and critical infrastructure.
“We are monitoring and we are working closely with Ukrainian partners or with our NATO partners,” Melnis said, adding that Latvia’s threat assessment is a continuous process and that hybrid activity is increasing.
Melnis said he did not believe Russia currently had the capacity to launch a conventional offensive against a NATO country while sustaining its war in Ukraine.
“Russia stopped in Ukraine, they are not achieving the goals,” he said, pointing to Ukrainian counteroffensive operations and arguing that Moscow would face major difficulties trying to conduct two large-scale military operations simultaneously.
He described cyberattacks, pressure through migration from Belarus -- which Minsk has been accused of facilitating to destabilize its neighbors -- and other hostile activities as part of the new security environment confronting Latvia and its allies.
Latvia is also strengthening defenses against drones. Melnis said the country had deployed interceptor systems and additional radar along its borders with Russia and Belarus, drawing heavily on lessons from Ukraine. NATO fighter aircraft provide another layer, while Latvia is procuring medium- and short-range air defense systems.
Melnis said Russian drone incursions could become a growing feature of the Baltic security environment, citing recent incidents involving Lithuania, Poland, and Romania. Latvia, he said, is preparing for more such incidents.
US Role In European Defense
Melnis was in Washington to deepen defense cooperation with the US, including discussions involving the Michigan National Guard, procurement programs, and capability development.
He said he remains confident that the US will maintain a military presence in Europe despite adjustments to deployments in individual countries. US forces, he said, remain in Latvia, and Washington continues to recognize the strategic importance of the region.
At the same time, Melnis said European allies must assume a greater share of the burden for their own defense. He credited US President Donald Trump with pushing NATO members to increase defense spending, saying Latvia is committed by law to spending at least 5 percent of gross domestic product annually on security beginning next year.
NATO members agreed at their 2025 summit in The Hague to spend 5 percent of GDP annually on defense and defense-related priorities by 2035, up from the alliance’s previous 2-percent benchmark. Latvia has moved faster, with its parliament requiring national defense spending of at least 5 percent of projected GDP from 2027.
But Melnis said greater European responsibility would go hand in hand with continued US support.
“The United States will provide. They will be there. They will fight with us if needed,” Melnis said, while stressing that Europe must do more.

articles.title: CENTEF report reveals Hezbollah acquired $157m of weapons in 2024, majority provided freely by Iran
articles.body:
Hezbollah acquired an estimated $157 million worth of weaponry in 2024 despite its war with Israel, with the vast majority donated by the Islamic Republic at no cost to the Iran-backed group, according to Israeli Center for Research of Terror Financing’s new research published on Thursday.
The report, titled Hezbollah Financial Statements, is the first installment in a series set to expose Hezbollah's media spending, payments to wounded fighters, and spending on its military infrastructure.
Based on open-source information and valuations of known Hezbollah military assets, CENTEF estimates that Iran provided roughly $129 million worth of weapons and military equipment as an in-kind grant, while Hezbollah itself spent approximately $28 million in cash on its acquisitions.
Seeking to understand Hezbollah’s expenses as a business entity, to better assess the terror group’s financial health and identify ways to weaken it while avoiding the costly airstrikes that can have significant consequences for Lebanese civilians, the researchers examined the group’s weapons procurement and manufacturing costs, as well as its ability to sustain its arsenal if the Islamic Republic’s capacity to supply it were reduced.
Explaining the rationale behind the analysis, CENTEF CEO Sharon Gal told The Jerusalem Post that breaking down Hezbollah’s finances as a business could help legislators and operators efficiently identify and prioritize key supply chains to disrupt, creating pressure points on Iranian-backed terror groups.
Researchers aim for interactive tool on Hezbollah finances
Expanding those efforts, researcher Marc Cohen told the Post that they plan to release an interactive tool to help civilians understand Hezbollah’s financial statements, with the hope that it can raise awareness of Hezbollah's negative impact on the Lebanese economy and the scale of its operations.
The researchers looked at the different types of military equipment Hezbollah is estimated to have acquired in 2024, including rockets, missiles, drones, ATGMs, air-defense systems, ammunition, launchers, naval equipment, and IED-related assets.
Hezbollah’s own investment in its weapons is limited to small arms, ammunition, drone components, dual-use equipment, and equipment obtained through its international procurement networks.
Because Hezbollah’s weapons acquisitions are clandestine, the researchers had to estimate how many weapons the group acquired in 2024 rather than rely on procurement records. They used three methods: Analyzing Hezbollah’s historical rate of replenishing its arsenal, assessing Iran’s capacity to manufacture and deliver weapons, and comparing global benchmarks for the costs of equipping, training, and mobilizing military forces.
The first method was based on Hezbollah’s growth over the past two decades. According to estimates from the Center for Strategic and International Studies, Hezbollah had approximately 15,000 rockets in 2006 and had expanded its arsenal to roughly 150,000 by 2024, amounting to an average increase of about 7,500 rockets per year over 18 years of Iranian resupply.
Acknowledging that Hezbollah's replenishment likely varied year-to-year, it estimated that the disruption to Hezbollah's supply chain and manufacturing abilities during the 2024 fighting resulted in them acquiring approximately 4,500 to 6,500 rockets and missiles during the year.
The second method considered Iran’s ability to actually supply Hezbollah. The researchers noted that Iran can only manufacture and physically deliver a limited number of sophisticated weapons, and those weapons must be distributed among Iran’s own forces and multiple proxies.
Iran is estimated to produce approximately 50 to 240 ballistic missiles per month and 1,800 to 3,000 attack drones per year total. This places a ceiling on how many guided missiles and drones Hezbollah could realistically have acquired in 2024. With that in mind, researchers analyzed the value of weapons in Hezbollah’s arsenal to understand exactly what Iranian support was worth and confirm that Hezbollah would be unable to afford such advanced weaponry without Tehran’s patronage.
Hezbollah arsenal includes heavy Iranian Falaq rockets, Katyushas
A staple of Hezbollah’s arsenal is the Katyusha rocket, alongside Iran’s heavier Falaq-1 and Falaq-2 rockets, which have 240mm and 333mm warheads respectively, and the crude, large-warhead Burkan rocket. The 122mm Katyusha is one of the few systems for which there is a publicly available price, at approximately $300 per round, while the Burkan is estimated to cost around $400 per rocket. Based on OSINT, the researchers estimate that Hezbollah acquired approximately 4,000 of the short-range rockets, 400 Falaq rockets, and 120 Burkan rockets in 2024.
Hezbollah’s inventory also includes Iran’s Fajr series and Syrian-origin heavy rockets. The Fajr-3 is a 240mm artillery rocket armed with a 45-kilogram warhead, while the Fajr-5 is a 333mm rocket with a GPS-guided Fajr-5C variant. CENTEF estimates that Hezbollah acquired approximately 600 rockets across this class in 2024, at an estimated cost of $2,000 to $10,000 per unit.
The inventory also includes the unguided Zelzal-2, which costs an estimated $25,000 per rocket, and the GPS-guided Fateh-110/M-600, a high-priority transfer estimated by JINSA to cost $110,000. The transfer can also be fitted with a $5,000 to $10,000 GPS guidance kit to turn them into a guided weapon. With Iran’s missile production shared among several recipients and the supply corridor repeatedly disrupted during 2024, Hezbollah’s acquisition of these systems was thought to have been tightly constrained and it is understood the group acquired only 60 Zelzal rockets, 40 Fateh-110/M-600 missiles, and 150 guidance kits.
The inventory also includes Iran’s Paveh land-attack cruise missile, which has a range of approximately 700 to 2,000 kilometers. Given its high unit value, CENTEF estimates that only about 12 were acquired in 2024.
Anti-tank guided missiles (ATGMs) accounted for about 20% of Hezbollah’s attacks on Israel during its attacks after October 8, 2023, and were likely its largest-value weapons category, according to the researchers The Russian-made Kornet, supplied via Syria, costs approximately $26,000 per round, while Iran’s reverse-engineered Dehlavieh costs an estimated $12,000 to $15,000. Hezbollah also uses the Iranian Almas, older Konkurs and Metis systems, and the RPG-29. CENTEF estimates that Hezbollah received approximately 700 Kornet and 500 Dehlavieh rounds, 500 Almas missiles, and 400 Konkurs/Metis missiles, along with 30 launchers in 2024.
The RPG-7 standard squad-level anti-armor weapon, with reusable launchers costs about $350 and rounds $100 to $500, and CENTEF estimated that Hezbollah acquired approximately 800 RPG launchers and 15,000 rounds in 2024, with some rounds procured on the black market.
Hezbollah also acquired drones and unmanned aerial vehicles, including the Iranian Mirsad-1 and Ababil-T and small Shahed-101-class loitering munitions. Loitering munitions cost an estimated $20,000 to $40,000, while commercial and FPV quadcopters range from $1,000 to $15,000. CENTEF estimates that Hezbollah acquired approximately 300 Mirsad and Ababil drones combined, 200 loitering munitions, 400 commercial and FPV drones, and several reconnaissance UAVs in 2024.
Hezbollah’s air-defense inventory includes MANPADS cost roughly $5,000 to $100,000 each depending on the model, and it is thought to have also received 358 of Iran’s loitering surface-to-air missile.
Small arms, IEDs relatively cheap for Hezbollah
Small arms are comparatively inexpensive. Hezbollah uses AKM and AK-103 assault rifles, along with PKM and DShK machine guns and SVD sniper rifles. CENTEF estimates that it acquired about 5,000 rifles, 900 crew-served weapons, 80 mortar tubes, 15,000 mortar rounds, and 8 million rounds of ammunition in 2024.
Given that IEDs are relatively cheap to manufacture, and can be produced in Lebanon, the researchers estimated the group invested in 2,000.
CENTEF is also gathering data on how Hezbollah spends money on its civilian arm, including through charities that provide assistance to residents of Lebanon’s south displaced through the group’s wars. Though still analyzing the cost of Hezbollah’s media landscape, it has already come to the estimation that Hezbollah spent $26 million to $28 million on media in 2024, with Al-Manar alone accounting for $16.5 million to $17.2 million.
The researchers said understanding these expenses, alongside Hezbollah’s military spending and Iran’s support, could provide a fuller picture of the group’s financial dependencies and generate more choke points to pressure it.

articles.title: Read the Full Transcript of Donald Trump’s 2026 Interview With TIME
articles.body:
President Donald Trump sat down for an interview with TIME at the White House on Sept. 28.
Over the course of the interview, Trump discussed a wide range of issues, including the war with Iran, the artificial intelligence boom, the Federal Reserve, the Supreme Court, and his outlook for the midterms.
Below is a lightly edited transcript of the interview conducted by TIME Senior Political Correspondent Eric Cortellessa and Editor-in-Chief Sam Jacobs. Click here to read our fact check.
Read TIME's interview with President Donald Trump and the fact-check of that conversation.
TIME: I'm curious about your dinner last night with Dario.
Trump: Oh.
Yes, exactly. Do you still disagree with his views on what he calls AI safety?
I spoke to him about his views, and they're much different, I think, than what is portrayed in the media. First of all, I liked him and his wife a lot. They had dinner, and we were going to meet at 7:00. But I was at the big Presidents Cup. I was the chairman of it in Chicago at Marion, which is great. Actually, that was yeah, Medinah, at Medinah, last year, Marion, this time of year, it was really great, and so I called, I said, "Could we make it a little bit later?" He actually saw the helicopter land, so we made it a little bit later. We got in at about 10. We stayed for more than two hours, talked about a lot of things. Very smart guy. Maybe different than I thought, a little bit. Really a little bit different. But no, he understands.
Look, I say, if you're going to seek regulation, they can put you out of business. Now you do have to be responsible for yourself, and there aren't a lot of people that understand what's going on. This is a new one that is much different than people have ever seen before. But my attitude is, we're winning against the world by a lot, and I want to keep winning. There are those that say it's bigger than the industrial revolution, and you would think not. But actually, if you look at the numbers—you ever see these numbers? They're like, they're like straight up in the air. And from our standpoint, we have trillions of dollars being invested in our country because it's probably the biggest business there is. We're the most advanced, we have the, we have the smartest people. And tomorrow I have a big meeting. We have everybody. All the—Dario's coming back.
I'm curious what exactly is going on with all these meetings with these AI leaders.
Well, look, you know, this isn't like I'm building a building, which I can do out of my back pocket. It's easier to do that for me, and it's what I've been doing. This is a whole new world, probably mostly good, but some bad too. And it's a very powerful world. It's a very—potentially really could be good for medical. I mean, some of the things they're coming up with now that they never even thought about. But with good comes bad, and we want them, we want all of them to behave for themselves. Tomorrow's meeting. What time is that meeting tomorrow? Two?
Natalie Harp: Noon, in the East Room.
Trump: So we have everybody. Give me a list of the people at the meeting.
Can I ask, Mr. President?
We had a good evening the other night, three nights ago, or two nights ago.
Given the news this week, I have to ask: Why should Americans believe that you respect the free press when you're restricting access of some of our colleagues to the White House?
No, but say it a little louder.
Why should Americans believe that you respect the free press when you're restricting access to the White House to some of our colleagues?
Because I do respect the free press, but I don't respect fake news. I'll give you an example. CNN and MSDNC, which is MS Now—they changed the name because it does so poorly. But I won the election. I won it handily by massive numbers. I won the popular vote. I won all seven swing states. They said if you won three swing states, I won all seven. I won the counties. It's very important, 86% popular vote. Everything, and very conclusively, I haven't had a good story on CNN for years. They're incapable of being—they're fake news. Same thing on MS NOW.
If I do the finest thing, if I found the cure to cancer, they would say, "Why didn't he move quicker?" They are just horrible people, and they're so bad. So I believe in a free press. I believe in an honest press, but I don't believe in fake news. And I know it's fake because I know the thing—I don't mind, you know, if I do something wrong, I don't mind having a bad story. He's written a couple of times about something. I said, well listen, he’s not wrong. But with the press, if somebody's going to call me, if every single story is—look, I've done a lot of good stuff. I'm in the Oval Office. I mean, the public is very smart. If I wasn't doing a good job, I wouldn't have won that election by a lot.
Are you going to ignore the courts when they say this this denial is—
Well, the court actually said that, if you look at the judge's decision, he's been a very anti-Trump judge, which is very interesting. But if you look at his decision, he really said process. He talked about—come back to us with process.
He's a Trump-appointed judge. He was appointed by you.
Yeah, he was. He was. It's one of those things.
You don't think you're ignoring what he ordered you to do? You don't think you're ignoring his order?
No, I'm not. I'm not ignoring his order. I'm just saying that when I don't have to go out of my way, these people write only bad stories. When they say orders, what order? I'm not even aware.
Steven Cheung: The judge basically ordered them to renew their access back to the White House, but that's different than allowing the pool into the events in the Oval Office or on Air Force One.
Trump: He actually said to the premises of the White House?
Can I just ask, why now? You've had this contentious relationship with the media for a while. What was the impetus to doing this at this moment in time?
Well, it's just bad story after bad story, and when I say bad story, I can handle bad stories. I've got a lot of bad stories. Most of them are fake, and it's not only CNN, and it's not only MSDNC. It's a lot of other people.
Let's talk a little bit about the war in Iran.
Just to finish.
Yeah, absolutely.
Because I don't think anybody should be forced to bear fake news, constantly bad stories, because I've done great things. I mean, I've done Venezuela. I've done—I can name, I can name 100 great things I've done. I never get good press. I never get fair press. Doesn’t have to be good. All it has to be is fair. So at a certain point, you say, "What's the purpose of like this crazy Kaitlan Collins?" She's a very average person. She's the most unhappy young person I've ever seen. If I did something spectacular by any standard, and they would write about it, they will only write badly. Sometimes I'm amazed at how they can—you know, yesterday I got tremendous applause from massive crowds that came to Duncan.
