OpenAI agents.
They're not allowed to do that, and if they do that, they, you know, could have penalties that are not going to be acceptable to them.
Can you tell us who you're meeting with—go ahead.
I don't have to destroy the industry. We're making a lot of money with that industry. That industry is the industrial revolution, but bigger. It's the internet, but much bigger. I don't have to destroy that industry. By the way, you know, I had a very good meeting with President Xi. We get along, right? We talked about it not much, but a little bit. But I told him, I said, we don't want—you know, we're leading them pretty good. He knows that. And I said, "We don't want to take this thing that we've done so well with and turn it off. I don't want to turn it off. It's tremendous amounts of money."
Now, when you talk about the debt, the growth is going to pay off the debt. Growth will pay it off. Now, it's pretty bad when they keep raising interest rates, and they only raise them because they have Trump derangement syndrome. And I don't blame Kevin. In fact, when he took the job, he's got mostly people from Barack Hussein Obama and Sleepy Joe Biden on the board. And I don't know what he's—I actually said, "What are you going to do?" But they would rather see the country do badly because I’m President. But we're blowing through interest rates because it's got—we got this thing going. If the interest rates were—even, if they were low, we should be paying the lowest interest rate of any country in the world, because all these countries that are making money, almost all, are only making money because of this.
Switzerland. They sell billions of dollars of watches. We didn't take their watch, and they're considered [unintelligible]. They have the lowest interest rate, one half of 1%, and we're paying much more than that. And yet, if I said to Switzerland, "Sorry, I don't want to lose $40 billion a year in order to have your watches." We just picked up $40 billion. I could do the same thing with 50 countries, more than that, much more than that, and we would make more money than any country has ever dreamed of. We should be the lowest interest rate with the most prime country—we should be the lowest interest rate in the world. In the old days, that would happen. When you did well, the interest rate used to—you could check. You did well, you announced good numbers. Now you announce good numbers, we're going to rock and roll and raise interest rates to try and kill it.
Well, they're concerned that the economy is too hot—
No, they’re concerned for inflation.
Well, yeah, exactly.
Okay, and frankly, this is hurting our country more than inflation is hurting our country. More than inflation.
Can you tell us about your meeting with—?
You know, inflation. Certain levels of inflation will also pay off that debt very rapidly. Very rapidly.
Cheung: Can I just jump in? We're coming up for about an hour.
Trump: Yeah, we said so. I’ve been doing this from about 5 o'clock in the morning. I got back last night at 10. I left at 6 o'clock in the morning. I got back, and I had, lo and behold, a dinner with Dario for two and a half hours.
Let's talk about the midterms. Do you expect Democrats to take control of Congress?
No, I think we'll do okay if I campaign, and I intend to. If I campaign…you don't give me enough credit. When I campaign, I give people a lot. We did a convention that had 107 million views, and it stupidly was put opposite the NFL opening, and we got more views. They got 25 million. We got 107. Very stupid thing to do, but we did it. Somebody tell you, some person did it.
No, I think that we're going to do well. If I campaign for people, those people are going to win. Lindsey Graham's sister is fantastic. I helped her, I endorsed. And she beat a very seasoned professional named Ralph Norman.
Thomas Massie is a sleazebag, comes from Kentucky. He was semi-popular, but not somebody that could be beaten. And I campaigned against him, and I beat him in the election.
Are you preparing at all for what might happen if you don't hold on to the House?
They'll probably go after me and I'll go after them.
You know what's really interesting is your relationship with Zohran Mamdani. You know, you saw him again last week and had lunch.
I get along with him. I disagree with his policy.
Well, a lot of Republicans—
A lot of people liked it. They said it's bipartisan.
Sure.
And I get along with him, but I just disagree with his policy. I don't think you should be driving people out of New York with money, because they’re the ones that are paying the taxes.
Well, a lot of Republicans are running ads, hosting him as a new voice of the Democratic Party. That he is, you know, in their depiction, a radical—
I don't think about it. I say I like him, I think he's great, but I think his policies are crazy. You can't have wealthy people leave. You can't have companies that employ tens or thousands of people leave and go to Florida, Texas. You’ve got to fight those companies that cherish—you've got to fight to keep them. And nobody's doing that. I've never seen anything like it. But I do—I like him, but I think his policies are not good.
Do you plan to dispatch ICE agents to polling places in the midterms?
Haven't thought of it.
Would you rule out declaring a state of emergency in the lead up to the midterms unless there's widespread violence in the streets?
I don't rule anything out or in. We'll see. You mean the Insurrection Act?
Yeah.
No, I've never used it. I could use it. A lot of people think I should use it sometimes. We have the best—look, we have the lowest crime in the history of our country. We have the lowest murder rate since 1900, 125 years. We have the lowest murder rate. That's despite the fact that they allowed 25 million people.
Mr. President, your polls have never been lower.
They're fake numbers. I would beat anybody running today by 20 points. Your numbers that you have are fake. The pollsters are corrupt. They're almost as corrupt as the writers.
Your own pollsters are not telling you that?
My own? No. I'll tell you what. I heard John McLaughlin told me they are much higher than the numbers. I don't ask him. I'm not running, but they said John McLaughlin is a good pollster. See, I'm doing very well. I think I am. Look, we have the strongest economy. We have the strongest industrial economy. Everybody said you’d never have jobs, and you’d never have you know manufacturing jobs. We got more manufacturing jobs coming online than at any time in the history of our country. Do you have any idea what's going on? Do you know how many factories were built? And I'm not talking AI. I'm talking about car factories, Pfizer, Merck, Lilly. They're all coming back. You know why? They're like me, but you know why they're coming back? Because they don't want to pay tariffs.
You said you're not running again. Looking ahead to 2028, who do you think is the strongest Democratic candidate?
Well, I thought that, frankly, Gavin Newsom maybe would have had the itch, then he gave an interview, which was the worst interview I've ever heard by a professional politician. He gave an interview that basically he was a dumb person, but he was smarter than the Black people that happened to be in the room. That's what he said, because he was talking to a Black audience. He said he's got bad boards. He can't read a speech. He's got all sorts of medical problems.
So if not him, then who?
I believe it was the worst speech. In fact, I put out a statement after I heard him, remember, saying that Gavin Newsom has just given up the presidency today. I believe it was the worst interview I've ever seen a professional politician—
Can we also ask about the building that you're doing? You showed us the helipad, the new ballroom, which you say is ahead of schedule. We can see it being constructed.
Everything I do is ahead of schedule.
Can you explain to people who say that these building projects don't have a connection to Americans who are struggling to pay bills? Why is this important for the American people?
So the White House is a very special symbol. It's a symbol of America. It's a symbol of our greatness. It's, I think, maybe the most important symbol that we have. The White House was a dump. The moldings were falling off the outside of the building. It hadn't been painted in…it was just a disgraceful dump. The doors were falling off. The locks were broken. And I said, I got to fix it. And I do that better than anybody else. Maybe I do it better than anything I do, and it's easy for me. It's actually relaxing. You know, for a lot of people, it drives them crazy.
For me, it’s relaxing. You see…And then the generals came. They said, Sir, they have new helicopters. I didn't buy them. Stupid Joe Biden, but they're very big and very powerful. They ripped the shit out of the grass, and I said—and they didn't know what to do, so they're going to use the old helicopters just for this one stop because they land on the grass. And I said, “Did you ever hear of building a helipad?” And everybody said, “Oh, what a wonderful idea. I never thought of that.” I said, "Why don't you design a helipad that's appropriate for these large helicopters?" And I built it. You see how I built it ahead of schedule.
You know how much money I spent on it? Zero. I got it from the company that built the helicopters, Lockheed, to build a helipad—close to $10 million—because they sold those helicopters and they didn't say you can't fly on grass. So I said to them, “Fellas, do you mind paying for it?” So I got it built for—I built it, but I built it with their money. The ballroom had $400 million in it. I had a judge who was a lunatic, and he said that I used the money in order to avoid getting a permit. I didn't. I don't own it. I'll be in it for just a relatively short period of time. Other guys will be in it for four years, seven years, eight years.
You take great pride—
And I had a judge that actually accused me of giving $400 million to go with that loan because I wanted to avoid permits. It's the craziest thing.
Are you willing to demolish the Kennedy Center?
It's in terrible shape. I'd be willing to save it, but it's in terrible, terrible shape. Only I can save it, and I'll tell you the biggest problem with the Kennedy Center. I can build it, but it will lose like many of those places. If you look at Carnegie Hall, New York, and all these places, the artsy places, they lose tens of millions of dollars. The Kennedy Center, long before I got there, was losing hundreds of millions of dollars. Do you know that? And if I'm going to go out and put up the money myself or raise that kind of money, I think the Trump Administration should be recognized. It's not just a building. I have $258 million. That's money to build. I got that, I got that from Congress. But the problem isn't that. The problem—and I'll make it nice. The problem isn't that.
The problem is that once it's built, as all houses of the art are doing, they lose—if you look at Carnegie Hall, if you look at some of the places like that, their numbers, they all lose a lot of money. The Kennedy Center was losing over the years hundreds of millions of dollars. Now I'm in a unique position. I'm a really good builder. I can fix it. I can fix it. And I'm also real rich where I can—and I have influence where I can put up money and I can also raise money. But we're talking about $60 to $125 million a year.
So, would you commit to not bringing in wrecking balls to Washington to demolish the Kennedy Center without the consent of Congress?
I'm not committing to anything. We're going to see how it plays out in court. But if I build it, and if I agree that for the rest of my life, I'm going to be putting up $100 million to have it open to people so they can see free—do you know the orchestra at the Kennedy Center? Do you know how much it costs for it? $22 million a year, that I've been paying. $22 million. It's a lot of money, and I said, if I'm going to do this, then I think the Trump Administration should be recognized.
And the judge is a Trump hater, radical left Trump hater. His wife uses a different name. Said. "No, you can't do that. Well, why would I want to stick with something that's going to lose hundreds of millions of dollars, and I'm not even recognized? It's not me; it's the administration. So I have people. He works hard on it. I have people that work hard on that because it's a financial loser. Always will be. Always has been. When I took it over, it was in extremely bad shape physically. The steel was rusted and rotted. The place was a dirty—like the White House. I fixed the White House, you know.
So, I get $550,000 a year as president. For the first term, I gave it. And I contributed to the White House renovation. I've done a great job. You would have come here a year ago, you would have seen walls that were falling off the outside of the White House. You would have seen beautiful ornamentation around the windows, where half of it was hanging off the window and the other half was up. Half of it, much of it, was actually gone. It was—it fell to the ground. It was removed. Fell to the ground, exploded, and it was removed. The place was in terrible shape. I made it beautiful.
You've seen the white marble floor, right? You've seen it, yeah. Nobody can do that. Very few people can do that. Well, I know how to do it. I made my money with luxury, and the White House, the White House, is a symbol of this country. Why should we have a White House—you know, when I came here, I was here maybe 20 years ago. I'll never forget. I came in. They had a meeting at the White House, and I came in and I looked at the walls as I got out of the car, and they were all broken, dented, the plaster was falling off them. That was 20 years ago. Now it's flawless.
[An aide comes in to say he has people waiting]
One thing, I just want to say this. I read a lot about, oh he's saying the White House was in very poor condition. It's now in better condition than when it was built. Could you give me those pictures, please? It's now in better condition than when it was built. Better, and it's not finished yet, but it's getting very close. And the White House is a symbol of America. When you look at a window and you see the ornamentation has fallen off half the window, or it's hanging from the final remaining screw that hasn't been rusted out.
Wiles: Or the chipping of the walls.
Trump: Oh the chipping. The walls? So bad. You know, over the course of 100 years, they were hit. I'll give you an example. Look at that board. See that woodwork? It's what I do best, I guess. Yeah. I say to people, am I a better builder or politician? See the walls. That wood was put there in 1901. It was in terrible condition. It was beat to shit. And what I did is I had it very gently by top top people stripped, Not easy to strip it and not destroy it. And there's a way of doing it that I can't tell you because that would be a whole other story. And look at it; it looks like it's in perfect condition. And then ended—solid gold. Look up and see the [unintelligible]. This office was in very bad condition. Now everyone loves it.
I know we got to get rolling. I do want to ask you. You know, you'd mentioned—
Here, just take a look. This was a while ago. This was work. This was 1949. Now, when I went through the court, they all said, "Oh, he's touching the White House.” This is the White House in 1949, 1949 means modern times.
You were three years old.
The White House was built in 1792, and the White House—look, this is the stairway going upstairs. That was in 1950. That's the stairway. This whole place was a wreck, and it was worse today. It was worse a year ago than it was here. It's just real fast. Now they said, they said, look, look at this, 1950. This is the interior of the White House. So when I do a little touch of a little paint, they say, "Oh, he's ruining the White House."
And I'll tell you, the East Wing was ripped down and rebuilt five times. That place, look at this. Just before it had—they changed the floor. If you want to do the floor, so that's in 1926. But the floor is terrible in here. If you want to do the floor, it's like a big deal. You want to put like a beautiful statuary or marble, which is the highest level. They'll say, "Oh, he's ruining the White House. Look at the condition of this place. So this is the East Room. Look, 1950, falling down. You see, that's where they had the event the other day for far too few people. Now, President Xi gave me a list, a lot of people. I said, if I give you that, I won't have anybody. Here's the State Dining Room in 1950, and I had to go through a courthouse with a judge who said, "You're destroying the White House.” It's the shit I have to go through. I brought it back to us, and I think the White House. See, there's your press room right there.
You mentioned the Democrats will come after you if they win. Are you considering pardoning members of your administration prior to the end of your term?
Yeah, sure I’d do that.
Is that something you would consider doing?
Well, Sleepy Joe Biden, he gave pardons to everyone. [Holds up pictures of White House] They're actually—see, this is the way it looks now.
Have you seen the videos of Mitch McConnell back in the Senate? Do you think he should resign because of his health condition?
It was a disappointment to a lot of Republicans. So that's just—well, Sleepy Joe gave pardons to everybody. He gave them to Fauci. He gave them to this. But you mean I'm not allowed to give them, but Sleepy Joe's allowed to give them? This ain't gonna be much of a story. Here we are doing this. You haven't asked me one fucking positive question. All of this. What about this? What about that? What about that? What about this? All negative. Why are you devoting all this time to the White House? You know how I do, I do that out of my back pocket. I pay for a lot of it, but I fix it because the White House should look like that. It shouldn’t look like—if you would have stood in that balcony and looked at that wall, half the wall was falling. It's actually dangerous. People are walking under, crap was falling off it all the time. Every time it rained, it was leaking, horrible. Now it's perfect, and I would say that I should be given credit for fixing the White House because I'm also doing very well with the war. I'm doing very well with another war that we already won, Venezuela. Do you notice you haven't asked me a question about Venezuela?
We did earlier.
No, no, I brought it up, and then you said—
You beat us to it. But yeah.
No, but I'm just thinking to myself, fake news. But I have a lot of respect. I like the owner, good guy. But I don't understand. I'm sitting here. I've done all this stuff. Look, this is nothing compared to what I've done, but I took the White House and made it beautiful again. Okay, and people look at it. People came up. President Xi looked at it two days ago. He said, "This is beautiful. Much better than I…" He was here 25 years ago with Obama. Think Obama knows it? Obama would not. He doesn't know if something's dirty or clean.
How did Xi's health seem to you? There are reports that Xi's in bad health. How did he seem to you?
I think he's in great health. I hope you quote me on that too, because I was with him for two days, extremely intense, a lot of visits to different places all over the place. I don't know, and he was in perfect health. I know when somebody’s not—
What will you miss the most about the White House?
This beautiful room that nobody should be allowed to rip down. The Oval Office. I've been asking Susie for six months to give me a statement. Will we save this room? Will we make it a federal landmark?
No one can change what you've done to it, you're saying
No.
No one can tear it down.
I see the Secret Service looking, and I say, "What are you guys looking at?” “Sir, we think the Oval Office should be taken down, and we'll build a new one, sir.” I said, "My ass, you can’t build a new one. This is a special place.” The cabinet room too, which I also think—show them the cabinet room when they go out, okay. The cabinet room’s gorgeous. That was a mess. It was a disgusting mess. This whole place was a disgusting mess, and now it's perfect. But Joe didn't do it. Well, I hope I get a decent story. I don't think—you know, it's hard to get a good story. Every question's a hit. I don't know what the hell's wrong.
We really appreciate your time. Thank you.

articles.title: From nuclear to hybrid: The key moments from the Euronews Defence Summit
articles.body:
Euronews hosted on Wednesday its first Defence and Space Summit. Here are the key moments from the day-long gathering, bringing together the NATO Secretary General, ministers, senior officials and industry leaders.
Is Europe ready to defend itself?
That was the central question at the Euronews Defence and Space Summit, which brought together policymakers, lawmakers and industry leaders as Europe grapples with the need to rearm and deter potential threats.
Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine has transformed Europe's security landscape, exposing longstanding weaknesses and forcing governments to rethink defence spending, military capabilities and industrial capacity.
As Russia continues its war in Ukraine and hybrid attacks against European allies increase, the pressure to act is growing.
Here are five key moments from Wednesday's summit.
Radev raises the alarm
Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev was among the day's most anticipated speakers. On Wednesday, he challenged the EU's strategy of supporting Ukraine, describing it as a failed attempt at "peace by force".
"The war in Ukraine challenged our critical thinking and realistic approach," he said.
"It challenged our ability to assess the strategic centre of gravity of the opponent. It challenged most of all our ability to design feasible political objectives and to translate them into a sound military strategy and to define a desired end state."
Radev called for greater diplomatic engagement with the Kremlin to end the war and avert what he described as the "worst-case scenario" of a nuclear attack against Europe.
Russia controls the world's largest nuclear arsenal, with an estimated 4,400 stockpiled warheads, including 1,796 strategically deployed.
"There is a nuclear card," Radev said.
"We need to have this into account. We cannot close our eyes (to the fact) that there are nuclear weapons on our continent, there are nuclear weapons in the arsenal of Russia. And this is part of the game calculation."
His remarks came hours after Reuters reported that Russia had sent a document threatening to "use the entire arsenal of forces and capabilities at its disposal, including nuclear weapons" to defend its territory.
Rutte reassures allies
NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte followed Radev with a very different message for Moscow: "Stop the nuclear threats."
Rutte declined to comment on the reported document but offered a glimpse of NATO's response to Russian President Vladimir Putin.
"Putin knows he can never win (against) NATO, so I don't take this seriously," he said. "Of course, we had to reply and make clear to him that NATO is a defensive alliance."
"I think the best way to deal with this is to have a bit of calm," he added.
Rutte also addressed the rise in hybrid attacks targeting Ukraine's allies, including an arson attack at a robotics defence company in Estonia and an attempted drone attack at Leipzig airport in Germany.
He described the incidents as attempts by Putin to divert attention from the stalled battlefield, fracture Western unity and weaken military support for Kyiv.
Seeking to reassure allies, Rutte said: "There is no immediate threat to NATO territory."
"We will defend every inch of NATO territory, every square kilometre, square mile," he said. "There's no doubt Putin knows this. So that threat is not there. And if anything happens, we are ready to counter it."
Rutte praised Ukraine's gains on the battlefield and its deep strikes inside Russia, but highlighted a critical weakness: air defence.
Russia has used sustained aerial attacks to pummel Ukrainian cities, putting pressure on Kyiv's stocks of air defence interceptors.
"It is crucial now to keep Ukraine strong," Rutte said, urging allies to provide Patriot interceptors. "But Ukraine is not doing worse (now) than some time ago."
Francken warns of 'dark winter'
Despite the reassurances, concern over Europe's security is growing.
Belgian Defence Minister Theo Francken warned that Europe was facing a "dark winter" of increasing interference.
"Russia, air attack, air attack, air attack. This is the biggest threat. So we need air defence, air defence, air defence," Francken told the summit.
"We need to have more stocks, more production, scale up production, and a large industrial base. Everything has to go faster."
Francken said Russia had decades of experience in hybrid warfare and argued that Europe should draw on Ukraine's battlefield expertise to keep pace with rapidly changing technology.
"I don't want to have 200,000 drones somewhere in a stock, and in two months you cannot even use them because they're outdated. So we have to adapt," he said.
Francken also acknowledged Belgium's long-standing underinvestment in defence.
"We were like the worst pupil of the NATO class. We had 1% of GDP in defence spending," he said, adding that spending had since doubled.
"But I cannot do in 18 months what has been neglected for 40 years."
Puzder aims at 'Made in Europe'
European security remains closely tied to the United States, NATO's largest military power.
Relations between Washington and European capitals have faced repeated tensions since Donald Trump returned to the White House and pursued an "America First" agenda.
Matthew Whitaker, the US ambassador to NATO, sought to reassure European allies that Washington remained committed to their security.
"We're not stepping back. We're just asking our allies to step forward and join us," he said. "We have continued to say that we're going to stay engaged in Europe."
Andrew Puzder, the US ambassador to the EU, struck a more confrontational tone, criticising the bloc's push to prioritise "Made in Europe" products in public procurement, including defence.
The policy, which originated in France, has gained support in other EU capitals, although its precise scope remains contested.
"When lives are on the line, capability and availability should determine the solution, not geography," Puzder said.
"One attack by a powerful adversary on a member state, and we'll all be glad that we focused on weapon superiority rather than regional economics."
Puzder instead promoted a "Made in NATO" approach, which would give US defence companies greater access to EU procurement.
"We're stronger when we work together," he said, calling for an alliance that confronts its adversaries with "unity and strength rather than division and self-interest".

articles.title: There is no risk of Russia using nuclear weapons against the Baltics, Rutte assures
articles.body:
NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte, the former Dutch prime minister, said there is no risk of Russia using nuclear weapons against the Baltic States in response to a question about Moscow's warning over Kaliningrad at the Euronews Defence and Space Summit in Brussels on 30 September, according to NATO's transcript of his remarks.
Russia routinely brandishes nuclear threats as a pressure tool against Europe, and its latest one targets the Baltic. In a written warning to NATO, Moscow claimed it was ready to use nuclear weapons if the alliance tried to isolate Kaliningrad, its exclave between Poland and Lithuania.
NATO tells Moscow to stop the nuclear threats
Rutte said NATO had responded to the Russian document by making clear that it is a defensive alliance and telling Moscow to stop its nuclear threats. "This is absolutely not called for and not helpful," he said.
Asked whether "the risk of nuclear weapons being employed against the Baltics is now real?" Rutte said: "No, it's not." He said Russian President Vladimir Putin knows he cannot defeat NATO and said he did not take the threat too seriously.
Rutte added that NATO should remain calm while continuing its work, and that Russian hybrid actions in Europe would bring more support for Ukraine, not less.
"We can allow a bit of calm, but also a bit of making sure we continue with what we are doing," he said.
Moscow warns of strikes on NATO decision-making centers
The Russian document, seen by Reuters, claimed NATO was pursuing a "dangerous and reckless course" carrying "high risks of the outbreak of a direct armed conflict." It warned that Russia could strike decision-making centers in NATO member states from the start of a conflict.
NATO said none of its exercises or activities pose a threat to Russian territory and called on Moscow to end its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, refrain from increasingly reckless behavior toward NATO members, and cease its "irresponsible nuclear rhetoric," according to the alliance's written response seen by Reuters.
Russian embassies take the warning public
Russia's Embassy in Ireland repeated the nuclear warning on 29 September, claiming NATO was preparing an air and naval blockade of Kaliningrad and that Moscow would be ready to use its entire arsenal, including nuclear weapons, if NATO countries tried to isolate the exclave from the rest of Russia. The embassy also claimed Russia had no plans to escalate tensions with Europe and accused European politicians of "playing a dangerous game."
The embassy linked its warning to statements by European politicians about an increased Russian "alleged hybrid campaign against European countries." Reuters said Russian embassies in at least three European countries had issued similar statements in the previous three days.

articles.title: Hegseth Unveils New Autonomous Warfare Command in ‘State of the Force’ Address
articles.body:
MARINE CORPS BASE QUANTICO, Va.—Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth announced plans for a new four-star command to lead the military-wide drive to field autonomous systems, as the Pentagon’s takes a bullish approach towards artificial intelligence and drone warfare. He also unveiled five other initiatives during what he promised will become an annual “State of the Force” address here Sept. 30.
Hegseth plans to launch the Autonomous Warfare Command within a year as a combatant command endowed with “service-like authorities, built to scale autonomous and robotic capabilities across the joint force,” he said. Its portfolio will include drones, artificial intelligence, and command and control systems.
Hegseth also announced the creation of a new program office, led by a two-star officer, to ensure military installations can generate their own power to isolate themselves from attacks on public grids. Bases in the homeland are increasingly seen as possibly contested environments where the U.S. military must be able to operate while under threat in a age of increasingly sophisticated cyberattacks and so-called hybrid warfare activities by America’s adversaries.
And he confirmed plans to slash the total number of generals and admirals across the military by 20 percent, a move Air & Space Forces Magazine and other outlets had reported would be part of Hegseth’s speech.
Other initiatives include:
- A new group, dubbed “Project Meridian,” to study the future of warfare led by tech leaders Palmer Luckey and Elon Musk and former Speaker of the House Newt Gingrich, who were in attendance.
- An initiative, called the “Next Great American Base,” to build a new military installation to host 15,000-25,000 service members. Hegseth said governors and adjutant generals from every state will be invited to the Pentagon to pitch locations.
- The creation of five new corps of cadets at Hillsdale College, Louisiana State University, Liberty University, Mississippi State University, and Tuskegee University, which will all be given priority in officer commissioning.
- A new “Office of Religious Affairs” reporting directly to the Secretary of Defense to give chaplains better access to senior leadership.
Exactly one year after Hegseth summoned hundreds of senior officers and enlisted from commands across the globe to Quantico for an address outlining his vision for the U.S. military, he spoke this time to an audience of around 600 E-6 enlisted members and O-3 officers, who the Pentagon said were selected by their units for their performance and leadership potential.
Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff Air Force Gen. Dan Caine briefly addressed the crowd and introduced Hegseth.
Autonomy
The new Autonomous Warfare Command will drive the design, development, and fielding of autonomous and semi-autonomous capabilities and systems.
“The autonomous and robotic revolution has enormous implications for equipment, doctrine, organization, and the assumptions that have governed warfare for decades,” Hegseth said. “Civilian leaders can provide direction and urgency, but lasting change must be anchored in military command structures and operationalized by leaders across our joint force.”
The Pentagon is already leaning heavily into autonomy, and the new command is designed to significantly accelerate that effort. Lawmakers in the Senate had proposed the creation of such a combatant command during deliberations for the 2027 defense policy bill. The measure cleared the committee, but the bill is still pending. To be authorized, the House would also have to approve the measure.
It is not yet clear how the new four-star command will be structured, who will lead it, or how it will work with the autonomy efforts already underway within the different services. In a memo, Hegseth wrote the Pentagon plans to work with Congress to stand up the command by October 1, 2027, a year on from the announcement.
Hegseth said it will start with an interim step, dubbed “Project Agincourt,” named for the Battle of Agincourt in 1415. Project Agincourt will draw from existing efforts like the Defense Innovation Unit and the Drone Dominance program, Hegseth said, and pair “operators with entrepreneurs in rapid adaptation cycles while distributing decisions and dollars closer to frontline units.”
Project Agincourt will be guided by DIU director Owen West and Navy SEAL Senior Chief Max Strasiser, the first enlisted SEAL to graduate from Navy Test Pilot School. Creating Autonomous Warfare Command will take place “over the course of several months,” Hegseth said.
The Air Force and Navy are already developing Collaborative Combat Aircraft: semi-autonomous drones designed to work alongside crewed fighters. The Air Force is also pursuing a lower-cost intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance drone with autonomous capabilities under its Massed Modular Aircraft program, and the Navy is working to field an unmanned tanker drone, the MQ-25.
The growth of autonomomy and the Penatagon’s future plans to harvest technology with its new command represent the “fastest peacetime shift in modern military history,” Hegseth said.
“Drone warfare supercharged by SI-enabled targeting is the biggest battlefield revolution in generations,” he added, using an acronym for so-called super intelligence, President Donald Trump’s favored term for AI.
At AFA’s Air, Space & Cyber conference earlier this month, Air Force leadership made it clear they see autonomous systems as central to the service’s future. Air Force Chief of Staff Gen. Ken Wilsbach told Air & Space Forces Magazine at the conference that while true autonomous aircraft are a “few years off,” the service is leaning heavily into autonomy in its current future Force Design model.
“The FQ-42 and the FQ-44 [Collaborative Combat Aircraft] are autonomous fighters, and then we’re going to have perhaps other platforms that are autonomous, where you don’t actually need a crew to do a fighter mission,” Wilsbach said during a session with reporters. “You just send the aircraft off, and it does its mission because it’s automated.”
The Pentagon has deployed uncrewed surface vessels operationally in the Middle East for a few years for maritime surveillance. This summer, a U.S. Navy drone boat was even able to rescue two downed Army Apache pilots near the Strait of Hormuz. U.S. Southern Command, which has been conducting strikes on boats suspected of smuggling drugs for over a year, recently established an autonomous warfare branch that will employ its own uncrewed vessels and aerial intelligence-gathering platforms. On the southern border, the U.S. military is now using 10 uncrewed surface vessels to patrol the Rio Grande River, Assistant Secretary of Defense for Homeland Defense and Americas Security Affairs M. Roosevelt Ditlevson told Air & Space Forces Magazine in a recent interview.
“We’re moving into next-generation tools here that we’re going to employ to make sure that we hold these narcoterrorists at bay,” Ditlevson said, referring to the drug smugglers. “I’m very excited about what is going to happen in the autonomy space and how we’re going to employ these different systems.”
But the Pentagon is automating more than aircraft, ships, and vehicles.
The Pentagon’s Maven Smart System has become a key tool for the U.S. military, a system aggregating sensors, intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance, and command and control as part of the targeting process. Maven is used for operations ranging from targeting assistance in the Middle East to, more recently, counter-drone and anti-smuggling efforts on the southern border.
Ditlevson said AI, through Maven, will also feed into the Pentagon’s sweeping Golden Dome missile defense shield. “Maven Smart System is going to feed into the Golden Dome picture,” he said.
At the border, the Defense Department also uses autonomy software called Fortress, an adaptation of Anduril’s Lattice, which integrates data and sensors using AI. “All of our systems must be compatible with Maven Smart System,” Ditlevson said. “Everything that we have, that data needs to be integrated into Maven and into Lattice.”
To support all these new autonomous systems, Hegseth said, each military service will phase in new military occupational specialties for autonomy.
“We need institutional knowledge and career paths for a new generation of autonomous warfighters,” he said.
Fortress America
Hegseth also said the Pentagon is creating a new initiative called “Fortress America” to ensure military installations are able to generate their own power. The Pentagon has been working on building nuclear microreactors at key U.S. bases in the homeland and has previously said it plans to field a nuclear reactor at a military base by September 2028.
The Air Force in particular is working on a microreactor at Eielson Air Force Base, Alaska, with plans to build more at other bases in the coming years. The service has also explored using alternate power sources like solar panels, geothermal plants, and more to create so-called “microgirds” for bases so they’re not entirely reliant on local civilian power grids.
The drive to give bases their own energy sources is driven by concerns that adversaries may target critical infrastructure, around 80 percent of which is currently in the commercial sector, to kneecap the military’s ability to generate forces. The Pentagon chief referred to the program as “nation’s insurance policy” in a memo directing the establishment of Fortress America.
“If an adversary takes down the grid by cyber attack, by sabotage, or by any means, our bases stay lit, our aircraft keep flying, our command centers never go dark,” Hegseth said.
Hegseth is also slashing the number of general and flag officers, cutting billets by 20 percent. That doubles down on the 10 percent cut to general and flag officers he ordered last year, which he dubbed the “less generals, more GIs” policy.
“The number-crunchers say we fired 10 percent of the generals and admirals across the force, and that number sounds about right,” Hegseth said. “And I know because I directed it that we’ve also reduced the overall number of general officer slots by an additional 10 percent. So yes, 20 percent reduction across the board.”
Generals and admirals make up less than 1 percent of the military. According to the Congressional Research Service data, there were about 850 general officer positions in 2023. Some of those positions were unfilled at the time, as is the case today.
The maximum number of general officers allowed per service is set by law, though those caps do not apply to joint positions. The law also sets a minimum number of general officers in joint jobs.
The Air Force has roughly 250 generals. The Space Force has roughly 30 generals, and has plans to continue to grow that number.
A year ago, most senior military leaders gave stoic reactions during politically charged speeches from Hegseth and Trump, keeping with the military’s apolitical tradition. The troops at this year’s addres gave Hegseth a more vocal reception, particularly during his reference to Musk, Luckey, and Gingrich, and Hegseth exited to applause from the troops, though service members appeared to avoid visual reactions to Hegseth’s more ideological comments. Attendees were separated by branch, and were given a “War Department Field Manual,” a collection speeches by Hegseth with a forward written by Trump. Earlier in the day, the service members in attendance participated in a physical training session with Hegseth on the grounds of the Pentagon.

articles.title: Belgium will send three F-16 fighter jets, but maintenance delays may keep Ukraine from using them
articles.body:
Less than 50% of the F-16 fighter jets delivered to Ukraine may be operational, Defense Express reports, citing a Wall Street Journal (WSJ) editorial published on 29 September. On the same day, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that Belgium would deliver three F-16 fighter jets this year.
F-16s are used extensively to intercept Russian cruise missiles and drones. As the number of Russian attacks has increased, these aircraft have become particularly important for Ukraine. However, the jets Ukraine receives are old, and keeping them flying takes regular maintenance, extra work, and hard-to-find parts.
Routine inspections are taking as long as 40 weeks in Belgium, retired US Navy Rear Admiral Mark Montgomery told the WSJ.
The maintenance process for these aircraft for Ukraine is lengthy
A likely reason for the problem is the lengthy maintenance process handled by Belgian company Sabena Aerospace Engineering, according to the WSJ, whose questions the company declined to answer. This process, according to Defense Express's estimates, takes 6–20 times longer than maintenance in the United States, which usually takes between 2 and 6 weeks. Ukraine uses the services of the Belgian company, meaning its F-16s are not being serviced quickly enough.
Delivering three additional fighter jets will not significantly help the Ukrainian military until the issue with aircraft maintenance times is resolved, Defense Express notes. The lengthy turnaround may be caused by a large maintenance backlog at the company, limited capacity, or logistical constraints, and older jets may need extra work and scarcer parts.
The delivery is part of an earlier commitment. Belgium plans to provide seven fighter jets this year: three for operational use and four for spare parts, Belgian Defense Minister Theo Francken said in June.
"I'll propose to the government to send all our F-16s to Ukraine in the coming years. It depends on having the F-35s in place because, of course, we have DCA [dual-capable aircraft] capacity. We have our role in the nuclear doctrine of NATO," Francken said.
Belgium has pledged its entire F-16 fleet of 53 aircraft as F-35s replace them, according to Defense Express.
F-16s in Ukraine have already shot down several thousand Russian aerial targets
F-16s operated by Ukrainian pilots have shot down more than 3,150 aerial targets. These include 666 cruise missiles and around 2,500 drones of various types. The aircraft have also carried out more than 650 strikes against Russian ground targets, Lieutenant General Anatolii Kryvonozhko, Commander of the Ukrainian Air Force, said during a meeting between a Ukrainian Air Force delegation and representatives of Lockheed Martin on 29 September.
At the meeting, Conor McGuire, Lockheed Martin's head of F-16 capability development, highly praised the combat use and operation of F-16s by Ukrainian pilots and the entire ground aviation personnel. He also expressed his intention to help Ukrainians enhance the capabilities of the existing platform, the statement said.

articles.title: Ukraine war latest: Russia uses drone with warhead designed to cut power pylons for 1st time, Zelensky adviser says
articles.body:
Ukraine war latest: Russia uses drone with warhead designed to cut power pylons for 1st time, Zelensky adviser says
Key developments on Sept. 30:
- Russia uses drone with warhead designed to cut power pylons for first time, Zelensky adviser says
- Drone crashes in Moldova, Romania scrambles fighter jets amid Russian mass attack on Ukraine
- Missile alerts cost Ukraine $45 million for every hour businesses stop, economy minister says
- Zelensky visits Lyman sector, says Operation Vivaldi reclaimed 125 square kilometers
Russia has for the first time used a jet-powered drone equipped with a warhead designed to destroy high-voltage power pylons and steel bridge structures, presidential adviser Serhii "Flash" Beskrestnov said on Sept. 30.
The development comes as Moscow renews its large-scale campaign against Ukraine's energy system ahead of winter, launching its heaviest combined attack on energy infrastructure in months overnight on Sept. 30.
"Bad news. Today, the enemy for the first time used a special shaped-charge cutting warhead on a jet-powered unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV)," Beskrestnov, an adviser to President Volodymyr Zelensky on defense technologies, wrote on Telegram.
According to Beskrestnov, the warhead was developed specifically to destroy high-voltage pylons and steel bridge structures. It consists of a 40-kilogram main charge and four additional destructive modules.
"I think the enemy plans to attack important high-voltage power transmission lines," he said.
Russia's overnight assault involved nearly 190 attack drones as well as ballistic missiles, Zelensky said. Energy infrastructure in Kyiv and Kyiv Oblast was the primary target, while critical infrastructure was also struck in several other regions.
By the evening, emergency power outages had been introduced in the capital and surrounding region as well as in Chernihiv and Zhytomyr oblasts following repeated Russian attacks on energy infrastructure, according to the Energy Ministry.
The Sept. 30 attack marked a sharp escalation in Russia's renewed campaign against Ukraine's power system.
"Since the summer, there has been practically no day when the enemy has not attacked energy infrastructure. But such a massive and combined attack has occurred for the first time since the end of the last heating season," Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi said following the attack.
read also
Drone crashes in Moldova, Romania scrambles fighter jets amid Russian mass attack on Ukraine
A drone flew into Moldovan airspace, crashed outside a village, and exploded in the early hours of Sept. 30 amid a Russian mass attack on Ukraine, Moldova's Defense Ministry said.
The drone entered Moldovan airspace around 5:43 a.m. local time and fell down near the village of Hirbovat in the central Anenii Noi district, where it exploded, according to the ministry.
According to preliminary information, no injuries were reported from the explosion. Moldovan police and army teams were headed to inspect the site.
Romania's Defense Ministry said that its radars detected an aerial target east of Izmail during the night and two F-18 fighter jets of the Spanish air force stationed in the NATO country scrambled as a precaution. No object entered Romanian airspace, the ministry said.
Overnight, Russia attacked across Ukraine with 188 drones, 86 of them jet-powered, as well as with Zircon, Onyx, and Iskander missiles, according to Ukraine's air force. The air force said it shot down or suppressed 5 missiles and 155 drones.
read also
Missile alerts cost Ukraine $45 million for every hour businesses stop, economy minister says
Missile alerts cost Ukraine an estimated $45 million for every hour they force businesses to stop operating, Economy and Environment Minister Oleksandr Kravchenko told the Guardian in an interview published on Sept. 30.
"If people are in a bunker, business stops," Kravchenko told the Guardian.
Kravchenko said prolonged missile alerts can bring large parts of the economy to a standstill as workers move into shelters, with some alerts lasting for hours.
Ukraine introduced a two-tier air raid warning system on Sept. 2 to reduce the economic disruption caused by prolonged alerts. Red alerts are issued when there is a missile threat and require businesses to halt operations and people to seek shelter. Yellow alerts warn primarily of drone threats and allow many businesses to continue operating.
Russia has intensified its aerial campaign against Ukrainian cities and critical infrastructure. Kravchenko said more than half of businesses continue operating during yellow alerts, but those warnings do not mean there is no danger.
On Sept. 28, a Russian jet-powered drone struck the National Academy of Sciences building in central Kyiv during a yellow alert while employees were still inside. The attack killed an aide to former National Security and Defense Council Secretary Volodymyr Horbulin and injured others.
"What we had not fully anticipated was how quickly Russia would develop these jet-powered drones and use them to target everything," Kravchenko said.
Russian attacks have caused an estimated $10 billion in damage to fixed assets in Ukraine this year alone, according to Kravchenko. Steel plants, warehouses, logistics hubs, and data centers have all been hit as Moscow increasingly targets infrastructure supporting the country's economy.
Russia has also stepped up attacks on Ukraine's Black Sea ports and maritime export infrastructure, adding pressure on one of the country's main trade routes.
The government is now discussing ways to allow more private companies to purchase Ukrainian air-defense systems to better protect their facilities, Kravchenko said, while acknowledging that businesses cannot fully shield themselves from Russian missiles and drones.
read also
Zelensky visits Lyman sector, says Operation Vivaldi reclaimed 125 square kilometers
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky visited the command post of the 66th Separate Mechanized Brigade in the Lyman sector running across Donetsk and Luhansk oblasts to award soldiers and meet brigade comannders on Sept. 30.
Zelensky thanked the troops for returning more than 125 square kilometers of territory from Russian occupation to Ukrainian control, in cooperation with other units of the Third Army Corps as part of Operation Vivaldi.
"Thank you for protecting our state, sovereignty, and territorial integrity," he said.
In his talks with the commanders, the President discussed issues of procurement, especially pick-up trucks for brigades, and increasing funding for drones, simplifying procurement, and expanding staffing, Zelensky said. He also highlighted the need for long-range artillery.
Ukrainian forces under the command of the 3rd Army Corps liberated three villages in northern Donetsk Oblast as part of the ongoing Operation Vivaldi, corps commander, Brigadier-General Andrii Biletskyi said on Sept 28.
The villages of Ridkodub, Nove, and Katerynivka were liberated, while full Ukrainian control was restored over Karpivka and Novomykhailivka.
This phase, described as the "third season" of Operation Vivaldi, inflicted over 2,000 Russian losses and saw over 250 Russian soldiers taken prisoner, according to Biletskyi.
The two previous "seasons" of Operation Vivaldi were each announced in similar updates, first on Sept. 15 when the offensive was given its name, and then on Sept. 20, when the liberation of the villages of Shandryholove and Derylove were announced.

articles.title: Explainer-Why Russia's Kaliningrad is a potential flashpoint with NATO
articles.body:
Explainer-Why Russia's Kaliningrad is a potential flashpoint with NATO
Sept 30 - Russia has warned NATO that it would be ready to resort to nuclear weapons if the Western alliance tried to cut off or attack the Russian region of Kaliningrad.
WHERE AND WHAT IS KALININGRAD?
It's a highly militarised exclave - separated from the main mass of Russian territory - that is wedged between NATO members Poland and Lithuania and also borders the Baltic Sea. It has a population of about 1 million and is slightly bigger in area than the US state of Connecticut.
HOW DID IT COME TO BE RUSSIAN?
Kaliningrad, formerly the German city of Königsberg and capital of East Prussia, became part of the Soviet Union after the Red Army captured it in April 1945 and the victorious allies divided East Prussia at the end of World War Two.
WHAT MAKES IT STRATEGICALLY IMPORTANT?
It provides Russia with a platform for air defence, missile and naval forces that can project power deep into northern and central Europe. At the same time, it is a potentially vulnerable pressure point for Moscow because of its boxed-in location between two NATO states and the difficulty of maintaining supply lines or reinforcing it in the event of a war.
WHAT HAS LED TO THE LATEST SPIKE IN TENSIONS?
These have been rising steadily since Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine, which led NATO to move decisively to strengthen its eastern flank. The alliance has expanded in the region, with Finland and Sweden joining in 2023 and 2024 respectively.
Russia perceives a growing Western threat to Kaliningrad. In May 2026, it slammed remarks by Lithuania's foreign minister as "verging on insanity" after he said NATO had to show Moscow it was capable of "penetrating the small fortress they've built in Kaliningrad" and razing Russian air defences and missile bases there.
A Western military source told Reuters that dozens of aircraft from NATO members were involved in an unannounced operation in the airspace around Kaliningrad in mid-August, demonstrating the capability to cut off the exclave's radio and radar links as well as its air defences in the event of a conflict with Russia.
In social media posts, Russian embassies in Europe have highlighted what Moscow sees as threatening NATO military movements in the Baltic and hawkish rhetoric on Kaliningrad from policymakers and in the media.
NATO says it has increased its presence in the Baltic Sea partly in response to concerns about threats to critical undersea energy and communications infrastructure. In its response to the Russian warning, it urged Moscow to halt its "increasingly reckless behaviour" and "irresponsible nuclear rhetoric".
WHAT DO EXPERTS FEAR COULD SPARK A CRISIS?
European states have been walking a fine line since 2022 - supporting Ukraine with weapons, intelligence and sanctions against Russia while stopping short of joining the conflict themselves - though Moscow said this week they are already "waging war" against it.
Security analysts say any miscalculation could lead to a direct military confrontation - and Kaliningrad, by virtue of its location, would be a potential flashpoint.
Among the possible triggers could be drone incidents, disruption of critical infrastructure, major new missile deployments or anything perceived by Moscow as amounting to a NATO attempt to impose a blockade on the exclave. REUTERS

articles.title: Russia Sends NATO Formal Nuclear Warning Over Kaliningrad
articles.body:
- Category
- World
Russia Sends NATO Formal Nuclear Warning Over Kaliningrad
Russia privately threatened NATO that it could use nuclear weapons if the alliance attempted to isolate Kaliningrad, Russia’s heavily militarized exclave between Poland and Lithuania, Reuters reported on September 30.
In a diplomatic note sent to NATO and reviewed by Reuters, Moscow accused the alliance of pursuing a “dangerous and reckless course” that carried “high risks of the outbreak of a direct armed conflict.”
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The warning comes amid growing concern over Russian hybrid operations across Europe, including sabotage, arson, cyberattacks, and other hostile activity that governments have linked to Moscow. UNITED24 Media recently detailed how these operations have intensified across the continent.
The document warned that such a confrontation could include “Russian strikes against decision-making centers in the alliance’s member states right from the outset.”
“Russia will be ready to use the entire arsenal of forces and capabilities at its disposal, including nuclear weapons, in order to defend its territory should NATO countries undertake any attempt aimed at isolating the Kaliningrad Region from the rest of the country,” the note stated.
Kaliningrad is a heavily militarized Russian exclave on the Baltic Sea between NATO members Poland and Lithuania. Reuters noted that Moscow has increasingly portrayed allied military activity around the region as a direct threat.
NATO rejected the accusation in a written response also reviewed by Reuters, stating that it is a defensive alliance and that its exercises do not threaten Russian territory.
“None of NATO’s exercises or activities pose a threat to the territory of the Russian Federation,” the alliance stated. “We urge the Russian Federation to refrain from increasingly reckless behaviour towards the Allies and to cease its irresponsible nuclear rhetoric.”
Nikolai Sokov, a Vienna-based nuclear analyst and former Russian diplomat, told Reuters that the warning could reflect growing concern in Moscow over Western arms supplies to Ukraine, sanctions, military exercises, intelligence flights, and possible restrictions on Russian shipping in the Baltic.
“They expect more action, including a blockade of the Baltic Sea — just below the level of war in European calculation, but for them this will be open war,” Sokov stated. “I see a risk of mutual miscalculation.”
Russian embassies in at least three European countries have also issued warnings in recent days accusing NATO of escalating tensions around Kaliningrad, Reuters wrote. Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov described the statements as diplomatic reminders to “hotheads in Europe.”
A NATO diplomat characterized the Russian note as another attempt to intimidate European countries and emphasized that the alliance would continue supporting Ukraine. A senior European defense official told Reuters it was the first threat of this kind from Russia since the Cold War and described it as serious.
A day earlier, Russia had already threatened nuclear retaliation if NATO attempted to blockade or attack Kaliningrad, with its embassy in the UK warning that Moscow could respond using “all means available,” including nuclear weapons.

articles.title: Ukraine’s war chest is running low at the worst possible moment
articles.body:
The building of the private medical clinic Dobrobut burns following a Russian drone strike on central Kyiv on Sept. 28, 2026. | Nikoletta Stoyanova/Getty Images
KYIV — Vladimir Putin is intensifying Russia’s pressure on Ukraine, smashing cities, factories, bridges and ports with constant waves of killer drones and missiles.
Prime Minister Sergii Koretskyi warned journalists this week that Ukraine faces a $27 billion defense funding gap this year, with Kyiv hoping to cover about $7 billion domestically and looking to partners for the rest. Some EU financing remains tied to reforms Kyiv must pass to unlock the money, while other allies have yet to fill the remaining gap.
Advertisement
Overnight, Russia launched more than 190 missiles and drones in a nationwide assault that heavily targeted energy infrastructure, causing blackouts in Kyiv.
“Since the summer, there has been virtually not a single day when the enemy has not attacked energy infrastructure. But an attack of this scale and intensity has not occurred since the end of the last heating season,” Koretskyi said Wednesday.
Following the attack, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy renewed his call for allies to send more air defenses. “Every interceptor missile truly saves lives,” he said. “And the closer we get to winter, the more of this protection we need. We must do everything we can to ensure that Russia’s strategy of ballistic and drone terror does not succeed.”
Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy walks to the dais during the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly in New York on September 23, 2026. | Spencer Platt/Getty Images
Russia, in recent weeks, has escalated near-continuous drone and missile attacks. Air raid alerts are relentless — day and night — in Kyiv. The strikes have hit railways, energy plants, ports, factories and other critical infrastructure across the country, hammering Ukraine’s economy and adding to pressure on public finances. The government is also considering tax increases as it looks for domestic methods to close part of the defense gap.
“Of course, raising taxes is never ideal, but in wartime, we cannot afford the luxury of populism or pretend we can avoid asking anything of the public,” said Oleksandra Myronenko, an economist with the Center for Economic Strategy think tank.
Without money, Ukraine’s ability to continue resisting Russia would be undermined, Koretskyi warned. Kyiv needs cash now to place advance orders for weapons and ammunition due next year.
Advertisement
“This applies particularly to long-range drones — our ability to carry the war back to where it came from. This is a critical need that needs to be fulfilled,” he said.
Koretskyi told reporters that Kyiv will have to shift spending to keep the country fighting and basic government services functioning.
“This entails a strict regime of public finance austerity and the deferral of certain non-priority expenditures. These funds are intended to ensure payments to military personnel and support for their families,” Koretskyi said. “First and foremost, we are financing: defense, pensions and social payments, as well as salaries for teachers, doctors and other budget employees.”
Newly appointed Ukraine’s Prime Minister Sergii Koretsky delivers a speech to member of Parliament during a session of the Ukrainian parliament in Kyiv on July 16, 2026. | AFP via Getty Images
Zelenskyy underlined this week that his administration’s “clear task” is to “meet Ukraine’s current defense funding needs. Everything we can do together with our partners, using their funding — and this applies first and foremost to defense orders — must be 100% complete by the end of the year.”
Russia also feels the pain
Ukraine is not alone in feeling the financial strain. Moscow is also being forced to absorb rising fiscal costs — but its larger economy and ability to raise taxes give it more room to sustain the war.
The federal budget deficit reached 5.8 trillion rubles (€60.4 billion) in the first half of the year, which is being financed by a host of tax increases. Russia plans to spend 17.1 trillion rubles (€180 billion) on defense in 2027, Reuters reported, a 27 percent increase on what it had previously budgeted for that year and accounting for more than a third of all budget spending.
Advertisement
The Kremlin has lowered its estimates for oil and gas revenue for next year; Ukraine’s ongoing bombing campaign against refineries and energy infrastructure has wrought havoc with production.
The Russian military has suffered more than 1.5 million casualties in the war, according to Ukrainian estimates. Russian President Vladimir Putin this week raised the authorized size of the armed forces to about 2.4 million personnel, the fourth expansion since the full-scale invasion began in February 2022.
A woman walks past a billboard advertising contract service in the Russian army as an Unmanned Aerial Vehicle operator for a period of 12 months, offering 5.4 million rubles per year with a two-month training period, in Tambov, on September 9, 2026. | Igor Ivanko/AFP via Getty Images
Despite the cash crunch, Ukraine is still able to exert a painful toll on Russia.
Ukraine’s army reported last week that its ongoing Operation Vivaldi had pushed Russian forces back in part of the eastern front and captured more than 250 prisoners. Kyiv is also investing heavily in domestic long-range missiles and drones to strike targets inside Russia.
Europe under pressure to pay up
But Ukraine needs money to fund that war effort.
That’s putting pressure on European allies, which supply the bulk of Kyiv’s weapons and finances after the U.S. ended most new aid when Donald Trump returned to the White House last year.
Advertisement
The EU is currently paying out installments on its two-year €90 billion loan to Ukraine, but Kyiv is asking for the money to come faster to fill the budget gap. “The funds are needed this fall … especially given the mobilization that the enemy is planning right now,” Defense Minister Evgeniy Khmara urged this week.
But before releasing more funds, Brussels wants Ukraine’s parliament, the Verkhovna Rada, to complete crucial reforms that are part of the country’s roadmap to eventual EU membership.
“As reforms in the Rada progress, more budget support too. We have €37 billion still available in this calendar year,” European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen wrote after meeting Zelenskyy at the U.N. General Assembly earlier this month.
Kyiv, for its part, is also putting pressure on Brussels to revisit the more than €200 billion in Russian central-bank assets immobilized across the EU. “We need our friends, our European politicians, to be brave enough and to make some bold actions,” said Ukrainian Finance Minister Serhii Marchenko.
Next year looks even more fraught.
Marchenko told donors in Brussels this week that Ukraine would require $52.6 billion in aid in 2027, while about $32.6 billion remains unfunded.
“Ukraine has no reserve funds to cover its entire spending. If we fail to get external financing, we’re facing a strong cut of all non-priority expenditures — and could even extend to protected expenditures,” said Myronenko, the economist.
“If we don’t have the actual cash in our accounts, we won’t have the means to pay military salaries, pensions, and so on. So, if there is no international aid, then everything will be very bad,” she added.

articles.title: Ukraine Needs 20mm F-16 Ammo to Down Russian Jet Drones
articles.body:
Ukraine wants to purchase tens of hundreds of thousands of 20-millimeter rounds for its F-16 fighter aircraft to shoot down Russia’s increasingly deployed jet-powered attack drones.
Kyiv is negotiating with several European countries and ammunition manufacturers about potential supplies, Bloomberg reported on Wednesday, Sept. 30, citing people familiar with the discussions.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The ammunition would be fired from the F-16’s built-in cannon, offering Ukraine a potentially cheaper and more widely available alternative to using scarce air-to-air missiles against each Russian drone.
According to Bloomberg, destroying one drone may require approximately 150 rounds. At the current intensity of Russian attacks, Ukraine could need around 10,000 such rounds per day.
Cheaper option against Russian drones
Ukraine has used AIM-9 Sidewinder and AIM-120 AMRAAM missiles launched from F-16s to intercept Russian aerial targets. These guided missiles are considerably more expensive than cannon ammunition and are also needed by ground-based air defense systems.
Ukrainian F-16 pilots are already using their aircraft’s 20-millimeter cannons against jet-powered drones when other intercept options were unavailable.
The F-16 carries an internally mounted M61A1 Vulcan six-barrel rotary cannon that fires 6,000 rounds per minute. Using it allows pilots to preserve guided missiles for cruise missiles and other high-priority targets.
Each aircraft carries 500 usable rounds of semi-armor piercing, high-explosives, incendiary (SAPHEI) PGU-28 20mm cartridges.
Pentagon Commits Nearly All $400M in Ukraine Aid a Day Before Deadline
In employing the gun against airborne targets, pilots usually fire half-second bursts which puts out 50 exploding bullets in each brief trigger squeeze. And the trigger is positioned in the same place as it is when shooting a firearm – under your right index finger.
The tactic nevertheless requires pilots to approach drones at relatively close range. Shahed drones are approximately 1/10 the size of an average fighter, which at maximum range for the typical gunshot of 4,000 feet slant range, the target is about 2 milliradians or about the size of the smallest item in the heads-up display (HUD) which is a dot, or about the size of a decimal or period on this page.
Falling debris from destroyed drones and overspray from the natural dispersion of projectiles that don’t hit the target may also endanger people and property within the Vulcan’s ground projected elliptical footprint when intercepts take place over populated areas.
Bloomberg reported that global supplies of 20-millimeter ammunition are more plentiful than stocks of Patriot and Western air-to-air missiles, potentially allowing Kyiv to obtain the rounds more quickly.
Russia expands jet-powered drone attacks
Russia has rapidly increased its use of jet-powered drones, which fly faster and higher than conventional propeller-driven Shaheds and are more difficult for mobile fire groups and existing interceptor drones to destroy.
According to Ukrainian Air Force, Russian launches of jet-powered drones rose from around 350 in June to approximately 2,850 in August.
President Volodymyr Zelensky said Russia launched more than 100 drones on Tuesday, including 29 jet-powered models. Ukrainian forces intercepted 18 of the faster drones, he said.
Ukraine is simultaneously developing high-speed interceptor drones and other domestic systems to counter the new threat. Zelensky said on Tuesday that officials had selected the first prototypes of a dedicated countermeasure and established deadlines, financing requirements and planned production volumes.
Kyiv has also received urgent deliveries of F-16 ammunition from Belgium, Spain and other partners. Belgium has agreed to transfer three additional F-16 fighters to Ukraine by the end of 2026.
“As Russia escalates its attacks every day, we need to add more capabilities to shoot down aerial targets and protect people,” Zelensky said.

articles.title: Kyiv Reshapes Responses to Russian Strikes
articles.body:
President Volodymyr Zelensky said Ukraine has adjusted its response system to what he described as Russia’s “terrorist operation” against Kyiv’s critical infrastructure, while ordering an urgent review of air defense and F-16 ammunition supplies.
He made the remarks following a conference call with military officials, government members, and the heads of services involved in protecting critical infrastructure.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“We have adjusted the response system to the Russian terrorist operation against Kyiv’s critical infrastructure. Protective measures must be fully implemented. We have determined the necessary reallocation of resources,” Zelensky said in a Telegram statement on Thursday.
He added that Kyiv’s local authorities must be prepared to make rapid decisions to support residents.
The statement follows reports of two drone strikes near the support structure of Kyiv’s Pivdennyi (South) Bridge, prompting authorities to suspend metro and surface public transport across the bridge.
“Two drone strikes near the support structure of the Pivdennyi (South) Bridge,” Kyiv Mayor Vitalii Klitschko said on Telegram.
Municipal specialists are inspecting the bridge to assess any damage.
Earlier, local Telegram channels reported that a Shahed drone struck the bridge as a metro train was crossing, allegedly blowing out windows in one car. They also circulated videos and photos purportedly showing the strike, fires near the supports, and drone debris on the roadway.
UAE Government Used Sanctioned Russian ‘Shadow’ Airline
Zelensky also ordered an urgent review of agreements with international partners on the supply of ammunition for Ukraine’s F-16 fighter jets and air defense missiles.
“The Ministry of Foreign Affairs, the Ministry of Defense, and the Office team will conduct an urgent review of agreements with partners regarding the supply of necessary ammunition for F-16s,” he said.
Ukraine has increasingly used F-16 fighter jets to intercept Russian aerial targets, including jet-powered attack drones.
Pilots have already used the aircraft’s built-in 20mm cannon when guided missiles were unavailable, helping preserve more expensive air-to-air missiles for higher-priority targets.
Russia has rapidly expanded its use of jet-powered drones, which fly faster and higher than conventional Shahed-type drones. According to Ukraine’s Air Force, their launches rose from around 350 in June to approximately 2,850 in August.
Earlier, Zelensky said Russia launched more than 100 drones on Tuesday, including 29 jet-powered models. Ukraine is also developing high-speed interceptor drones and other systems to counter the growing threat.
Per the latest Zelensky’s report, the review will cover air defense missile agreements with every partner, including the status of each package and an updated delivery schedule for Ukraine, which he said should be prepared by the following day.
“It is crucial that we receive additional missiles in October,” Zelensky said, adding that some agreements already reached with national leaders had not yet been implemented at the operational level.
Zelensky said he had been in contact with partner leaders and stressed the need to speed up the implementation of existing orders.
“I am grateful to Germany, Norway, Finland, and all other partners ready to act as quickly as possible,” he said.
Zelensky also revealed that the government was monitoring the implementation of resilience plans in every region and key city on a weekly basis.
According to him, delays have been identified in some communities. He instructed the military command and government officials to prepare additional measures to improve safety and ensure the continuity of resilience efforts.
“I look forward to the report from the Prime Minister of Ukraine and the Commander-in-Chief of the Armed Forces of Ukraine regarding the steps outlined today,” Zelensky said.
