articles.title: What Trump Has Built
articles.body:
Donald Trump struts onto the new White House helipad, an 80,000-sq.-ft. expanse of carved granite on the South Lawn. “Can you believe this?” he says, taking in the scene, the Washington Monument rising in the distance. The President lingers over the details of the project with obvious pleasure, pointing out the gray stone imported from Italy and describing how five separate sections were fitted together, with measurements he says are precise to an eighth of an inch.
Behind him rises a bigger renovation project: the new White House ballroom, its concrete skeleton consuming the former East Wing. Lawsuits have followed the endeavor, alleging that Trump demolished the historic structure and began building its replacement without congressional authorization or the required federal reviews. He kept building anyway. Trump points to the walls, calling them “nuclear concrete” (the sort, he says, used in nuclear facilities), and describes a military complex beneath the ballroom that will plunge six stories underground. There will be five separate floors, he says, with one side made entirely of glass, 6 or 8 in. thick. He holds his hands apart to demonstrate. “The steel goes up next week.” 
As we walk toward the Oval Office, Trump stops several times to inspect his handiwork. There are freshly painted doors, new gold doorknobs, the Rose Garden lawn ripped out and replaced with a Mar-a-Lago-style patio, where he now presides over dinners at what he calls the Rose Garden Club. “People say, why do you spend so much time on this?” he says. “But I find it relaxing.” Later, he returns to the subject again. “It’s what I do best,” he muses aloud. “I say, am I a better builder or a politician?”
One can understand Trump’s fixation on his construction projects. At one of the lowest points of his presidency, he is absorbed with the physical details of a world he can remake to his liking. There is something revealing in the contrast. Here, he can still point to a wall and say how thick it should be, decide where the grass ends and the stone begins, make demands and have them fulfilled. With his presidency seemingly spinning off course, Trump has busied himself with things he can control.
Outside these gates, events have become increasingly resistant to Trump’s will. The war in Iran, launched without congressional authorization and initially described by Trump as a four-to-six-week undertaking, is seven months old when we meet, with no end in sight. It has sent oil and gasoline prices soaring and convulsed the global economy. Inflationary pressures compounded by Trump’s tariffs have pushed the Federal Reserve—now led by his handpicked chairman—to raise interest rates over his objections, with another hike possible before year’s end. Mortgage rates have climbed to 7.5%, worsening an already punishing housing market.
The political coalition that returned Trump to power has frayed, with signs of discontent among independents, rural voters, and parts of the Latino electorate, even as his GOP base remains substantially loyal. A Reuters/Ipsos poll in September put his approval at 32%, the lowest of his political career; a recent Wall Street Journal survey recorded the lowest ratings of any President heading into midterm elections since 1990. Republican candidates have distanced themselves from his military actions and his deportation campaign. Voters have recoiled at his laissez-faire approach to the artificial intelligence industry and his accumulation of wealth while in office through crypto deals, thousands of disclosed stock trades, and an expanding empire of Trump-branded developments stretching from Saudi Arabia and Qatar to India and Vietnam.
Inside the Administration, senior advisers increasingly recognize that he has passed the apogee of his second-term power. Across the Republican Party, officials are preparing for the likelihood of losing the House—and perhaps the Senate—in the midterms. After two years spent almost entirely on offense, Trump may soon be forced onto defense. Democratic control of Congress would bring investigations and subpoenas, hearings, and potentially a third round of impeachment proceedings. Cabinet officials could be hauled before Congress. Trump describes the prospect in characteristic terms. “They’ll probably go after me,” he says, “and I’ll go after them.”
Yet with so much at stake—for the country and the world, for his party and his own power—Trump can seem curiously preoccupied. During a 75-minute Oval Office interview with TIME, he was discursive and grievance-fueled, veering from the crises of his presidency to resentments old and emerging. He said he regretted appointing Neil Gorsuch, Brett Kavanaugh, and Amy Coney Barrett to the Supreme Court, after they ruled against him on tariffs, mail ballots, and birthright citizenship. “I gave them the position of a lifetime,” he said, “and they voted against me often.” On his expectation of fealty, he was unapologetic: “I do like loyalty, yeah.” Again and again, he returned to the condition of the White House itself, complaining that his predecessors had left the building in disrepair and deriding Barack Obama as someone who “doesn’t know if something’s dirty or clean.”
Trump dismissed widespread opposition to the rapid build-out of data centers, including among his own base, as a prescription for a poorer America. When pressed on the limits of his power, Trump left himself ample room: He would not rule out declaring a national emergency or invoking the Insurrection Act around the midterms, nor promise to refrain from bringing wrecking balls to the Kennedy Center without congressional approval. “I’m not committing to anything,” he says. “We’re going to see how it plays out in court.”
In Trump’s telling, he is simply doing what has to be done, even when that means breaking foundational promises to his voters. He campaigned as a president of peace, but is now waging a war he says was necessary to prevent Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon. He points to Venezuela, where his removal of Nicolás Maduro and the elevation of Delcy Rodríguez have brought the country into Washington’s orbit, as proof that his projection of U.S. power can produce results. He touts most-favored-nation drug pricing and restricting institutional investors from buying single-family homes as measures that will lower costs for Americans. New GDP and inflation figures suggest the economy remains strong.
When asked why he remains consumed with construction projects so removed from the country’s concerns, Trump offers a rationale: “The White House is a very special symbol. It’s a symbol of America. It’s a symbol of our greatness.” He speaks of his building projects in the language of legacy—monuments meant to endure long after he is gone. But while Trump obsesses over stonework and fixtures, gold and glass, the more important parts of his legacy are being built too—in the decisions he makes from inside these walls, and the consequences unfolding far beyond them. 
In late April, the President summoned Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and a retinue of military and national security officials to the Oval Office. By Trump’s own timeline, the war with Iran was supposed to be over already, with a new regime in place and a nuclear program throttled. But the Islamic Republic had proved resilient and resourceful, choking off oil through the Strait of Hormuz and sending tremors through the global economy.
Now there was another problem. Trump had learned from a New York Times report that the U.S. military was running low on certain munitions after firing more than 1,200 Patriot missile interceptors. To replenish the losses, the Pentagon was drawing on assets stationed in Asia and Europe, potentially weakening American defenses in other theaters. “What the f-ck is this?” Trump said to Hegseth, according to two officials familiar with the exchange, handing him a printout of the story.
According to those officials, Hegseth borrowed one of Trump’s favorite terms of derision, telling the President it was “fake news.” The Secretary of Defense insisted that the reporters had taken the facts out of context and exaggerated them to make the Administration look bad. But the reporting emerged from an official DOD inspector general’s assessment. (A spokesperson for Hegseth denied the exchange.)
Trump’s frustration went beyond munition stores. The war was polling miserably. At the time, 13 U.S. service members had been killed and nearly 400 wounded. (Those numbers would increase to 19 killed and more than 800 wounded by the end of September.) Gasoline prices had risen more than 40% since the opening attacks on Feb. 28. The conflict had already cost more than $25 billion, and the consequences were beginning to bleed into the midterm campaign. The President found himself without an exit ramp. That dynamic appears to hold true: Instead of concluding the war, Trump tells TIME, he may ramp up the bombing after the midterms if they can’t reach a satisfactory deal. “Because by annihilating Iran, we’ve created peace in the world,” he says. “With Iran, I don’t think you could ever have peace.”
In recent months, Trump’s relationship with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has grown more acrimonious, according to a senior Administration official. Netanyahu urged Trump toward war with Tehran but has since complicated Trump’s efforts to end it, including by striking Hezbollah targets in Lebanon after Trump told him not to, multiple U.S. officials tell TIME. Trump says he does not believe reports that Netanyahu was warned by Egypt and the UAE ahead of the Oct. 7 attacks, but stops short of endorsing him for re-election as Israelis prepare to vote in late October for the first time since the worst security failure in the country’s history. Asked whether he might work better with Netanyahu’s leading challenger, former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, Trump leaves the possibility open. “Well, I don’t know,” he says. “I don’t hear bad things about him.”
The decision to attack Iran was a hinge point in Trump’s second term. His first year back in power had unfolded as a frenetic exercise in presidential will, a barrage of executive actions and dismantled guardrails that had largely gone according to plan. Then his second year opened with the raid on Caracas and capture of Maduro, a daring operation that reinforced Trump’s conviction that audacity could succeed where caution had failed. The subsequent attack on Tehran would test the limits of that conviction—and reveal how quickly confidence born of success could lead to overreach.
A cascade of crises followed. Though Trump has dismissed the pain of rising gas prices, he concedes the war has depleted a subset of U.S. munitions. “Some forms of ammunition are a little bit lower than other forms,” he says. Trump says he has struck deals with leading defense manufacturers, including Raytheon and Lockheed Martin, to replenish the arsenal and expand production. “They’re building four, five, six plants,” he says, citing Patriot and THAAD anti-ballistic-missile facilities. “They’re building tremendous amounts of capability.”
When asked what this will cost American taxpayers, Trump offers a curious metric: less, he says, than America makes in a single month from Venezuelan oil. Yet Americans have so far felt little benefit from that arrangement. Major U.S. oil companies have returned to Venezuela and begun extracting from the world’s largest proven crude reserves, but gas prices remain at record highs for September. Meanwhile, Trump’s tariff regime strained America’s global relationships and reverberated through the economy. 
Trump points to low unemployment, robust consumer spending, and a stock market at record highs as evidence that his economic program is working. By those measures, the economy has remained strong. But they coexist with a harsher reality: the cost of everyday life remains painfully high.
By summer, Trump was growing angrier with U.S. allies that had refused to come to America’s aid against Iran—from the European powers and South Korea to Canada. Trump has directed much of his ire over the issue at America’s neighbor to the north, according to a close aide. “He doesn’t like the fact that we essentially protect them because of their proximity to our military might, and doesn’t think they give us enough in return,” says a Trump senior adviser. On July 20, Trump invoked a 1930 statute to impose a 50% tariff on Canadian goods. The trade war with America’s second largest trading partner hit steel, aluminum, and lumber especially hard, disrupting supply chains and raising the cost of materials that went into everything from factories to new homes. 
Borrowing costs were becoming their own problem. For Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, preventing a sell-off in the bond market from becoming a broader crisis was an increasingly urgent task. By late September, only 25% of Americans believed Trump’s policies had improved the economy, according to a Wall Street Journal poll, while 60% said they had worsened it. Trump had returned to office promising cheaper energy, lower prices, and an economic boom. Instead, voters were finding the opposite. “It’s not lost on any of us,” a Trump adviser tells TIME. “When voters aren’t happy with the economy, they tend to vote against the party in charge.”
Since returning to office, Trump has marveled at AI’s capabilities. He is increasingly in thrall to the tech executives courting him. In December 2025, Elon Musk returned to the Oval Office for a clandestine meeting. Trump spent hours asking Grok, Musk’s AI chatbot, questions about his presidency and legacy, according to an official present. At the time, Trump was ordering missile strikes against Venezuelan boats he alleged were smuggling drugs into the U.S. He asked Grok how Venezuelans would react if the U.S. captured Maduro. According to the official present, the chatbot responded that Maduro was a repressive and deeply unpopular dictator and that many Venezuelans would likely celebrate his downfall. After Trump ordered the mission to seize Maduro, the following month, celebrations broke out in the streets. Trump, according to officials, came away thinking Grok was ingenious.
Along with his fascination with the technology came two related concerns. One was economic: that enthusiasm for AI’s potential was propping up the stock market. The other was geopolitical, reinforced in conversations with industry titans such as Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang: that China could gain a decisive advantage over the U.S. if it developed more powerful AI first. Trump was committed to giving American companies the freedom to build faster than their foreign competitors. That meant embracing the unprecedented infrastructure build-out required to support the industry’s computing needs. After watching a cable news segment about the backlash, Trump fired off a Truth Social post. “The only reason that communities throughout the U.S.A. should not want Data Centers is if they want to end up being backwards and poor,” he wrote Aug. 31. “If they want to be successful and rich, with far lower taxes and jobs all over the place, let Data Reign.” 
Days later, aides showed Trump surveys from his longtime pollster, Tony Fabrizio, showing pervasive anxiety about AI: fears of lost jobs, rising costs, and technology eventually escaping human control. Fellow Republicans facing voters in November were increasingly eager to put distance between themselves and the issue. Trump “really just didn’t seem to care,” one aide says. “He wants to do what he wants to do. He’s used to generating outrage and then watching everyone eventually crawl back to him. It’s hard to convince him to do anything at this point.”
Trump was unfazed by the burgeoning bipartisan calls for new AI regulations. “I don’t have to destroy the industry,” he says. “We’re making a lot of money with that industry. That industry is the Industrial Revolution, but bigger. It’s the internet, but much bigger.” The details don’t appear to concern him. When TIME asks about OpenAI agents’ meddling with federal government websites, Trump responds: “Who breached it? They’re not allowed to do that.”
Trump’s contribution to the debate about AI safeguards has been to announce the formation of an “AI Force,” which he now wants to rename the “SI Force”—part of his effort to rebrand artificial intelligence as “super intelligence.” Asked what the group will do, Trump responds: “It’s going to be super intelligent.” Pressed further, he explains that it will consist of industry leaders advising him on government policy. On Sept. 29, he met with AI leaders at the White House, where the President and top executives from six leading tech companies signed a “constitution” to police themselves—a covenant of self-regulation in lieu of government oversight. An Administration official present said they left with a “no surprises if something happens” understanding between the White House and the industry. 
It was an example of how Trump has surrounded himself with industry leaders, seeking their advice, favor, and political donations. A recent CNN poll found 75% of Americans viewed artificial intelligence with more fear and concern than excitement, with broad bipartisan support for greater federal oversight. But Trump waves away AI fears, placing them in a familiar catalogue of what he considers manufactured panics. “They said that our country was going to burn down because of global warming,” he says. “Then they changed the name to climate change because global warming turned out to be a hoax. Russia, Russia, Russia was a hoax.” Asked who, exactly, is perpetrating the supposed hoax of AI concern, Trump throws his hands in the air. “The whole country is based on fake stuff,” he says, “because these people have Trump derangement syndrome.”
Inside the Oval Office, Trump’s redesign is impossible to miss. There is gold everywhere, from the decorative plasterwork to the inscriptions on the ceiling and the gilded frames crowding the walls. The room is so dazzling you practically need sunglasses. Trumpian tchotchkes are scattered about: a FIFA “World Peace Prize” sits next to the Resolute Desk, where the President keeps a commendation given to his uncle during his years as an MIT professor. 
At times, Trump’s train of thought was difficult to keep up with, his conversation moving in streams and eddies before circling back to familiar obsessions. He recounted conversations that sometimes sounded improbable. At one point, Trump claimed the Secret Service had wanted to tear down the Oval Office and rebuild it, only for him to intervene. “I said, ‘My ass, you can’t build a new one. This is a special place.’”
Whatever happens in November, people close to Trump expect him to devote more of his remaining presidency to foreign affairs, as second-term Presidents often do, with particular attention to the western hemisphere, where ideologically sympathetic governments have given him opportunities to expand American influence. At home, they expect another emphasis altogether: Trump’s campaign against what he calls “lawfare” and his effort to reshape cultural institutions, including the nation’s museums, in his battle against what he calls “woke” ideology.
Looking ahead to the midterms, Trump dismisses unfavorable polls as fake and insists Republicans can prevail. “I think we’ll do OK if I campaign, and I intend to,” he says. So far, he has done little beyond a two-day midterm convention and a few fundraisers, but top advisers say the President is preparing a campaign sprint to help Republicans stave off disaster in the midterms: visiting 32 competitive districts in the next month, with the MAGA-style rallies that powered his political rise.
Inside the White House, advisers are already contemplating what a divided Washington would mean. “I think if the worst happens in the midterms, we’ll be forced to think more bipartisan,” one top official says. “I would hope that if we win, we can still do that, because for two years we’ve run a completely partisan play. When you’re looking back on your time, I don’t think that’s what you should be proud of, even if it was successful.”
Trump’s political operation boasts a $400 million war chest, but he has only recently begun opening his checkbook. Aides say he has been reluctant to spend because he wants to preserve cash for future elections as a means of keeping his grip on his party. “He wants to have as much money in his account as possible when he’s no longer able to raise the kind of money he can now,” a Trump aide told TIME this fall. “He doesn’t seem to care that much about the midterms, thinks they’re a lost cause anyway, and wants to preserve future possibilities.”
Aides are bracing for turnover after the midterms as Trump sheds officials who have frustrated him. A source close to the President says he has openly mused about firing the FBI Director Kash Patel and has expressed frustration with Hegseth. Trump says he intends to protect those who remain. When TIME asks whether he plans to issue pre-emptive pardons to aides and associates before Democrats—or a future Administration—can pursue them, he suggests he will, offering a familiar justification: “Sleepy Joe gave pardons to everybody.”
As the conversation moves between war and peace, his own grip on power, and the possibility of impeachment, Trump keeps returning to the trappings of the office. He asks Natalie Harp, his ever present aide, to bring in photographs of earlier White House construction projects, including renovations from the 1930s and the Truman-era reconstruction. He studies the pictures as evidence for his case, lamenting the judges and injunctions now complicating his own efforts. Holding up a photograph of work being performed on the State Dining Room in 1950, Trump complains about a judge he says accused him of destroying the White House. “It’s the sh-t I have to go through,” he says. 
Toward the end of our interview, I ask what he will miss most when his presidency is over. This time there is no digression, no grievance, no story. Trump does not need a moment to think: “This beautiful room.” 
—With reporting by Leslie Dickstein, Simmone Shah, and Olivia B. Waxman

articles.title: Hegseth announces new AI and drone command
articles.body:
Hegseth announces new AI and drone command
The Pentagon will set up a new Autonomous Warfare Command to design, produce and field robotic systems across the military, US Secretary of War Pete Hegseth has said in his ‘State of the Force’ address.
The announcement comes as experts sound the alarm about the threat posed by military AI, saying that over-reliance on it could lead to the erosion of human critical thinking, increase the risk of accidental escalation due to the unpredictability of the decision-making by the algorithms and make warfare even more dangerous for civilians.
During his speech at Marine Corps Base Quantico in Virginia on Wednesday, Hegseth said that the AutoWarCom would be granted “service-like authorities built to scale autonomous and robotic capabilities across the joint force in the fastest peacetime shift in modern military history.”
“Drone warfare supercharged by SI-enabled targeting is the biggest battlefield revolution in generations,” he stressed.
A day earlier, US President Donald Trump signed an executive order replacing the term “Artificial Intelligence” (“AI”) with “Super Intelligence” (“SI”) in the US government’s vocabulary.
The lessons of the Ukraine conflict, in which both sides actively rely on drones, have been one of the main motivations for launching the new command, according to the secretary of war.
In a memo published the same day, Hegseth noted that the Pentagon’s long-time strategy “of buying fewer, increasingly sophisticated weapons” has lost its effectiveness.
“Warfare… has changed dramatically and suddenly. Advanced computing now enables precise, low-cost weapons to be produced at massive scale. These systems increasingly threaten our costly legacy platforms and disrupt our force projection. Urgent change is required,” he wrote.
The Autonomous Warfare Command, which will be led by a four-star general, should become operational by October 1, 2027, the secretary of war said.
Bloomberg reported last month that heavy reliance on AI, staff cuts and rushed targeting procedures contributed to a US missile strike on an Iranian girls’ school in Minab on February 28, in which at least 157 people, including 123 children, were killed.
Officials involved in the Pentagon investigation told the agency that some US Central Command (CENTCOM) personnel expected Palantir’s Maven Smart System to flag stale or inconsistent intelligence when selecting potential targets, but it failed to do so. The US hasn’t publicly acknowledged responsibility for the Minab strike.
Last week, CNN reported that AI almost caused a serious incident between US and China in spring. The American forces were about to intercept a Chinese vessel, which, according to an intelligence report, was carrying components for a nuclear weapon to Iran. The mission was called off at the last moment when it became clear that a chatbot used by the analyst misidentified the cargo, according to the broadcaster.
During a defense conference in Beijing in mid-September, Thailand’s Defense Minister Adul Boonthumjaroen warned that the world was at “a critical turning point” due to the emergence of the military AI. “The most pressing is not who will be the most powerful, but rather, how can we build an international order,” he said.

articles.title: “I Don't Take This Seriously”: NATO Chief Rutte Dismisses Russia’s Nuclear Threat Over Kaliningrad
articles.body:
- Category
- World
“I Don't Take This Seriously”: NATO Chief Rutte Dismisses Russia’s Nuclear Threat Over Kaliningrad
NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte dismissed Russia’s threats to use nuclear weapons if NATO members attempt to isolate the Kaliningrad region, saying he does not consider the threat credible and stressing that NATO remains a defensive alliance.
Rutte made the remarks on September 30 while speaking to journalists on the sidelines of the Euronews Defence & Space Summit 2026 in Brussels.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The NATO chief declined to disclose details of an unofficial letter reportedly sent by Moscow containing the threats, saying he was not authorized to make its contents public. He said, however, that NATO had responded directly and clearly to Russia.
Rutte stressed that NATO is a defensive alliance and called on Russia to end its nuclear threats, describing them as inappropriate and unhelpful. He also urged Moscow to end its war against Ukraine, which he described “unprovoked war of aggression.”
Asked whether there was a genuine risk that Russia could use nuclear weapons against NATO members, including the Baltic states, Rutte said there was not.
“Putin knows that he can never win from NATO. So I don't take this that serious. But of course, we had to reply and make clear to him that NATO is a defensive alliance, as I said, and stop the war in Ukraine and stop the nuclear threats because it's not helpful,” he stated.
He reiterated that Russia should end its war against Ukraine and stop issuing nuclear threats, saying such rhetoric serves no constructive purpose.
Rutte also stressed that NATO members must continue strengthening their own defense capabilities while maintaining support for Ukraine despite threats from the Kremlin.
According to the NATO chief, Moscow is using such messages and broader hybrid activities in an attempt to divide NATO members and divert their attention from Ukraine.
“What Putin tries to do… is to divide us and and lose the focus on Ukraine. We will not. So every hybrid whatever happens in Europe will be met with more support for Ukraine, not less support for Ukraine,” Rutte added.
Russia privately warned NATO that it could resort to nuclear weapons if the Alliance sought to isolate Kaliningrad, Russia’s heavily militarized exclave located between Poland and Lithuania, Reuters reported on September 30.
In a diplomatic note reviewed by Reuters, Moscow accused NATO of following what it described as a “dangerous and reckless course,” warning that such actions carried a significant risk of triggering a direct military confrontation.
The reported warning comes amid mounting concerns over Russian hybrid activities across Europe, including sabotage, arson, cyberattacks, and other hostile operations that European governments have attributed to Moscow.
Some countries in the region, meanwhile, are taking steps to strengthen critical infrastructure against potential drone attacks and sabotage. Lithuania is preparing enhanced security measures for the planned Gizai power substation near Russia’s Kaliningrad region.
Located about 30 kilometers west of Kaliningrad, the substation is set to feature reinforced fencing capable of resisting a vehicle carrying explosives, sensors designed to detect possible underground tunnels, and concrete barriers intended to protect transformers from drone strikes.

articles.title: Ukraine is downing Russia’s fastest drones—just not often enough, and scaling up comes down to money
articles.body:
Ukraine is stitching together a layered answer to Russia's faster, jet-powered Shahed drones, leaning on electronic jamming, fighter jets, and a new class of homegrown interceptors, RBC-Ukraine reported. Each tool has limits, and the new interceptors still bring down only the occasional jet drone. The bottleneck now is money and factory output, not ideas.
Russia is pouring faster jet-powered drones into the air war as winter nears, a campaign Western analysts say is meant to wear Ukraine's defenses down—and holding those skies now turns on which side can keep out-producing the other's cheap weapons.
Fighter jets help, but they run on imported rounds
Electronic jamming can work against some of the drones, and Ukraine is also sending combat aircraft up after them. But aviation has a catch: the jets need air-to-air missiles and cannon rounds, and for the F-16 and Mirage those are imported and not always in stock. Flying over Kyiv adds danger to the civilians below and to the pilots, so Ukraine would rather catch the drones out on the approaches.
New interceptors are landing hits—just not enough
The newest piece is a wave of Ukrainian interceptor drones built to chase the jet versions, which fly three times faster than the propeller Shaheds. Ukrainian crews have been downing the jet Gerans in a recent run: on 19 September, presidential adviser Serhii Beskrestnov, known as Flash, confirmed one Geran-5 shot down, and in late September, operators of the National Guard's Separate Artillery Brigade brought down a Geran-4 with the Bullet interceptor made by General Cherry, the first Geran-4 that drone has downed, Ukraine's National Association of Defense Industries said. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said several prototypes have proven themselves in combat.
Russia is now wiring its attack drones into one network in flight, so a single drone can scout, strike, and relay for the rest
Across all methods, Ukraine now intercepts about 57% of the jet drones Russia launches, Zelenskyy said on 28 September—a rate that has climbed but still trails the 90%-plus it manages against slower Shaheds. Kills by the new interceptors specifically remain isolated. In August, Air Force spokesperson Yurii Ihnat said jet drones can make up as much as two-thirds of the drones in some raids—though not every time. One promising route is reworking Ukraine's own long-range strike drones into interceptors. Kyiv is in talks with partners over the money; on 28 September, Ukraine's Defense Minister Yevhenii Khmara asked the EU to help finance the interceptors so enough reach the front quickly.
Hitting the launch sites and jamming the controls
Ukrainian forces strike the Russian airfields the jet drones launch from, RBC-Ukraine's sources said, though the raids have not forced Russia to abandon the attacks. On 20 August, military intelligence hit drone storage and launch sites at Primorsko-Akhtarsk, one of the launch bases RBC names, and at occupied Donetsk airfield. Ukraine also keeps going after the Belarusian relay towers Russia strings into a mesh network to steer the drones in, RBC's sources said.

articles.title: Russia sends nuclear warning to NATO as tensions rise in the Baltic
articles.body:
Russia has warned NATO it would be ready to resort to nuclear weapons if the Western alliance attempted to cut off Kaliningrad, a Russian exclave that borders the Baltic Sea.
In a document sent to NATO and seen by Reuters, Moscow accused the alliance of a "dangerous and reckless course" that entailed "high risks of the outbreak of a direct armed conflict."
The document said this included the possibility of "Russian strikes against decision-making centers in the alliance's member states right from the outset."
"Russia will be ready to use the entire arsenal of forces and capabilities at its disposal, including nuclear weapons, in order to defend its territory should NATO countries undertake any attempt aimed at isolating the Kaliningrad Region from the rest of the country," the diplomatic note said.
The warning highlighted Moscow's urgent concern at what it has presented as a growing NATO threat to Kaliningrad, a heavily militarized Russian territory that is wedged between Poland and Lithuania and is slightly bigger than the US state of Connecticut.
Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova, in a commentary on the ministry's website, cited statements by dignitaries from NATO states which she said demonstrated "Russophobia" and a readiness to wage war with Moscow.
These figures, Zakharova wrote, "need to be brought back down to earth. We hope that our warnings will be heard by those to whom they are addressed."
"If Europe attacks Russia, it will be a completely different sort of war – a very short war."
NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte said the alliance had responded to Russia's message by declaring: "We are a defensive alliance. And stop the nuclear threats. This is absolutely not called for and not helpful."
In its response to the Russian document, seen by Reuters, NATO also said that none of its "exercises or activities pose a threat to the territory of the Russian Federation."
"We call upon the Russian Federation to end its unprovoked full-scale invasion of Ukraine. We urge the Russian Federation to refrain from increasingly reckless behavior towards the Allies and to cease its irresponsible nuclear rhetoric," it said.
Asked if the risk of nuclear weapons being used against the Baltics was now real, Rutte told a defense conference in Brussels hosted by broadcaster Euronews: "No, it's not. Putin knows that he can never win (against) NATO, so I don't take this that seriously."
Risk of miscalculation
Nikolai Sokov, a Vienna-based nuclear analyst and former Russian diplomat, said it was becoming increasingly hard for Western countries to keep stepping up their support for Ukraine without tipping into direct confrontation with Moscow.
He said the Russian warning may indicate that hardliners are gaining influence in a debate over how to respond to Western actions that include arms supplies to Kyiv, new sanctions on Moscow, interceptions of Russian ships, frequent military exercises and intelligence flights near Kaliningrad.
"They (Russia) expect more action, including a blockade of the Baltic Sea - just below the level of war in European calculation, but for them this will be open war. I see a risk of mutual miscalculation," Sokov said.
In an online interview, he said Russia and Europe were on a collision course. Both sides needed caution and calculation.
Instead of this, the Europeans were applying "full-court pressure," and Russia was delivering a serious warning that this was highly risky, Sokov added.
Europe says it faces 'hybrid war', Russia denies it
In addition to the private warning, Russian embassies in at least three European countries have issued statements in the past three days accusing NATO of escalating tensions through military exercises and planning scenarios involving Kaliningrad.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov described these as diplomatic reminders to "hotheads in Europe."
Relations, already dire since Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine, have sharply worsened this year, with European governments accusing Moscow of stepping up a "hybrid war" on the continent through acts including sabotage and arson.
Russia denies that, and rejects repeated statements by Western politicians that it is gearing up for a possible military attack on a NATO country.
A NATO diplomat said: "I would say that the Russian letter is only another Russian attempt to intimidate Europeans, and that the response by NATO is firm and responsible. (It) reaffirms that we will not be dissuaded from supporting Ukraine."
A senior European defense official said: "(This is the) first time since (the) Cold War that Russia is threatening us like this. So this is serious."

articles.title: Zelenskyy visits frontline troops, discusses air defenses with Finnish president
articles.body:
Elena Teslova
30 September 2026•Update: 30 September 2026
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Wednesday that he visited frontline troops in eastern Ukraine and discussed strengthening air defenses with Finnish President Alexander Stubb following Russian strikes.
Zelenskyy said on Telegram that he visited the 66th Separate Mechanized Brigade’s command post on the Lyman front in the eastern Donetsk region, presented state awards and discussed the unit’s missions and needs.
He said the brigade, operating alongside other units of the Third Army Corps as part of Operation Vivaldi, had brought more than 125 square kilometers (48 square miles) of territory back under Ukrainian control.
Separately, Zelenskyy said he spoke by phone with Stubb about strengthening defenses following “a new escalation of attacks” against Ukrainian cities and communities.
Ukrainian officials reported at least four deaths in overnight Russian attacks on Kyiv and the surrounding region. Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko reported three deaths in the capital, while emergency services said a child was killed in Vyshgorod.
"Almost throughout the entire day, since the night, air raid alerts have continued in Kyiv and other cities and regions, with a constant threat from jet-powered Shaheds. There were also ballistic strikes at night," said Zelenskyy.
The two presidents discussed how best to strengthen Ukraine’s defenses, including F-16 fighter jets and air defense capabilities, according to Zelenskyy.
The attacks have also disrupted economic activity.
Oleksandr Kravchenko, Ukraine’s economy and environment minister, told The Guardian in an interview published Wednesday that missile alerts cost the country an estimated $45 million for every hour they halt business as workers take shelter.

articles.title: Russia continues strikes on Ukraine as Zelenskyy visits frontline – Europe live
articles.body:
French high school protests escalate with reported violence
France‘s prime minister convened a crisis meeting on Thursday and cancelled ministers’ trips to focus on the nationwide spread of protests, some violent, by high school students venting against under-resourced schools, long hours and other complaints, AP reported.
The demonstrations erupted in Paris-region schools last week and have snowballed, with police making hundreds of arrests in clashes with the young protesters.
Authorities have reported many dozens of injuries, including from hurled objects but also, in some suspected cases, from police riot-control projectiles.
The protests are quickly blowing up as a hot topic in the election campaign to replace president Emmanuel Macron next May and heightening pressure on the government also beset by France‘s growing financial problems.
The office of prime minister Sébastien Lecornu said he asked ministers to cancel any planned official trips in the coming days, to enable authorities and police to focus on dealing with the demonstrations.
AFP reported that some 340 demonstrations were underway late morning, with police forces deployed to several schools.
University students joined in on Thursday, blocking physical access to around 30 campuses, including in Paris and the southern city of Marseille, a student union said.
In the northeastern city of Strasbourg, authorities ordered trams to grind to a halt to “restrict the movements of rioters and demonstrators”, the regional prefect said.
In the northern city of Lille, AFP reporters saw young people wearing black hoodies destroy the glass of a bus stop. Firefighters intervened to put out the flames on upturned dustbins set on fire.
What started as a nationwide student protest over the state of the French education system has now descended into full-blown “urban violence”, according to government officials, who briefered the media, including BFMTV and Le Figaro.
The authorities believe the protests and riots are supported by far-left groups, who seek to sow discord.
In public comments, education minister Édouard Geffray called the reported violence “extremely serious,” and saying they cannot be justified in any way.
Justice minister Gérald Darmanin has called a meeting with all regional prosecutors for later this evening to discuss their response.
But the far-left France Unbowed party’s coordinator, Manuel Bompard, rejected the accusations as “conspiracy theories.”
French high school protests escalate with reported violence
France‘s prime minister convened a crisis meeting on Thursday and cancelled ministers’ trips to focus on the nationwide spread of protests, some violent, by high school students venting against under-resourced schools, long hours and other complaints, AP reported.
The demonstrations erupted in Paris-region schools last week and have snowballed, with police making hundreds of arrests in clashes with the young protesters.
Authorities have reported many dozens of injuries, including from hurled objects but also, in some suspected cases, from police riot-control projectiles.
The protests are quickly blowing up as a hot topic in the election campaign to replace president Emmanuel Macron next May and heightening pressure on the government also beset by France‘s growing financial problems.
The office of prime minister Sébastien Lecornu said he asked ministers to cancel any planned official trips in the coming days, to enable authorities and police to focus on dealing with the demonstrations.
Sikorski says Poland would welcome Britain back to EU 'with open arms'
Jakub Krupa
After France’s Emmanuel Macron and Spain’s Pedro Sánchez yesterday, Poland’s foreign minister Radosław Sikorski is the latest EU leader to offer his take on Britain’s renewed push to reset its relationship with the European Union, a decade on from Brexit.
In a post on X aimed partially at his domestic opponents ahead of Poland’s 2027 parliamentary election, he said:
“If [Britain] were to apply for a return to [the EU], which Poland would welcome with open arms, it would mean that after a decade of analyses, London has concluded that membership is the optimal form of participation in the single market.
Let us not be swayed by the Europhobes into believing that a better alternative exists.”
Ukraine made net gains in September with counteroffensive push against Russia
Ukrainian troops have regained ground in a counteroffensive in the Donetsk region, according to an AFP analysis of data from the Institute for the Study of War (ISW).
Operation “Vivaldi” was launched in September with the aim of pushing Russian forces back from the cities of Sloviansk and Kramatorsk.
The Ukrainian military has retaken small patches of territory from Russia, for total gains in the Donetsk region of 172 square kilometres (66 square miles), an area more than 1.5 times the size of Paris.
Elsewhere, Ukraine retake small areas in the regions of Kharkiv in the north (seven square km) and the eastern regions of Dnipropetrovsk (12 square km) andLuhansk (13 square km).
By contrast, Russian offensives in Zaporizhzhia (south) and Sumy (north) enabled Kremlin forces to seize 104.5 square km and 20 square km respectively.
Overall, Ukraine made a net territorial gain of 80 square km in September, according to the data.
Joint EU–Ukraine statement says they have 'identified means' on budget shortfall
The European Commision and Ukraine have said in a joint statement they had “identified the means” to cover Kyiv’s budget and defence needs for this year. It read:
Today through coordinated joint efforts, we have identified the means to cover Ukraine’s budget and defence needs for 2026. We have also reconfirmed the steps needed to ensure their timely release.
Finland investigates suspected break-ins at MPs homes
While that press conference was going on, AFP have reported that Finnish authorities are investigating a slew of suspected break-ins at the homes of members of parliament, which the prime minister said could “very likely” be linked to a foreign power.
Petteri Orpo said “If someone tries to destabilise Finland, our sense of security, or our support for example for Ukraine, it has the opposite effect. It strengthens our unity.”
Speaker of parliament Jussi Halla-aho confirmed that parliament had been made aware of a “significant” number of break-ins and signs of attempted intrusions at the homes of several politicians.
A determined show of unity amid growing tensions with Russia - snap analysis
Jakub Krupa
It’s a determined show of unity from Nato’s Rutte, the Netherlands’s Jetten, and Germany’s Merz.
The signal is clear and in line with the warnings of recent weeks: while there is no imminent threat of a military attack from Russia, Moscow’s “campaign of hostile actions” against allies would persist over the winter.
And the three leaders reiterated the urgency in accelerating defence planning, and the importance of supporting Ukraine as the situation there worsens.
'I hope Putin gets the message' as he is 'failing to intimidate us,' Rutte says
Nato’s Rutte thanks Germany and the Netherlands for increased defence spending.
He says:
“I hope Putin gets the message. It’s not just Ukrainians who are suffering. The whole of Russia is paying a huge price for his war of choice.
Putin is sending tens of thousands of young Russians to their death each month, and for nothing. He is failing on a battlefield and he is failing to intimidate us.”
The three leaders take no questions after their statements.
'We see Russia testing us across Europe,' and 'must be prepared for hostile actions,' Nato chief says
Nato’s Rutte is speaking now.
He says the three leaders just met the soldiers of the 1st German-Netherlands Corps, and thanks them for their service.
He also thanks for the 2026 International Westphalian Peace Prize that he will pick up later today on behalf of the alliance. He credits all soldiers and people working for Nato.
Russia 'poses rapidly increasing threat' to Nato, Dutch PM says
Dutch PM Jetten is next.
He says the message of deterrence is “more vital than ever”, as Russia “poses a rapidly increasingly threat to the Nato alliance,” whether in the Baltics or in Germany, as he points to a recent drone incident in Leipzig.
“Europe needs to show what it’s made of, show that we are prepared to do whatever it takes to protect our security,” he says.
He says Europeans are “ramping up our intelligence cooperation to an unprecedented level so we can combat hybrid threats,” and “reaffirming and stepping up our support for Ukraine.”
He says the Netherlands is increasing its defence spending, too.
Germany’s Merz begins by stressing the importance of Nato, as “our continental peace order is being challenged by violent revisionism emanating from Russia.”
He says the Russian aggression on Ukraine was “unleashed by Moscow in utter disregard and contempt for law and order,” causing direct threat to Europe.
Merz says the focus remains on finding “a diplomatic solution,” even as “Moscow has so far shown no willingness to come to the negotiating table.”
He adds that Europe’s support for Ukraine will continue as “we refuse to be deterred by Moscow’s hybrid attack.”
He says the work is under way to “ensure credible deterrence” against Russia, pointing to Germany’s “determined investments” in its military and general resilience.
“We know that a good future for our country is only possible within a free, secure, and united Europe,” he says.
He also repeats his lines that Europe needs to “make Nato more European so it can remain transatlantic.”
He also stresses the importance of military cooperation between Nato member states, specifically in this context with the Netherlands.
Russian drone hits grounds of nuclear research facility in Kyiv
Meanwhile, a Russian drone hit the grounds of a nuclear research facility in Kyiv, causing a fire but leaving the facility’s test reactor undamaged, Ukraine’s nuclear safety watchdog said, and AFP reported.
The regulator did not say where the drone landed or provide imagery of the attack, which happened on Wednesday.
Several of Ukraine’s nuclear sites have come under fire since Russia invaded in February 2022, raising fears of a nuclear accident.
The research reactor at the site has the capacity to generate around 10 Megawatts, around a hundredth of the generating capacity of a conventional nuclear reactor. There are four nuclear power plants in Ukraine, the largest of which was seized by Russian forces in 2022.
Rutte, Merz, Jetten about to speak at joint press conference in Germany
Nato’s Mark Rutte, Germany’s Friedrich Merz, and the Netherlands’s Rob Jetten are about to speak on a visit to see the 1st German-Netherlands Corps in Münster, Germany.
I will bring you all the key lines here, or you can watch along:
Germany's Jürgen Klopp disgusted by claims national team are ‘not white enough’
Kate Connolly
in Berlin
In other news, Jürgen Klopp has reacted with disgust to a social media debate questioning whether the Germany team he is in the process of forming are “white enough”.
Klopp said he believed there was no point in giving room to “such people and their utterances”, dismissing them as “complete nonsense”.
Asked to respond to the debate as to whether the national team were “not German enough” or “not white enough”, he said: “There is absolutely no reason to pay attention to these people. You won’t get my thoughts on this. I have little time in everyday life for idiocy – and even less on social media.”
“The great crux of our lives is that everyone is allowed to express their opinion … it’s insane when something like that exists.”
Klopp said watching sportspeople interact with each other was proof to him that mutual respect was still possible. “The world could learn a thing or two from a sports changing room … There, everyone is respected based on the facts and not discredited based on false opinions.”
Klopp, whose plans for Germany since he took over as coach in the summer have attracted huge attention, said the players he had gathered at the national team camp, including several players with a migrant background, “could not be better united than they are”.
The barrage of racist and generally offensive commentaries on social media followed Germany’s 1-0 defeat by Greece last Sunday, in the Nations League, marking the first time Greece had beaten Germany.
It is also reflective of plenty of utterances from MPs of the far-right Alternative für Deutschland (AfD), the largest opposition party in the Bundestag, who have repeatedly and consistently criticised the diversity and ethnic makeup of the national team, often referring to the squad in derogatory terms such as a “politically correct mercenary force”.

articles.title: Putin’s Valdai keynote: Russian president addresses renowned forum
articles.body:
Putin’s Valdai keynote: Russian president addresses renowned forum
Published 1 Oct, 2026 12:05 | Updated 1 Oct, 2026 14:49
Russian President Vladimir Putin is delivering his annual keynote to the Valdai discussion club international forum, outside Moscow.
Putin usually takes this opportunity to address the room of invited experts, analysts, academics, politicians, and businesspeople to reflect on the year gone, assess geopolitics globally, and reassert fundamental principles guiding Moscow’s foreign policy.
This year, we can expect some reflections on the emerging multipolar world, particularly in terms of strengthening ties with China and India, and the notable success of the ASEAN Summit in Kazan in June.
Putin’s speech will be followed by a Q&A session, where some of the world’s top Russia analysts and Russia-focused academics can put questions to the Russian president. Previously he has issued warnings about nuclear risks, told oligarch jokes, and “confessed” to being behind the phantom drone spectre that haunted Western Europe last year.
More seriously, Putin has used the Valdai speeches to consolidate and refine key points of Russian policy, from a warning to the West after his Munich Security Conference speech in 2007, through to a declaration of a new world order in 2014, to drawing explicit red lines in policy and conflict escalation thresholds in 2025.
Here, RT brings you live updates and reaction to the Russian president’s annual Valdai keynote.
- 01 October 2026 14:42 GMTPutin’s Valdai address comes a day after he outlined economic, social and security priorities at the opening session of Russia’s newly elected State Duma. He stressed that Russia has the resources to achieve its goals without outside assistance, saying, “we don’t need handouts.” He called for a balanced budget, full funding for social commitments and national projects, greater investment and fewer administrative barriers for businesses. Putin also urged lawmakers to strengthen defense, support troops and their families, and “do everything for our victory.” He further called for continued reconstruction of Russia’s four new regions, now represented in the State Duma for the first time, and said September’s elections demonstrated national unity in the face of “historic challenges.”
- 14:40 GMTPutin’s address comes at a time of significantly heightened rhetoric and self-defeating claims of “hybrid warfare” from an increasingly hysterical Western bloc. RT unpacked the claims around the “Fairford incident” at the weekend that saw UK deep state media go into overdrive.
- 14:39 GMTRussia is not considering using nuclear weapons and urges European officials to keep their emotions in check, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters ahead of the start of the Valdai meeting. “The president has repeatedly said that Russia is not threatening anyone in Europe in any way, because we simply have no problems with Europe,” he said. Asked how Moscow would respond to a NATO blockade of Kaliningrad Region, Peskov said Russia’s doctrine sets clear conditions for using different weapons, all aimed at protecting its territorial integrity and the state’s existence. If NATO is not planning action against Russia, the bloc has no reason to worry, he said.
- 14:32 GMTWhat is the Valdai Discussion Club? 
 For those who are unfamiliar with the Valdai Discussion Club, here’s a bit of background on why its annual forum is such a significant part of the calendar for anyone interested in Russia and its foreign policy direction:
 • The Valdai Discussion Club was set up in 2004 and takes its name from Lake Valdai near Veliky Novgorod – the site of the club’s first meeting.
 • Symbolizing the club’s importance, Russian President Vladimir Putin was among the officials to attend that first gathering more than 20 years ago. This year’s forum is the 23d annual Valdai gathering.
• In 2014, management of the club was taken over by the Valdai Club Foundation, under the auspices of Russian think tank the Council for Foreign and Defense Policy, the Russian International Affairs Council, Moscow State Institute of International Relations, and the Higher School of Economics.
- 13:58 GMTPutin’s address comes amid escalating rhetoric from European NATO members, particularly after Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski recently proposed to deploy additional troops near Russia’s Kaliningrad Region so that Moscow would be “uncertain of what we will do.” Putin has since ordered all relevant Russian agencies to take the necessary measures to ensure the security of the exclave, according to presidential aide Nikolay Patrushev.
- 13:43 GMTThe topic of this year’s Valdai forum is “Responsibility for the Future: Limits of the Possible or Unlimited Possibility?” Vladimir Putin’s speech is expected to draw parallels to his historic 2014 address about the collapse of the unipolar world and his 2025 Valdai speech about the rise of multipolarity and the need to shift to agreements based on mutual respect between countries.
- 12:39 GMTParticipants from 40 countries are attending this year’s Valdai forum, with about 60% of attendees coming from foreign states, including the UK, Germany, USA, France, Iran, India, China, Brazil, Türkiye, South Africa, Japan, and others.
- 12:18 GMTPutin’s upcoming speech at the Valdai plenary session is one of several annual addresses that is eagerly awaited by “the whole world,” Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov has said. He stated that Putin will begin his address after 4:00 PM Moscow time. After the event, the president is expected to meet with Russia’s chief rabbi, Berel Lazar, and the president of the Federation of Jewish Communities of Russia, Aleksandr Boroda.

articles.title: Russia strikes Ukrainian power pylon with steel-cutting drone for 1st time, Zelensky's adviser says
articles.body:
Russia strikes Ukrainian pylon with steel-cutting drone for 1st time, as power outages hit 3 regions
Russia has for the first time used a jet-powered drone equipped with a warhead designed to destroy high-voltage power pylons and steel bridge structures, presidential adviser Serhii "Flash" Beskrestnov said on Sept. 30.
The development comes as Moscow renews its large-scale campaign against Ukraine's energy system ahead of winter, launching its heaviest combined attack on energy infrastructure in months overnight on Sept. 30.
"Bad news. Today, the enemy for the first time used a special shaped-charge cutting warhead on a jet-powered unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV)," Beskrestnov, an adviser to President Volodymyr Zelensky on defense technologies, wrote on Telegram.
According to Beskrestnov, the warhead was developed specifically to destroy high-voltage pylons and steel bridge structures. It consists of a 40-kilogram main charge and four additional destructive modules.
"I think the enemy plans to attack important high-voltage power transmission lines," he said.
Russia's overnight assault involved nearly 190 attack drones as well as ballistic missiles, Zelensky said. Energy infrastructure in Kyiv and Kyiv Oblast was the primary target, while critical infrastructure was also struck in several other regions.
Ukraine's Air Force said that between 6:30 a.m. and 6:30 p.m. local time, Ukrainian air defenses intercepted 254 of 285 drones. Russian forces launched 174 jet-powered drones, 146 of which were intercepted by Ukrainian forces.
As of around 6:30 p.m., 10 drones remained in Ukrainian airspace, the Air Force said.
By the evening, emergency power outages had been introduced in the capital and surrounding region as well as in Chernihiv and Zhytomyr oblasts following repeated Russian attacks on energy infrastructure, according to the Energy Ministry.
Earlier in the morning, the ministry said some consumers in Kyiv and five oblasts had been left without electricity due to Russian strikes, although no nationwide restrictions were initially expected during the day.
The Sept. 30 attack marked a sharp escalation in Russia's renewed campaign against Ukraine's power system.
"Since the summer, there has been practically no day when the enemy has not attacked energy infrastructure. But such a massive and combined attack has occurred for the first time since the end of the last heating season," Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi said following the attack.
Ukraine's electricity system was already under strain before the renewed fall attacks.
During the summer, increased demand put additional pressure on the grid during hot weather, while Russian attacks periodically caused temporary outages in different regions. Ukrenergo, Ukraine's state-owned national power grid operator, repeatedly urged consumers to reduce electricity use during peak hours.
Last winter, repeated Russian strikes severely damaged power and heating infrastructure across Ukraine, leaving thousands of homes without heat and power for prolonged periods during freezing temperatures.
Officials have warned that the upcoming winter could be even harsher than the last one. Ukraine has yet to secure funding for its 5.4 billion euro ($6.2 billion) energy resilience plan, according to previous reporting.
The renewed attacks are also coinciding with the first cold spell of the season. Ukraine's State Emergency Service warned that overnight temperatures could fall to between 0 and 3 degrees Celsius (32-37 Fahrenheit) across Ukraine from Oct. 1-3.

articles.title: Trump Again Blames Ukraine for Rising US Diesel Prices, Dismissing Middle East War Impact
articles.body:
US President Donald Trump has again blamed Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries for rising diesel prices in the United States, arguing that the disruptions to Russia’s fuel production are a bigger factor than the war in the Middle East.
Speaking from the Oval Office on Wednesday, Sept. 30, Trump said a potential US ban on diesel exports could reduce domestic diesel prices, although he warned it would also have a negative impact on gasoline prices.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Trump said the war in Ukraine, including attacks by both sides that have disrupted energy production and exports, was the main factor behind rising diesel prices.
“It’s going to start to come in. You know, diesel is really hurt much more, not by the Middle East, but by what’s going on in Russia, because those diesel refineries are being knocked out at a pretty alarming rate,” he said.
“And if that didn’t happen, we wouldn’t have a diesel problem. What’s happened in Russia with Ukraine has been really the biggest problem for diesel,” Trump added.
US energy secretary points to broader disruptions
US Energy Secretary Chris Wright offered a broader explanation for the tightening diesel supply, pointing to disruptions in several major exporting regions.
“We’ve lost some diesel exports from the Middle East, although we’re restoring those, and we’ve lost diesel exports from China,” Wright said. “So that’s a lot of interruptions.”
ISW Russian Offensive Campaign Assessment, September 30, 2026
He added that the administration expected European countries to announce additional diesel supplies soon.
According to Reuters, gasoline prices in the US have risen by more than 40% over the past year, while diesel prices reached a record $6.53 per gallon a week ago, according to AAA data.
The price surge has been driven largely by a combination of tighter supplies linked to the war with Iran and refining disruptions, including those caused by Ukrainian attacks on Russian energy facilities, Reuters reported.
The issue also carries political significance in the US, where the Trump administration and Republican candidates face pressure to bring down fuel costs ahead of the November midterm elections, while Trump’s economic approval ratings remain under strain.
Ukraine’s refinery strikes
In mid-September, Trump called on his Ukrainian counterpart, Volodymyr Zelensky, to stop targeting Russia’s energy industry, arguing that Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries were driving up diesel prices in the US.
Trump said Ukraine’s long-range drone strikes against Russian refineries were the main reason global diesel prices had spiked and urged Zelensky to halt the attacks.
“Mr. Zelensky has to do one thing: He has to stop knocking out diesel fuel in Russia. Let him go after targets – but not diesel fuel, because he’s causing a shortage of diesel,” he said.
“This isn’t done by the Middle East. This is done by what’s happening with Russia and Ukraine... There are plenty of other targets. Don’t hit diesel fuel because that’s hurting the world,” Trump told a gaggle of Irish and international reporters.
Trump’s remarks came after a record month of Ukrainian strikes against Russia’s energy sector. In August 2026, Ukrainian drone forces hit 21 Russian oil refineries – a wartime record, according to data from Ukraine’s national long-range strike database, DeepStrike UA, and strike statistics published by the Ukrainian Unmanned Systems Forces (USF).
The targeted refineries were located in Omsk, Saratov, Syzran, Perm, Yaroslavl, Krasnodar, Samara, Tatarstan, Tyumen and Orsk. Strikes hit some facilities repeatedly, while others – including refineries in Omsk, Perm and Tyumen – were targeted for the first time during the war, according to Kyiv Post records.
The August figure was 50% higher than July’s 14 refinery strikes and twice the monthly strike pace recorded by USF units in October 2025, when seven refineries were hit.
Trump’s criticism echoed earlier remarks by US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who in early September blamed Ukrainian drone strikes on Russia for a global “energy shock” that he said was driving up energy costs.
However, energy industry analysts have pointed to other factors as the main drivers of the global surge in crude and refined-fuel prices. A US-Israeli war with Iran has brought tanker exports through the Strait of Hormuz close to a halt, while worsening Red Sea disruptions following the Houthi capture of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait have further constrained tanker traffic.
Russian President Vladimir Putin has also downplayed the impact of Ukraine’s strikes on Russia’s energy infrastructure. In comments aired by Russian state-controlled media on Aug. 22, he said the attacks had failed to produce the battlefield effect Kyiv intended.
“How effective are they – are they effective at all? And do they have any impact on the situation along the line of contact as a whole? The ultimate result for the adversary turned out to be the exact opposite of what was expected. No turning point occurred,” Putin said.
At the same time, Ukraine’s strikes have significantly disrupted Russia’s fuel production. A Bloomberg estimate published on Aug. 28 and widely cited by Ukrainian media said the attacks had reduced Russia’s production of gasoline, aviation fuel, diesel and other petroleum products by more than 30%.
Russian industry analysts have similarly estimated that fuel-processing capacity has fallen by roughly one-third, saying that restoring the damaged capacity could prove difficult as Russian air defenses struggle to intercept Ukrainian drones.

articles.title: Ukraine’s air-raid sirens can sound for 10 hours a day. Its economy minister says every hour costs $45 million.
articles.body:
Ukraine’s air-raid sirens can sound for 10 hours a day. Its economy minister says every hour costs $45 million.
Air raid alerts warning of Russian attacks cost Ukraine about $45 million an hour, Ukrainian Economy and Environment Minister Oleksandr Kravchenko estimated in an interview with The Guardian. He said Ukraine sometimes spends up to 10 hours a day under alerts, which regularly force most businesses in the country to suspend operations while employees take shelter.
To reduce the economic damage, Ukraine’s government introduced a new two-tier alert system: a “red” alert signals the threat of a missile strike and requires people to take shelter, while a “yellow” alert signals a drone threat and allows businesses to keep operating.
More than half of businesses keep operating during “yellow” alerts, Kravchenko said, although the danger remains. On the afternoon of September 28, during a “yellow” alert, a Russian drone struck a building in central Kyiv belonging to Ukraine’s National Academy of Sciences. Two people were killed.
The Kremlin intends to paralyze Kyiv before winter, The Economist reported. Several senior Ukrainian officials told the publication that Vladimir Putin had ordered strikes on civilian sites. One of the officials said, “They want people to be afraid of going to the supermarket.”
Russia did step up its attacks on civilian infrastructure in August and September. Kravchenko sees this as an attempt to “destroy pretty much the entire economy” of Ukraine. He estimated that attacks on factories, warehouses, data centers, and other sites have caused about $10 billion in damage since the start of the year. These losses are putting increasing pressure on the budget.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky recently estimated the shortfall in the 2026 budget at about $27 billion. The figure raised concerns among EU leaders. Kravchenko said spending cuts had reduced the deficit to $20 billion. But Kyiv will need $52.6 billion in external financing next year. Less than half of that amount has been secured so far, and the authorities are discussing further spending cuts and tax increases.
But Kravchenko does not attribute the deficit to mismanagement, corruption, or excessive spending under former Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov. “The cost of war is simply increasing,” he said.
Ukraine now needs to strengthen its air defenses and speed up development of drones capable of intercepting Russia’s new jet-powered drones, Kravchenko said. He said Ukraine is better prepared this year for what could be the hardest winter of the war.
The war in photographs: Kyiv and Vyshhorod
Overnight on September 30, Russia attacked Kyiv and the Kyiv region with drones and various types of missiles. Two people were killed in the capital, and four others were injured. In Vyshhorod, in the Kyiv region, a child was killed, and three people were rescued from the rubble of a destroyed house.
At Meduza, we are committed to transparency about our use of artificial intelligence in the newsroom. The story you’re reading was written by one of our living, breathing journalists and translated from Russian using an AI model configured to follow our strict editorial standards. This translation process is the result of extensive testing and refinements to ensure our English-language coverage is timely and accurate. A Meduza editor reviews every draft before publication.

articles.title: Ukraine persists with Russian oil refinery strikes in defiance of Trump
articles.body:
Ukraine is pressing on with strikes on Russian oil refineries, defying Donald Trump, who blames the attacks for exacerbating a global diesel shortage and pushing up fuel prices.
Kyiv struck an oil facility in Russia’s southern Samara region overnight, Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Thursday in a statement on social media. The Ukrainian president added that a Russian vessel in the Black Sea was hit, as well as a launch and storage site for attack drones in the Oryol region.
Trump has urged Zelenskyy in a private phone call to halt attacks on Russian refineries and repeatedly suggested in public that Ukraine’s strikes are to blame for the squeeze on global fuel supplies. “Diesel is really hurt much more, not by the Middle East, but by what’s going on in Russia, because those diesel refineries are being knocked out at a pretty alarming rate,” Trump said on Wednesday.
Diesel prices in the US have risen to record highs in recent weeks, adding to cost of living pressures that have helped push Trump’s approval ratings to a career low before next month’s crucial midterm elections.
Energy analysts, however, have pointed to the war in Iran and wider disruption to global oil markets as the leading drivers of the price increases.
Ukraine’s long-range strikes on Russian refineries have nevertheless emerged as an additional headache for Trump, with the attacks also contributing to tighter diesel supplies at a politically sensitive moment for the US president.
Ukraine’s campaign in recent months has knocked out more than 45% of Russia’s refining capacity, according to Ukrainian estimates, prompting fuel rationing in some regions and long queues at petrol stations.
Earlier this week, Russia – traditionally the world’s second-largest diesel exporter – extended its ban on diesel exports until the end of October, adding further pressure to a global supply crunch.
Mykola Bielieskov, a military analyst at Ukraine’s government-run National Institute for Strategic Studies, said it was unlikely Kyiv would stop targeting Russian oil infrastructure as long as Moscow continued its daily attacks on Ukraine. “There is no rationale for Ukraine to continue exercising restraint while it is being bombarded and major urban areas are under constant attack,” he said.
“We need to deprive Russia of revenue,” he added.
Zelenskyy has been pushing for a US-brokered energy ceasefire with Russia, but Putin has shown little interest in the proposal, instead vowing to intensify strikes on Ukraine.
Meanwhile, Russia has continued its deadly missile and drone strikes on Ukrainian cities, targeting energy infrastructure, commercial warehouses and other businesses in an apparent effort to cripple the country’s economy and render Kyiv increasingly uninhabitable.
A Russian drone struck a school in Kyiv on Thursday morning, but no one was injured because the children were sheltering in the basement, mayor Vitali Klitschko said.
A key bridge in the Ukrainian capital was also hit, forcing authorities to suspend metro services and other public transport.
Kyiv has experienced near round-the-clock Russian attacks in recent weeks, at times increasingly resembling a frontline city in what many see as the most challenging period for the capital since the early days of the full-scale invasion.
Russia’s newer jet-powered drones have proved particularly difficult for Ukrainian air defences to intercept, with success rates significantly lower than for the slower Shahed-type drones.
The sustained attacks have revived fears of another winter with prolonged power and heating outages, after similar strikes last year left parts of Ukraine without electricity during temperatures that fell as low as -20C.

articles.title: Ukraine war briefing: Russia pounds power grid with seven killed in biggest energy attack in months
articles.body:
- 
  Russia has unleashed a widely anticipated air campaign against Ukraine’s energy grid, hitting power facilities and infrastructure around Kyiv and other regions in the heaviest combined attack on energy sites in months. The strikes on Wednesday, in which Ukrainian officials said seven people were killed, came after days of intensifying drone barrages primarily on the capital, a prelude to what many Ukrainians expect to be a winter of attacks intended to plunge cities into cold and darkness while Ukraine is short of air defences. State power grid operator Ukrenergo said it had imposed emergency power cuts as a result of the attack in Kyiv and three surrounding regions – the first time such a measure had been imposed in the capital since the spring.
- 
  “Russia has escalated to massive strikes on energy infrastructure,” the prime minister, Sergii Koretskyi, said on X after the overnight attacks. A child was among the seven dead across Ukraine, Volodymyr Zelenskyy said, with critical infrastructure coming under attack in five regions. Further damage was reported in another five regions, the Ukrainian president added. Forecasters say they expect freezing temperatures at night in Kyiv in coming days.
- 
  Zelenskyy visited a military command post near the town of Lyman near the eastern frontline and praised what he said were gains against Russian forces during a counteroffensive. Ukrainian forces had recaptured 176 sq km (29.3 sq miles) of territory since the start of the operation, he said. “A serious operation, important in many ways for our defence overall and in Donbas in particular,” Zelenskyy wrote, referring to eastern Ukraine’s Donbas region, which Russia aims to capture in its entirety. Zelenskyy said the operation had prevented Russian forces from breaking through the rear of defensive lines around Sloviansk and Kramatorsk, part of the network of “fortress cities” Ukrainian forces are defending.
- 
  Ukraine is urging the US to impose sanctions on several Russian entities it says are helping develop Moscow’s Rassvet satellite network as a domestic alternative to SpaceX’s Starlink, its acting ambassador said. Denys Sienik, deputy chief of mission at the Ukrainian embassy in Washington, said Russia was rapidly expanding the Rassvet satellite network and that its goal to start operations in 2027 would pose grave risks to Ukraine. Kyiv planned to issue its own national sanctions against the entities linked to the network, Sienik said, adding: “If these entities are not sanctioned, it will actually make this program possible for Russia and that will be a gamechanger.”
- 
  Papal envoy Cardinal Matteo Zuppi discussed humanitarian issues in the Ukraine war in talks with Russian officials and visited Ukrainian prisoners of war, Russia’s foreign ministry said. Zuppi’s three days of talks coincided with an appeal by Pope Leo to Russia and Ukraine to sit down and discuss how to end the four-and-a-half-year war. The pontiff also decried national leaders who he said were “beginning to speak about nuclear weapons and wars that are becoming ever more destructive”. The foreign ministry said on Wednesday that Zuppi also discussed conditions in the Russian-occupied town of Oleshky in Ukraine’s Kherson region, where Ukrainian officials said Kyiv’s military used drones last weekend to deliver food and medicine to civilians.

articles.title: Zelensky discusses strengthening air defense with Stubb
articles.body:
Zelensky discusses strengthening air defense with Stubb
The Ukrainian president reported this on Facebook, according to Ukrinform.
"Alex and I discussed what can make the biggest difference to our defenses, strengthen our F-16s, and bolster our air defense overall. Thank you for being ready to help!" Zelensky wrote.
He said he had briefed the Finnish president in detail on the situation following Russia's strikes and the latest escalation of attacks against Ukrainian cities and communities.
In particular, Zelensky said that air-raid alerts had continued for almost the entire day, beginning overnight, in Kyiv and other Ukrainian cities and regions, with a constant threat from jet-powered Shahed drones. Ballistic missile strikes were also reported overnight.
As previously reported, Zelensky said the day before that Belgium would provide Ukraine with three F-16 fighter jets and ammunition for them by the end of the year.
The president also said today that Ukraine had received new packages of air-defense support in recent days.
