articles.title: Air Force Names 7 to Vie for New MMA Drone Program
articles.body:
The Air Force and the Pentagon’s Defense Innovation Unit have narrowed the field to seven companies which will be invited to compete to develop low-cost, semi-autonomous drones to succeed the MQ-9A Reaper, multiple sources confirmed to Air & Space Forces Magazine.
Anduril, Chaos Industries, General Atomics Aeronautical Systems, Grid Aero, Otto Aerospace, Shield AI, and Swarm Aero all made the cut to continue to develop their candidates for the Massed Modular Aircraft. The companies got the word Sept. 30.
The Air Force and DIU did not immediately respond to queries. Spokespeople from each of the companies either declined to comment or did not respond to queries. It is unclear how many companies submitted proposals, and therefore how many firms were cut from the competition.
An industry source said each company will now submit a proposal to build a prototype MMA.
The Air Force wants to field 500 MMAs by 2032, Air Force Secretary Troy Meink said Sept. 14 at AFA’s Air, Space & Cyber Conference.
DIU—an acquisition office created to tap into commercial and non-traditional suppliers—sought on July 7 proposals for cheap, attritable drones that could take on the MQ-9’s trademark missions of persistent intelligence, surveillance, reconnaissance and strike. The Air Force soon confirmed it was working with DIU on the concept.
The solicitation followed the loss of dozens of MQ-9s in operations against Iran earlier this year. DIU said at the time that the military’s reliance on “exquisite” aircraft that cost $30 million or more per tail has become “unsustainable against adversaries utilizing layered defenses enabled by increasingly low-cost antiaircraft capabilities.”
The MQ-9As that were lost did not cost that much, but General Atomics no longer makes that model and instead is offering a larger MQ-9B that can approach or exceed the $30 million level, depending on how it is equipped.
MMA is aiming for a lower price point. DIU’s solicitation sought drones that could fly together in groups large enough to overwhelm an enemy, even if several were shot down, while also forcing the enemy to expend precious anti-aircraft munitions. The Air Force must be able to affordably replace aircraft lost without busting the budget.
Air Force leaders said in a Sept. 3 briefing that they expect to pay about $10 million per MMA airframe, plus whatever sensors or other capabilities are added to it. During that briefing, Lt. Gen. Christopher Niemi, the Air Force’s new chief modernization officer, said Secretary Meink pushed to accelerate the MMA fielding schedule in the wake of the Iran losses. Maj. Gen. Joseph Kunkel, DIU’s military deputy, told reporters that the Pentagon wants to see a prototype within a year of issuing a contract, and field it at scale as soon as 2029.
Responding to the summer solicitation, industry rapidly moved to pitch their concepts. General Atomics pitched a new drone called Wildfire that could carry at least two Long Range Anti-Ship Missiles, four Joint Strike Missiles, or a similar combination of heavy stand-off weapons.
Swarm Aero, a California startup, proposed a new Group 5 drone dubbed Gamera, and displayed a full-scale model at the Air, Space & Cyber conference.

articles.title: Kremlin says states hosting nuclear weapons near Russian borders fuel escalation
articles.body:
Elena Teslova
01 October 2026•Update: 01 October 2026
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov warned on Thursday that countries deploying nuclear weapons near Russia's borders are adding fuel to escalation and tension.
Speaking at a press briefing in Moscow, Peskov said states agreeing to deploy nuclear weapons near Russia’s borders are deeply mistaken if they believe this will enhance their security.
"Those countries that reassure themselves by saying, ‘Let’s install and deploy nuclear weapons near the Russian borders,’ are deeply mistaken. This will not bring them any security, on the contrary, it will further lead to escalation and increased tensions,” he said.
Commenting on Putin’s recent letter to NATO warning of consequences from a blockade of Russia’s Kaliningrad region, Peskov said the message should not be viewed as confrontational.
"The letter and its publication should not be perceived as a confrontational statement," he said, drawing a parallel with Putin’s 2007 speech at the Munich Security Conference, which he said had also been widely perceived in the West as "confrontational."
Peskov said Kaliningrad is an integral part of Russia, and Moscow would ensure the security of the region in accordance with Russian law.
The official noted that Putin's warning came amid rapid militarization across Europe and the involvement of most European countries in the Ukraine conflict through arms and ammunition supplies and the provision of military instructors.
"If you take part in a war on someone’s side, you cannot avoid consequences of various kinds," he said.
Peskov said neither Ukraine nor Europe had moved closer to negotiations, adding that European countries continue to hinder the resumption of the negotiating process.
At the same time, he welcomed recent remarks by Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev on the need to use every opportunity for dialogue with Russia.
"Such a manifestation of political will for dialogue is undoubtedly a very positive phenomenon, we note and register it," he said, adding that such calls had so far not translated into practical steps or changed Europe’s anti-Russian and confrontational policy.
Peskov said European countries were developing their own security arrangements after concluding that NATO, led by the US, could no longer guarantee their security.
The official noted that Europe was building those arrangements on the same model as NATO.
"NATO was created in its genesis as a confrontational mechanism, it is not a mechanism aimed at ensuring security," he said.
Turning to contacts between Russia and US representatives, Pesko said they are continuing, with envoy Kirill Dmitriev discussing economic issues and the possibility of launching major projects in various sectors with his American counterparts.
"Indeed, implementing economic projects in various areas, including major ones, would be highly beneficial for both Russia and America," he said.
He said Washington continues to link such cooperation to a settlement in Ukraine.
Russia, meanwhile, believes economic projects could begin without waiting for a settlement, but dialogue with US representatives remains ongoing, he said.
"Americans, unfortunately, still link this entire process with the settlement in Ukraine, saying -- first the settlement, then the implementation of projects," he said. "We believe we could work for our mutual benefit right now and not wait, but contacts and dialogue are continuing, and this is quite a lengthy process."
Asked whether Russian citizens were aboard a Flydubai flight that made an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia on Wednesday while traveling from Dubai to Tel Aviv, Peskov urged journalists to await information from the special services investigating the incident.
"The event happened only yesterday, and an investigation is now underway. We should show a little patience, and we will receive the information that the investigation considers possible to publish," he said.

articles.title: Ukraine’s intelligence reveals data on 23 Russian companies producing Pantsir missiles
articles.body:
Ukraine’s intelligence reveals data on 23 Russian companies producing Pantsir missiles
Ukrinform reports this, citing HUR’s post on Facebook.
The data have been published on the War&Sanctions portal.
“Pantsir” is a family of Russian self-propelled short-range anti-aircraft gun-and-missile systems designed to provide air defense for important areas and individual military and industrial facilities.
Russia also uses these systems to strengthen air defense at low and extremely low altitudes and to protect against mass attacks involving air-launched weapons. Since 2023, the Russians have been installing Pantsir systems on rooftops in Moscow. This year, another modification of the system, the Pantsir-SMD-E, was spotted there. Unlike earlier variants, it uses smaller TKB-1055 Gvozd missiles instead of automatic cannons.
Previously, the HUR published information on more than 50 companies involved in producing the 72V6 combat vehicle used in the Pantsir-S1 anti-aircraft gun-and-missile system.
Now, data on another 23 companies involved in producing 95Ya6 missiles have been disclosed. The 95Ya6 is the main medium-range missile used by various Pantsir modifications.
A key role in developing these missiles is played by the Academician Shipunov Instrument Design Bureau, the main developer and manufacturer of 95Ya6 missiles. The company is already known for its involvement in producing weapons for the Orion unmanned systems, Krasnopol guided projectiles and cannons for Su-family fighter aircraft.
At the same time, about one-third of the companies whose information was published today are not under sanctions imposed by any country in the sanctions coalition.
They include:
Komponent plant – a manufacturer of proximity target sensors for 95Ya6 missiles;
Sergo Ordzhonikidze Saratov Electrotechnical Plant – manufactures and supplies emission and power-supply units for these missiles;
Tambov Elektropribor plant – a manufacturer of steering units for 95Ya6 missiles.
The HUR emphasizes that, to effectively weaken Russia’s military potential, it is important to coordinate restrictions against companies involved in the production of the full range of Russian weapons, rather than offensive systems alone.
Air defense capabilities, including Pantsir systems, protect Russian enterprises that manufacture cruise and ballistic missiles, as well as Russian troop formations during offensive and defensive operations in Ukraine and other important facilities in Russia.
As previously reported by Ukrinform, the HUR has released data on 14 banks, financial intermediaries and payment systems that enable Russia to conduct international transactions while circumventing sanctions restrictions.
Photo credit: Main Intelligence Directorate

articles.title: Bulgarian PM Warns Putin Holds a ‘Nuclear Trump Card’
articles.body:
Both the NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte and Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev, spoke at Wednesday’s Euronews’ Defence and Space Summit 2026 held in Brussels, but the two speakers could not agree on how best to deal with the threat from Russia.
Responding to a secret Kremlin diplomatic note reportedly threatening nuclear strikes if NATO took what Moscow called “aggressive” action against its Kaliningrad exclave, Rutte condemned the rhetoric, urged Russia to stop issuing nuclear threats, and called for an end to its illegal war against Ukraine.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
According to Reuters on Wednesday, Moscow accused the alliance of pursuing a “dangerous and reckless course” that carries a “high risk of a direct armed conflict,” warning that Russia would immediately strike “decision-making centers in alliance member countries.” Similar threats were echoed in statements by Russian embassies and across official social media channels throughout the week.
In his address, Rutte said Russia does not currently pose a direct threat to the alliance. However, he stressed that if a military conflict were to occur, NATO’s combined military strength exceeds Russia’s, leaving Moscow with no realistic prospect of defeating the alliance.
Rutte added that he does not take Russia’s nuclear threats seriously.
Bulgaria’s dissenting voice
On the contrary, Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev said he took Russia’s nuclear threats seriously and urged European leaders to pursue a more diplomatic approach toward Moscow to avoid what he described as a potential “the worst-case scenario.”
Russian Radicals Baptize Moon to ‘Make it Orthodox’
He warned that President Vladimir Putin still holds a “nuclear trump card” and could be tempted to use it if he feels weakened or cornered.
“We must always consider the worst-case scenario. Are we prepared for it? Is anyone even talking about risk assessment? After all, we are trying to achieve a conventional victory over the world’s largest nuclear power,” Radev said.
He also expressed the view that diplomacy was the only way to both prevent a nuclear conflict but also to end the war in Ukraine.
In June, Radev announced that Bulgaria would no longer participate in NATO’s continuing provision of financial and military aid to Ukraine.
The European position
Speaking at the same summit, European Commissioner for Defense Andrius Kubilius, dismissed calls for renewed engagement with Moscow, arguing the past attempts at diplomacy with Russia had consistently failed to change the Kremlin’s behaviour.
In relation to the war in Ukraine, he said: “Russians are standing with their position very clear: Ukraine needs to surrender – that is their diplomatic position.”
Kubilius also called for a tougher European response to the growing number of hybrid attacks orchestrated by Moscow as part of Putin’s efforts to win “the hearts and the minds” of Europeans.
He said that it was time to reject those who call for diplomatic engagement with the Kremlin and ensure Russia feels the pain of a concerned European response to ongoing hybrid attacks.

articles.title: Ukraine spots “whiskered” Shahed aimed at power lines
articles.body:
- Ukrainian volunteer Serhii Sternenko published video of a jet-powered Shahed fitted with whisker-like contacts, likely to detonate on power lines.
- Presidential adviser Serhii Beskrestnov said Russia appears to have used a jet drone carrying a 40-kg cutting warhead built for pylons and bridges.
A previously unseen version of Russia’s jet-powered Shahed attack drone has appeared in Ukraine fitted with whisker-like rods on its nose, a modification that Ukrainian volunteer Serhii Sternenko says is designed to detonate the warhead on contact with high-voltage power lines.
Sternenko, a Ukrainian volunteer and activist who runs one of the country’s largest drone fundraising efforts, published video of the drone on X, saying the “whiskers” are most likely there to close an electrical contact and set off the charge when the drone strikes something as thin as a power cable. A similar modification has been seen at another location, though Sternenko did not say where either drone was found or whether it was intact.
“And this is a whiskered Shahed with a specialized warhead for attacks on high-voltage power lines. Most likely the whiskers were added to close a contact and initiate the warhead when hitting small targets such as power lines,” Sternenko wrote.
A standard impact fuse needs a solid surface to trigger, so a drone that clips a cable or the open lattice of a transmission tower may fly through or fall without exploding. Rods sticking out ahead of the airframe would let the drone detonate as soon as they touch a wire.
A second development points in the same direction. Serhii Beskrestnov, known as “Flash,” a specialist in drones and electronic warfare who serves as President Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s adviser on defense technology, said Russia appeared to use a special warhead on a jet-powered drone for the first time on Sept. 30. He identified it as a shaped-charge cutting payload, known by its Russian initials KRSN, designed specifically to destroy high-voltage transmission towers and steel bridge structures.
According to Beskrestnov, the KRSN consists of a 40-kg (88-pound) main charge and four additional strike modules. A cutting charge focuses its blast along a line to slice through metal, which makes it suited to severing the legs of a steel pylon or the girders of a bridge rather than causing broad blast damage. Beskrestnov did not say where the drone carrying it struck or what damage it caused.
Russia has attacked Ukraine’s power system throughout the war, mainly with missiles and Iranian-designed Shahed drones aimed at power plants and substations. Ukraine’s long transmission lines, which run across open country and are hard to defend, have been less frequent targets because individual towers and cables are small and difficult for a drone to hit and destroy. The jet-powered Shahed variants, which fly much faster than the original propeller-driven model, also give Ukrainian air defenses less time to react.

articles.title: Russia launches major attack on Ukraine’s energy grid, causing power cuts
articles.body:
Russia launches major attack on Ukraine’s energy grid, causing power cuts
Russia launched its heaviest combined assault on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure in months on Wednesday, killing seven people and triggering emergency power cuts in Kyiv and nearby regions. The strikes came as officials warned of a difficult winter amid Russian attacks on Ukraine’s power and heating infrastructure.
Russia unleashed a widely anticipated air campaign against Ukraine's energy grid on Wednesday, hitting power facilities and infrastructure around Kyiv and other regions in the heaviest combined attack on energy sites in months.
The strikes, in which Ukrainian officials said seven people were killed, followed days of intensifying drone barrages primarily on the capital, a prelude to what many Ukrainians expect to be a winter of attacks intended to plunge cities into cold and darkness when Ukraine is short of air defences.
Ukraine's state power grid operator Ukrenergo said it had imposed emergency power cuts as a result of the attack in Kyiv and three surrounding regions – the first time such a measure had been imposed in the capital since the spring.
Russian attacks last winter, which brought record-low temperatures, ravaged power and heating systems, forcing Ukrainians to adapt to dire circumstances.
Read moreUkraine’s grid operator orders emergency power cuts in Kyiv after Russian strikes
Capital shrouded in smoke
Some of the capital's trams and trolley buses ground to a halt due to the outages as people headed home from work. Kyiv's water utility said pressure in the water system was reduced.
"Russia has escalated to massive strikes on energy infrastructure," Prime Minister Sergii Koretskyi said on X after the attacks overnight.
"Since summer, there's barely been a day without an attack on our energy infrastructure. But a combined strike of this scale hasn't happened since the end of last heating season."
Kyiv residents awoke on Wednesday to a city shrouded in fog from the smoke of attacks, which authorities said damaged a key power plant and other energy facilities around the capital.
Ukraine's air force said its air defences had intercepted 254 of 285 Russian drones deployed until early evening.
It said 174 drones were high-flying and faster jet-propelled models, which are harder to intercept. Russian forces had also launched a ballistic missile attack.
Read moreRussian attacks kill eight in Ukraine after Moscow vows to continue war
A child was among the seven dead across Ukraine, President Volodymyr Zelensky said, with critical infrastructure coming under attack in five regions. Further damage was reported in another five regions, he added.
Zelensky visited a military command post near the town of Lyman near the eastern frontline and praised what he said were gains against Russian forces during a counteroffensive.
He said Ukrainian forces had recaptured 176 sq. km. (29.3 sq. miles) of territory since the start of the operation.
Russia said its forces had struck power plants in the Kyiv region, an industrial complex in Odesa region, and port infrastructure in Ismail in the southwest.
Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said debris had been found at a Western embassy, but offered no further details. The overnight attack triggered a more than 12-hour air-raid alert.
Drone strikes continued in Kyiv into the early evening.
Near-constant daytime sirens and explosions have become a fixture of daily life in Kyiv, where drone attacks have killed around a dozen people over the past week alone.

PM orders power backup checks
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha described Wednesday's attack by Russia as a "deliberate" distraction from its grinding battlefield offensive in eastern Ukraine, which has slowed since last year.
"Moscow is increasing the pressure on Ukrainian civilians as winter approaches, trying once again to turn cold, darkness, and disruption of normal life into weapons," he said on X.
Forecasters say they expect freezing temperatures at night in Kyiv in the coming days.
Russia, which began its full-scale invasion in February 2022, denies targeting civilians although it has pounded cities and towns across Ukraine.
Koretskyi, the prime minister, said he had instructed local authorities to check the readiness of backup power systems at critical facilities and speed up installations.
Authorities in recent weeks and months have been building protective facilities and aiming to diversify energy generation before Russia's expected winter campaign.
However, Ukrainian human rights ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets said there was a critical shortage of urban shelters, describing the civil-defence system as having "completely failed".

Drones cross into Moldova
In Moldova, on Ukraine's western border, the defence ministry said three drones had crossed into its airspace over the course of the day.
NATO members Romania and Poland both scrambled military jets, the countries said, and flights at the Polish airports of Lublin and Rzeszow were suspended for a time.
Ukraine has also stepped up attacks on Russia, striking oil refineries and online retailers to undermine its war effort.
(FRANCE 24 with Reuters)

articles.title: The Prime Minister of Bulgaria called on the EU to engage more actively in dialogue with russia and criticized arms supplies to Kyiv
articles.body:
The Prime Minister of Bulgaria called on the EU to engage more actively in dialogue with russia and criticized arms supplies to Kyiv
Kyiv • UNN
Rumen Radev called on the EU to intensify diplomatic dialogue with russia in order to end the war and reduce the nuclear risk. He criticized arms supplies to Ukraine.
The European Union should become more actively involved in diplomatic dialogue with Russia in order to end the war in Ukraine and prevent a devastating nuclear strike. This was stated by Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev, reports UNN, citing Euronews.
Details
He also criticized the continued supply of weapons and ammunition to Ukraine, calling it an unsuccessful strategy of "peace through strength."
There is a limit to simply transferring weapons and providing support, because the ultimate architecture of the world will be shaped by diplomacy, not by arms supplies. Therefore, we call for listening to one another more closely and opening channels of communication. The problem is that no one is raising the issue of the nuclear risk. Does it exist? Perhaps not, I do not know, but it is a risk
He recalled a statement by Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov, who said that a war between Russia and Europe would be "quite different" and "very short." Radev criticized "this manner of speaking" by the Kremlin, but called on European leaders to consider what further escalation could lead to.
"There is a nuclear trump card. We must take this into account. We cannot turn a blind eye to the fact that there are nuclear weapons on our continent and that nuclear warheads are held in Russia's arsenal. And this is part of the calculation in this game," the Bulgarian prime minister concluded.
We remind you
In September, another ammunition depot exploded in Bulgaria; previously, facilities belonging to this company had been linked to attacks by Russian agents.

articles.title: Russia threatens NATO with a nuclear strike if the alliance tries to blockade Kaliningrad
articles.body:
Russia threatens NATO with a nuclear strike if the alliance tries to blockade Kaliningrad
Russia’s embassy in Ireland posted a nuclear warning on social media, citing unspecified “reports coming in” about NATO preparations for an air and naval blockade of the Kaliningrad region:
There should be no mistake – Russia would be ready to use all its arsenal, including nuclear weapons, to defend its territory if NATO countries try to isolate [the] Kaliningrad region from the rest of the country.
Russia “has no plans to escalate tensions with Europe,” the embassy said, while “Europe’s irresponsible and shortsighted political elite is playing a dangerous game.”
The same warning appears in a document Russia sent to NATO and Reuters obtained. In it, Moscow accuses the alliance of pursuing a “dangerous and reckless course” that carries “a high risk of direct armed conflict.”
In its written response, NATO said none of the alliance’s exercises or activities threaten Russian territory. “We urge the Russian Federation to refrain from increasingly reckless behavior towards the Allies and to cease its irresponsible nuclear rhetoric,” it said, according to Reuters.
The embassy’s post responded to statements by European politicians about an increase in Russian hybrid attacks against Ukraine’s allies.
At Meduza, we are committed to transparency about our use of artificial intelligence in the newsroom. The story you’re reading was written by one of our living, breathing journalists and translated from Russian using an AI model configured to follow our strict editorial standards. This translation process is the result of extensive testing and refinements to ensure our English-language coverage is timely and accurate. A Meduza editor reviews every draft before publication.
If you find any errors in this translation, please contact us at [email protected].

articles.title: Russian intelligence says Ukraine's corruption prevents peace settlement between Moscow and Kyiv
articles.body:
Elena Teslova
01 October 2026•Update: 01 October 2026
Corruption of the new leadership of Ukraine’s Security Service (SBU) is preventing Moscow and Kyiv from achieving a peace settlement, Russia's Foreign Intelligence Service (SVR) said on Thursday.
The SVR said in a statement that the SBU was behind corruption schemes to siphon off European taxpayers’ money.
"The new SBU leadership has organized another scheme to steal European taxpayers’ money through the supply of pistols from EU countries for the agency’s needs," it said in a statement.
According to information received by the SVR, the scheme involves purchasing weapons through intermediaries in Eastern Europe, tripling the price of each pistol from €250 to €750.
The intelligence agency identified a Polish company, Wytwornia Broni Jacek Popinski, as a key intermediary, alleging that it buys pistols, including from the Panamanian branch of Austrian arms manufacturer Glock, and resells them to Ukraine.
"For each batch of 5,000 pistols, €625,000 is transferred to the accounts of individuals trusted by the SBU leadership," the SVR said, adding that the purchases are funded by the defense ministries of Belgium and Germany.
The SVR noted that similar corruption could be taking place in the procurement of more expensive weapons, particularly scarce ammunition for air defense systems.
It linked its claims to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s recent statement that an unplanned $27 billion gap had emerged in Ukraine’s military budget, saying that European taxpayers would ultimately bear the cost.
"This information answers the question of why the gauleiter of Ukraine (Zelenskyy) and his entourage so stubbornly refuse to move toward a peaceful resolution of the conflict. Driven mad by easy money, they simply cannot stop and continue lining their pockets from a war that is disastrous for Ukrainians," the agency said.

articles.title: Focus on Saada: Yemen's Houthis amass forces near Saudi border
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Saada becomes focus of Yemen war as Houthis amass forces near Saudi border
Attention is turning to Saada province, the Houthi stronghold in northernmost Yemen, as the group steps up its military mobilisation and moves weapons and equipment to areas bordering Saudi Arabia.
These movements, confirmed by military and local sources to The New Arab, put the possibility a border confrontation, particularly as the group increases its threats against Saudi Arabia.
Saada has featured prominently in recent military statements by Majed Al-Nazili, spokesman for the armed forces affiliated with the internationally recognised government.
He included the Kataf and Al-Buqaa front and the Alab axis among the operations. These are important fronts because of their location along the Saudi border. Kataf and Al-Buqaa districts, the largest district in Saada by area, stretch along the Najran region and contain the Al-Buqaa border crossing. The Alab axis is located in Baqim district on the border north of Saada and is one of the advanced border fronts.
Meanwhile, Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree referred to Saudi strikes on Saada, while government military sources said the group was preparing to seek a breakthrough across the border.
A government military source familiar with the situation told The New Arab that the Houthis "are preparing for a confrontation on the border" with Saudi Arabia and are heavily mobilising for it, adding: "A border war is coming; it is only a matter of time."
The source said the group is seeking to launch an attack that would allow it to make an incursion into Saudi territory.
The source's account corresponds with information from other military and local sources in Saada, who told TNA that the Houthis have stepped up the moving fighters, weapons and equipment to border areas in recent days.
According to the government source, these transfers go beyond reinforcing the group's defensive positions and amount to preparations for an offensive, at a time when its forces and positions are being targeted on several fronts.
In this context, posts on Al Masirah, the Houthi's affiliated channel, two days ago included reports of strikes on the districts of Sahar, Al-Safra, Al-Dhahir and Majz, alongside rocket fire on Sahar.
The channel had reported the previous day that two strikes hit Al-Dhahir and that four rockets targeted eastern Saada city.
These areas are spread between the border strip, the vicinity of Saada provincial centre and routes connecting to the border—Al-Dhahir lies on the Saudi border, Al-Safra extends north to the border with Najran, Sahar surrounds Saada city and includes its outskirts, and Majz is connected to the road leading to Baqim and the Alab border crossing.
This distribution gives the strikes significance beyond pressure on the front lines, extending to pressure on the group's positions deep inside the province and areas connecting them to the border, and could disrupt the movement of reinforcements and supplies.
Saada, as the focus
Al-Nazili announced for the first time since the start of the latest escalation that Saada fronts were included in the operations.
In a statement posted on his account on X on 27 September, he said the forces had carried out 756 targeting operations during the previous 72 hours, covering Kataf and Al-Buqaa and the Alab axis, alongside the fronts in Al-Jawf, Marib, Al-Bayda and Lahj and Taiz, using air forces, drones, snipers, field artillery and rocket launchers.
Al-Nazili reiterated in a statement on 28 September that Saada fronts were included in the operations, announcing 356 operations during the previous 24 hours, and also included the coast, Haradh and Al-Tuwal in neighbouring Hajjah, as well as other fronts.
He said the operations overall targeted Houthi reinforcements and military capabilities, destroying command and control centres, weapons depots, artillery and vehicles.
A military source in government forces in the border areas told TNA, in response to a question on 26 September, that the latest escalation had also included Saada.
However, operations there were less intense at the time than on the active fronts in Taiz, Marib, Hodeidah and Al-Jawf, the source said.
The source explained that the Yemeni air force launches occasional strikes against Houthi reinforcements and targets in Saada districts, alongside artillery, drone and rocket-launcher operations.
The succession of reports coming from Saada reflects the province's growing presence in the military scene.
Targeting reinforcements, depots and vehicles has gained additional importance in light of the mobilisation because it could disrupt Houthi preparations for a potential confrontation on the border, and pressures Saada's role in mobilising fighters and supplying the group's other fronts with fighters and equipment.
The current mobilisation recalls the experience of the border fronts after Operation Decisive Storm began on 26 March 2015, when the Saudi-led coalition intervened at the request of then-President Abd-Rabbu Mansour Hadi.
In May that year, Houthi shelling extended to Najran and Jizan, turning the border into a confrontation zone and forcing Saudi Arabia to deal with a direct threat to its border areas.
The Houthis and their allies announced incursions at the time into positions inside Saudi territory and released footage they claimed showed breaches they had carried out there.
That precedent shows how a border incursion can provide a propaganda gain and a tool for putting pressure on Riyadh, even if the group's ability to hold territory is limited by military standards.
The group is betting more on the political and security impact of an incursion than on maintaining long-term control.
Houthi rhetoric
The current mobilisation has coincided with an explicit escalation in the group's rhetoric, as Houthi media outlets have recently intensified their attacks on Saudi Arabia.
The presenter of an Al Masirah report on 27 September, whose political and mobilisation-focused rhetoric reflects the group's positions and the messages it seeks to convey, spoke of moving from "restraint to deterrence through attack".
The presenter threatened to put Riyadh into "a state of unprecedented all-out war" and hinted at options that "had remained ruled out but are now possible, painful and decisive", without specifying the nature of these options.
Since the start of the latest round of fighting on 10 September, the Houthis have justified their attacks by referring to what they describe as the "Saudi blockade", citing airports and ports and what they said were restrictions on movement.
They later added almost daily accusations against Saudi Arabia of launching strikes on Yemeni provinces and targeting civilians.
This sequence allows the group to present any expansion of the confrontation as a response to Riyadh.
The Al Masirah account on Telegram published more than 90 breaking news reports about Saada during the past month, most attributed to its correspondent in the province.
They included reports of civilian injuries, including five shoppers in the Al Thabet area of Qatabir on 24 September, according to the channel.
Saree continued to include Saada in his statements, announcing on 28 September that 38 airstrikes and rocket strikes had taken place in Saada, Taiz and Hajjah.
The following day, he reported 35 strikes on Saada, Taiz, Al-Jawf, Amran and Hodeidah, adding that the strikes had hit telecommunications networks, schools and other civilian sites.
He raised his cumulative figure to 1,158 missiles since the start of the escalation across various provinces.
While the Houthis attribute these strikes to Saudi Arabia, government forces attribute the announced operations to their own forces.
The military source in the border areas said in a statement on 26 September that the Houthis combine government forces' operations with limited artillery strikes carried out by Saudi border guards against smuggling operations, then attribute them all to the kingdom.
Military and local sources said artillery fire linked to smuggling routes is known to residents and that its frequency had not increased recently, according to their monitoring.
The motives behind Houthi pressure on Saudi Arabia go beyond battlefield needs to the group's efforts to push Riyadh towards a direct agreement that would consolidate its position and limit support for the Yemeni government by raising the cost of confrontation for Saudi Arabia.
These calculations are specific to the group but overlap with Iranian interests in putting pressure on Riyadh and energy and trade routes in order to ease the pressure of the US war on Iran, according to observers.
While Yemeni army operations are putting pressure on Houthi positions and reinforcements in Saada, the mobilisation towards the border gives the group's threats a military dimension.
If these preparations turn into an attack on Saudi territory, according to the scenario anticipated by military sources, the group may be betting on an incursion that imposes a direct security and political cost on Riyadh and strengthens its ability to extract concessions from it, even if its ability to hold territory remains limited.
Article translated from Arabic by Afrah Almatwari. To read the original, click here.

articles.title: Zelenskyy convened a meeting on missiles for air defense and F-16s - he expects results on deliveries for October
articles.body:
Zelenskyy convened a meeting on missiles for air defense and F-16s - he expects results on deliveries for October
Kyiv • UNN
By October, the President expects missile deliveries to be accelerated. This concerns, among other things, air defense systems and F-16s. The protection of Kyiv’s critical infrastructure is also to be strengthened.
It is important for Ukraine that there be additional missiles in October, including for air defense and F-16s. The relevant agencies have been instructed to prepare an updated schedule for deliveries to Ukraine by tomorrow. Particular attention was paid to protecting Kyiv’s critical infrastructure. Relevant reports are expected. President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy said this following a conference call on October 1, UNN reports.
The President held a "conference call with the military, government officials, and all heads of services working to protect the infrastructure." He also set a number of tasks.
Weapons supplies
First: the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, the Ministry of Defense, and the Office team will conduct an operational review of agreements with partners concerning the provision of the necessary ammunition for F-16s. The same applies to the supply of air-defense missiles—for each country, all agreements, and every package—and by tomorrow, an updated schedule for deliveries to Ukraine. It is important that there be additional missiles in October. As of today, some of our agreements that have already been approved by the leaders of the countries have still not been implemented at the working level
At the same time, the Head of State thanked "Germany, Norway, Finland, and all other partners who are ready to work as quickly as possible."
"Yesterday and today, I communicated with the leaders: it is important to accelerate the implementation of the decisions," he added.
Resilience plans under control
"Second: for every region and key city, we record the status of implementation of resilience plans on a weekly basis. There are delays in some communities, and the military command together with government officials must prepare additional decisions to ensure greater security for the work," the President noted.
Protecting Kyiv’s critical infrastructure
"Third: we adjusted the response system to the Russian terrorist operation against Kyiv’s critical infrastructure. Protective measures must be fully implemented. We identified the necessary redistribution of resources. It is important that the local authorities in Kyiv be ready to make prompt decisions in support of the people," Zelenskyy stated.
I expect a report from the Prime Minister of Ukraine and the Commander-in-Chief of the Armed Forces of Ukraine on the steps that were determined today. Glory to Ukraine!

articles.title: Russian strikes on Ukraine are likely about to get worse, analyst says
articles.body:
Russia is stockpiling weapons to intensify attacks on Ukraine, analysts say
Kyiv — A daytime Russian attack on Ukraine Monday damaged civilian buildings and wounded more than 100 people across the country, according to local authorities.
A drone exploded into the National Academy of Sciences in the heart of Kyiv. Hours later, a second drone damaged a private medical clinic just blocks away. In Dnipro, Ukraine's fourth-largest city, emergency crews rushed to evacuate wounded civilians from a business center also hit in broad daylight.
And yet, the attack could have been much worse.
Ukraine's Air Force said Russia used 124 attack drones from 6:30 a.m. to 6:30 p.m. on Monday — much fewer than in previous barrages this year, which have regularly included more than 500 drones and 50 missiles within the same time frame.
Analysts and Ukrainian officials told CBS News that Russia is stockpiling weapons so that it can launch intensified late-autumn and winter barrages.
During Monday's attack, Russia used primarily "jet-powered drones," a new model of long-range strike drones that fly faster and are harder to intercept. Ukraine's Air Force said that 86 of the 124 drones used in the attack were jet-powered.
Since Russia began deploying the new models in June, Ukraine's interception rate against them is 57% — a sharp drop-off from the military's 90% to 95% success in intercepting older models.
Russia has two models of jet-powered drones, the Geran-4 and Geran-5, and has been stockpiling both. Come Back Alive, a Ukrainian military nonprofit, estimates that Russia will produce 1,200 Geran-4 and 800 Geran-5 in September, and projects those numbers to grow each month.
During his speech at the United Nations General Assembly earlier this month, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Russia has used just 7,700 jet-powered drones in attacks so far this year.
Viktoriia Chekalina, an analyst at the Come Back Alive Initiatives Center, estimates that Russia has stockpiled 450 to 700 units of the older non-jet-powered drones, the newer jet-powered models and dummy, non-explosive drones known as "Banderols" during each Russian attack this spring and summer.
"Despite the capacity to launch 600-1,000 units in a single massive attack, only about 150-300 drones were actually used," Chekalina told CBS News, explaining that attacks this autumn and winter "could reach around 1,500 units per one raid."
Because Russia has found success striking targets with relatively small barrages of jet-powered drones, it has also managed to save up its cruise and ballistic missiles, which are vastly more expensive and difficult to manufacture.
In the early spring and summer, Russia's attacks on Kyiv included barrages of over 70 cruise and ballistic missiles multiple times per month, according to estimates released by Ukraine's Air Force. In August, Ukraine stopped publicly releasing the numbers of missiles Russia used in each attack, but military analysts told CBS News that there was a drop-off in the number of mass-missile barrages in August and September.
Over this period, Russia has also increased its production of cruise and ballistic missiles. Chekalina said Russia has surpassed its missile production targets by 110% to 120% and estimated that it had stockpiled 130 ballistic missiles by August.
Solutions to countering Russia's ballistic missiles and jet-powered drones remain elusive. Ukraine continues to run dangerously low on American-made PAC-3 ballistic interceptors. And in an address this week, Zelenskyy said that while new defenses against jet-powered drones are being tested, they are not yet ready to be scaled, raising concerns that Ukraine may remain vulnerable heading into winter.
"Russia's goal during winter campaign will be complex: they will focus on attacking electrical and heating infrastructure as they are critical for civilians," Chekalina said. "At the same time, they will use turbojet drones along with missiles on local businesses, warehouses, and other targets."

articles.title: Why the US Air Force Needs to Invest in Electronic Warfare
articles.body:
United States air forces are engaged in combat operations today, and not all the aircraft are modern stealthy platforms like the B-2, F-22, or F-35. The venerable Lockheed Martin F-16 Fighting Falcon remains the backbone of the U.S. Air Force fighter fleet and will be in service for two more decades, yet combat operations in Operation Urgent Fury prove it needs electromagnetic warfare (EW) upgrades to survive in modern threat environments.
Our knowledge of the frequencies and waveform characteristics across the Electromagnetic Spectrum (EMS) and our ability to manipulate them with hardware and software have grown tremendously. We harness our knowledge and capabilities continuously for tracking, intelligence, communication, jamming, radar, and many other applications. Unfortunately, so do our adversaries.
To survive and accomplish combat missions, F-16 pilots need to first detect enemy threat systems, like surface-to-air missiles or air-to-air radars, via a Radar Warning Receiver (RWR) and then counter the threat with Electronic Countermeasures (ECM) that manipulate radio signals to jam guidance systems outright or deceive them in such a way that makes them ineffective. If it were only that easy.
In 2023, Commander-in-Chief of the Ukraine Armed Forces, General Valerii Zaluzhnyi, wrote a paper listing five reasons why the war with Russia had ground into static trench warfare. He cited the critical importance and rapid adaptation of electromagnetic warfare along with air superiority, counter artillery battery fires, minefield clearing, and reserve forces.
The electromagnetic spectrum is the tissue that continuously connects all our systems together and allows us to coordinate our actions, detect adversaries, deceive threats, survive, and win. Acknowledging the EMS’s asymmetric impact, both Russia and China created separate branches of service and senior commands specifically focused on electromagnetic warfare.
While superiority in the EMS is critical across all warfighting domains: land, sea, space, and cyber, it is particularly important in air operations.
While the U.S. Air Force has re-prioritized EMS for a portion of the F-16 fleet, approximately 50% of the remaining F-16 aircraft fleet across the active duty, Air National Guard, and Reserves will not have EW protection with no clear plan going forward.
International partners have invested over $1B in procuring Viper Shield systems for their F-16s over the past seven years. The Air Force could add EW pods and leverage foreign investment to save taxpayer money. This foreign investment is funding development, lab testing, flight testing, and current production of operational Viper Shield systems, which presents the U.S. Air Force with a massive savings opportunity to avoid those upfront costs.
As the Air Force considers options to resolve the F-16 EW capability gap, a modest number of advanced EW pods would be a reasonable expense for near-term capability to mitigate against potential program delays, maximize flexibility across the F-16 fleet, and reduce invasive internal modifications.
Furthermore, the pod version of Viper Shield offers maximum flexibility to rotate systems across deploying squadrons, share them among operational units during training periods, and maintain them without taking an aircraft off the flying schedule.
F-16 pilots today – and for the next 20+ years – deserve the capability an EW pod like Viper Shield brings to the fight.
Lt. Gen. Lance Landrum, USAF (Ret.), served over 30 years as an F-16 Weapons Instructor and operational fighter pilot in several deployed locations developing firsthand combat experience on the importance of Electromagnetic Warfare. During his role as the Joint Staff J8 Deputy Director for Requirements and Capability Development, he stood up and led the interagency Electromagnetic Spectrum Operations Cross Functional Team that developed the current U.S. EMS Superiority Strategy and subsequent implementation plan. His insights are based on that experience and from his efforts to champion EMS capabilities as the U.S. European Command J3 and Deputy Chair of the NATO Military Committee.

articles.title: Kubilius: Russian attack on arms factory would trigger NATO military response
articles.body:
BRUSSELS — A Russian bombing attack on a European weapons factory should trigger NATO's Article 5 mutual defense clause, the EU's top defense official said Thursday.
The call comes in the wake of a growing number of suspicious incidents at arms factories across Europe, some of which have been attributed to Russia.
"If Russia will hit our factories in European territories, that would be Article 5," European Defense Commissioner Andrius Kubilius told Polish television on the margins of a meeting of the European Parliament's Defence and Security Committee.
Advertisement
The remarks come after Russian foreign ministry spokesperson Maria Zakharova on Wednesday warned that "weapons factories in European countries that produce arms for Ukraine are potential military targets for Russia."
NATO chief Mark Rutte this week issued a strong rebuke of Moscow after Russia sent a note to the alliance threatening nuclear escalation over NATO activity near its border.
This week, Estonia said Russian secret services were behind last month's arson attack on arms contractor Milrem Robotics. Bulgaria, Poland, Slovakia and other countries are also investigating similar suspicious incidents.
An aide to Kubilius, granted anonymity to speak freely, confirmed that the commissioner's comments related specifically to an aerial bombardment or missile attack on a factory.
Yet Kubilius' statement is likely to stir unease within NATO given the sensitivity of discussions around Article 5 and the EU's non-military role compared to the alliance.
"When Kubilius will become secretary general of NATO he might be able to claim what triggers or doesn’t trigger Article 5," one NATO diplomat said.
NATO didn't immediately respond to a request for comment by POLITICO.

articles.title: Russia just accidentally crashed its first Tu-95 bomber in 11 years. Its missiles will keep striking Ukraine anyway
articles.body:
- A Russian Tu-95 bomber crashed on takeoff in Russia's Far East on Tuesday, the type's first crash in 11 years
- It's potentially the 11th Tu-95 the Russians have lost in the current wider war, and they can't build more
- But Russia still has enough bombers to keep up its missile raids on Ukraine
A Russian air force Tupolev Tu-95 Bear bomber crashed on takeoff, apparently from Ukrainka air base in Amur Oblast in Russia's Far East. The Russian defense ministry said the plane was on a training flight without munitions and blamed a technical fault. The crash, while reportedly accidental, is still a win of sorts for Ukraine. Every bomber the Russians lose is a bomber they can't immediately replace—and sortie for missile strikes on Ukrainian cities.
The problem for Ukraine is that Russia still has bombers to spare. It'll take more than a few crashes or drone raids on Russian bomber bases to cut into Russia's capacity to bombard Ukraine.
That's why Ukraine needs missile-armed fighters, ground-based self-propelled guns, speedy interceptor drones, and long-range surface-to-air missiles such as American-made Patriots, among other air defenses. The Ukrainians can't prevent missile attacks by destroying bombers or waiting for bombers to crash; they need to shoot down missiles as they near their targets.
A security camera on the ground recorded a large aircraft plunging toward the ground in Amur Oblast on Tuesday night. Video from the crash site confirmed it was one of the Russians' four-engine, propeller-driven Tu-95s, aging workhorses in Russia's escalating campaign of missile and drone attacks on Ukrainian cities.
The crash killed six crew and left one survivor injured, according to Russian state media. It is the first Tu-95 to go down in 11 years, Defense Express notes, and the first known non-combat loss of the type since the full-scale invasion.
It's potentially the 11th Tu-95 Russia has lost since widening its war on Ukraine in February 2022. Ukrainian drones caught two Bears on the ground at Engels-2 air base in Saratov Oblast in July and August. On 1 June 2025, Ukraine's Operation Spiderweb—coordinated strikes on Russian bomber bases by more than 100 small drones smuggled across Russia in trucks—destroyed as many as four Bears at Olenya air base on the Kola Peninsula and another four at Belaya air base in Irkutsk Oblast.
Now the Russian air force may be down to somewhere between 36 and 44 working Tu-95s, depending on the count, the youngest of which rolled out of the factory in the 1990s. That matters because the Tu-95 is, like the jet-propelled Tupolev Tu-22M bomber, out of production. Vendors have gone out of business. The skilled workers who assembled the types retired decades ago.
While the Russians can still build one or two Tupolev Tu-160 jet bombers every year, slowly growing a fleet that currently stands at around 18 active planes, that's far too few new bombers to replace combat losses as the wider war grinds through its 56th month.
Slow attrition
The Russians have also lost at least nine Tu-22Ms, and possibly far more: Defense Express estimates losses at up to 70% of the combat-ready fleet since 2022. All told, Russia's bomber force has shrunk to around 105 planes since the wider war began, or fewer.
Equally problematically for the Russians, the old Tu-95s and Tu-22Ms that carry out the majority of air-launched cruise missile strikes on Ukraine are wearing out from heavy use; not all are available for front-line use as more airframes spend more time in deep maintenance.
Ukraine is working down the short list of ships that shell its cities with cruise missiles. A Neptune reached one of them tied up at its own pier
But a Tu-95 carries as many as eight Kh-101 cruise missiles at a time; a Tu-22M carries up to three Kh-22s or Kh-32s. A Russian drone and missile strike might include just a dozen or so air-launched cruise missiles launched by a handful of bombers. A raid on 8 September involved just four Tu-95s and two Tu-160s.
The Russians don't need 105 bombers to sustain six-bomber raids once or twice a week, even as those bombers suffer more and more wear and tear. Ukraine would have to take out a lot more Russian bombers, and fast, to put a dent in Russian strikes.
Unless and until that unlikelihood happens, Ukraine will still need to defeat Russian raids inside Ukraine—by shooting down hundreds of incoming drones and missiles at a time. But that's getting harder as the Russians deploy faster jet-propelled Geran drones and more ground-launched Iskander missiles, combining them with the bomber-launched missiles in complex packages that routinely overwhelm ammunition-starved Ukrainian air defenses.

articles.title: The US has until 18 October to choose its Russia sanctions targets—if any. Kyiv’s wish list leads with the firms feeding Russia’s Starlink clone
articles.body:
Ukraine is about to tell Washington exactly which Russian targets it wants punished under America's new sanctions law, the Associated Press reported. A senior Ukrainian diplomat said Kyiv will hand the Trump administration and Congress a wish list of companies, ships, and people this week—and at the top are the firms supplying parts for Russia's answer to Starlink.
The law requires Washington to act but lets the president waive the sanctions if he certifies that doing so serves US national interests, and the first choice falls due in weeks. For Ukraine, a measure that names no targets changes nothing on the ground—which is why the fight now is over whose names make the list before the clock runs out.
A list topped by Russia's Starlink clone
Denys Sienik, chargé d'affaires at Ukraine's embassy in Washington, said the priority is a group of Russian firms making components for Rassvet, Moscow's homegrown satellite network, which Russia hopes to complete by the end of the year—though its own officials have put the start of service in 2027. Bureau 1440, the firm building Rassvet, is not itself on US sanctions lists, but its parent company, ICS Holding, is under US blocking sanctions, according to Militarnyi. The suppliers feeding the network parts are not sanctioned, and those are the ones Kyiv wants added to the list.
Russia sped up the project after Ukraine and SpaceX cut off the Starlink terminals its troops had used without authorization at the front. If Russia completes the constellation, Sienik said, it could strike Ukraine at will with real-time information—a danger he warned would bite hardest this winter. "If these entities are not sanctioned, it will actually make this program possible for Russia and that will be a game-changer," he told reporters, Reuters reported. Kyiv wants access to Starlink inside Russia, too, so it can strike targets there.
Euromaidan Press has reported how such a network would change the battlefield: the satellites transmit in high-frequency bands that are hard to jam, and a relay overhead would feed drones and missiles fresh coordinates mid-flight, letting them fly low under air defenses that struggle to see them.
Oil tankers and attacks on US firms
Ukraine is pushing for tougher action against Russia's shadow fleet, too—the aging tankers that sell its oil around Western restrictions—and is asking the administration and American industry to publicly condemn Russian attacks on US companies' operations inside Ukraine, Sienik said.
The deadline Washington is now facing
The requests arrive as the administration faces an 18 October deadline to decide which Russian entities, if any, to sanction under the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act, which US President Donald Trump signed into law on 18 September. The law directs the White House to impose tariffs on Russia's biggest oil buyers and to block its banks, officials, and tankers—but lets the president waive those measures, which is why Kyiv is lobbying for the toughest list it can get.

- 
							
							
								Russia’s answer to Starlink was written off as a failure—its satellites are still climbing
- 
							
							
								Ukrainian brigades detail Starlink crackdown: Russian terminals “became just bricks,” assaults disrupted

articles.title: Ukraine, Norway discuss strengthening air defence amid Russian attacks, need for F-16, MANPADS ammunition
articles.body:
During a phone call with Norwegian Defense Minister Tore Sandvik, Ukrainian Defense Minister Yevhen Khmara briefed him on the consequences of Russian strikes on civilianin Ukrainian cities and outlined Ukraine's urgent needs to strengthen its air defense, particularly regarding ammunition for F-16s and man-portable air defense systems (MANPADS).
Khmara told Sandvik about the consequences of the strikes Russia has carried out in recent weeks against civilian targets in Ukrainian cities, particularly in Kyiv.
"Ballistic missiles and jet-powered drones are the main challenges to air defense. Ukraine is developing its own capabilities to counter these threats. We have already achieved results in shooting down jet-powered UAVs. At the same time, our country is counting on continued support from our partners," the press service of the Ukrainian Ministry of Defense said on its Telegram channel citing the minister.
During the conversation, the Ukrainian side presented a specific list of urgent needs required to strengthen the defense of Ukraine's airspace. In particular, this includes ammunition for F-16s and man-portable air defense systems (MANPADS).
Khmara thanked Norway for its steady, consistent, and substantial support for Ukraine.
According to the Ukrainian Ministry of Defense, Norway allocates approximately 1.3% of its GDP – amounting to about $7 billion – to aid Ukraine each year.

articles.title: Jean-Luc Mélenchon will win young French voters – until they realise the size of his Russia blind spot | Alexander Hurst
articles.body:
Théodore Abitbol is a self-described “militant antifascist,” with degrees in political science and comparative literature, and a bookshelf that ranges from the gender and queer theory of bell hooks to the anti-capitalist social analysis of the Marxist theorist Mike Davis.
The 34-year-old is a regular participant in pro-Palestine protests, and has a decade of full-time activism under his belt: unions, strikes, protests, civil disobedience and vast protest encampments used to block construction projects, known in France as ZAD – for “zone à défendre”.
Abitbol should be an in-the-bag vote for Jean-Luc Mélenchon, the leader of La France Insoumise (LFI), a longtime fixture of hard-left French politics and a 2027 presidential candidate who is drawing significant support among voters under 35.
After all, LFI is doing something necessary by focusing on some of France’s most left-behind urban areas and giving voters in them a voice: Bally Bagayoko faced down racist abuse to win the mayoral race in Paris’s inner banlieue of Saint-Dénis. David Guiraud defeated the right for the first time since 1983 in Roubaix, one of France’s poorest large cities. The party’s success in these heavily working-class and minority areas is due its willingness to draw new lines around old identity debates, and an intransigent anti-capitalist attitude. LFI parliamentarians such as Clémence Guetté are actually making innovative and radical proposals, such as recognising close friendships and extending legal rights to them.
Yet Abitbol demonstrates the single biggest voter faultline between two incompatible French lefts: Mélenchon himself.
I mainly remember Abitbol, an acquaintance from my immediate post-student days, as being staunchly opposed to Macron’s economic policies. That hasn’t changed. But he also can’t stomach voting for Mélenchon, he confided when I reached out to him recently, , because of the LFI leader’s stances on Russia, Ukraine and the EU. “A part of the [French] left retains a cold-war mentality where Russia is an ally against American imperialism, without seeing that Putin and Trump are in agreement about almost everything in their foreign and domestic policies,” he told me.
I don’t believe Abitbol is alone. They might not admit it as openly, but I think there are millions of French voters who also crave the kind of rupture with capitalism and the status quo that Mélenchon is proposing, but have no desire to go where he would take France on foreign and European policy. French presidential elections rarely hinge on discussions of France’s place in the world. But the threat posed by Russia to Europe has already dominated the opening days of the 2027 campaign, including a special primetime TV interview with Macron.
Mélenchon consistently polls at around 17%, enough to qualify for round two of the presidential election. The combined non-Mélenchon left, split between the Ecologists, Socialist party and Communist party, just trails him, with Raphaël Glucksmann leading a split field with around 10% of a first-round vote. But polling also shows that Marine Le Pen would defeat Mélenchon 69% to 31% in a second round run-off.
If the divided and riven French left gets this wrong, it could leave millions of pro-European voters in an impossible position, and ultimately put Le Pen in power.
The term “zombie lie” is a good way to describe much of Russia’s propaganda about Ukraine. That Nato provoked the 2022 invasion by “expanding”; that Ukraine was full of neo-Nazis; that Ukraine was developing chemical weapons in secret Nato labs; that Russia – Ukraine’s former coloniser – has legitimate claims to parts of its territory anyway.
Since the mid-2010s, Mélenchon has consistently advanced many of these claims. In 2014, Mélenchon denounced the Maidan Revolution – when young Ukrainians filled the streets of Kyiv to demand a European future – saying that Russia would have to defend itself against “an adventurous putschist regime in which neo-Nazis wield a thoroughly reprehensible influence”. When Putin annexed Crimea shortly after Maidan, Mélenchon defended it by claiming that “Crimea has always been Russian”.
He didn’t stop there. In 2015, in response to Putin’s aggression, France cancelled the sale of two advanced “Mistral-class” helicopter carriers – both are now part of the French Mediterranean fleet based in Toulon. Mélenchon joined Marine Le Pen in decrying the cancellation as the “vassalisation of France to Nato’s bellicose rhetoric”, and accused the then president, François Hollande, of “unbearable betrayal” for having “devalued the worth of France’s word” by refusing to deliver the warships.
That is when Mélenchon lost Abitbol and others like him. “It’s easier [for Mélenchon] to grasp at phantoms than it is to face the reality that Russia is waging a hybrid war on us, and that tomorrow it will be a ‘classic’ war,” he says.
Mélenchon filled the next seven years alternately invoking international law to condemn the US’s unilateral action in Syria, and dispensing with the same international law when it came to defending or minimising Russia’s unilateral action and war crimes in Syria – which killed, by moderately conservative estimates, 20,000 civilians. All while denying Russia’s former Soviet colonies their right – under international law – to freely chose their alliances by joining Nato.
Accepting Georgia’s request for membership would be, he said, an “offensive and stupid provocation”. As for Estonia, Lithuania and Latvia (EU and Nato members since 2004, and some of Ukraine’s largest donors by GDP), Mélenchon’s dismissals have been scathing. “I feel nothing in common with them, it’s the end of the world, even the Romans never made it that far!” he said in 2017.
Mélenchon seems uninterested in examining why there would have been such huge interest among Russia’s immediate neighbours in joining a defensive military alliance. Apparently, in Mélenchon’s mind, it couldn’t possibly be because they had just been occupied by an aggressive and territorially expansionist petro-oligarchy – it’s because the US, and to a lesser extent western Europe, are the only ones with agency.
It’s little surprise, then, that Putin’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine did nothing to rock Mélenchon’s fixed position. Ukraine was “without a doubt” the aggressor, he claimed, whereas Russia felt “humiliated, threatened, aggressed” by the US’s decision “to annex Ukraine into Nato”. (The invasion, of course, hastened Sweden and Finland’s sovereign decisions to join.) In the four years since Putin’s war, Mélenchon’s personal blog and media appearances have been a grab-bag of the same type of ideas that Xenia Federova, former director of RT France, spewed on the rightwing news network CNews – until France issued an expulsion order and froze her assets. These included bringing Russia “back into the fold” and re-opening the Nord Stream gas pipelines; castigating Zelenskyy as “president of nothing” while promoting the Kremlin’s narrative about his lack of political legitimacy; and haranguing other Europeans for having “demonised Putin”.
Making common cause with “the enemy of my enemy” – whatever the consequences for the less powerful – as a shortsighted form of “realist” foreign policy is certainly nothing new. (Neither, in Mélénchon’s case, does it end at Europe’s borders: “Taiwan is China,” he told French TV in May). But how is any of this principled, or leftist?
After a summer when France burned and burned and burned, how is the frontrunner for the left a man who is calling for reopening the poison-drip of natural gas from a state that has been, for years, in an undeclared war hybrid war on France along with the rest of Europe? It seems Mélenchon, who has wanted to withdraw France from Nato for decades, has not updated his worldview since 1985 when he first held public office. But this is not the anti-American position it once was: it is simply to attack from the inside what Putin seeks to dismantle from the outside.
Mélenchon is not trying to hide his Eurosceptic ideas any more than he has tried to hide his positions on Ukraine. What he loudly said during the first presidential debate, in late August, is also in his programme: he will “assume confrontation with European institutions” and “disobey” EU rules “whenever necessary”.
This is not the way to lead and change an EU that, while imperfect, remains among France’s greatest foreign policy achievements. This is the way to destroy from within the best framework for tackling every modern challenge that transcends borders, from the climate crisis to inequality.
If the new guiding philosophy is that France can decide to “désobéir” whenever it sees fit, so can everyone else. How do we imagine the EU maintaining its emissions trading scheme, and the carbon border tax meant to protect it? How will these – or any other European-level policies – survive if, as Mark Carney might say, a member state’s word becomes something “written in pencil”?
The short answer is: they won’t. The EU will enter an institutional death cycle, of which a deteriorating US is only slowly becoming aware. This is what Europe’s far-right nationalists want. Is it what Mélenchon supporters want?
Mélenchon makes no secret of his desire for France to lead some non-aligned coalition of states geographically more remote, with even less coherent common interests than the existing 27 EU countries. What would all these other potential partners conclude if France were to show that it were ready, in a very Trumpian way, to do the very thing Mélenchon accused Hollande of doing? To walk all over its word, ratified in treaty with its closest neighbours, with whom it has shared a political community that France itself built?
When it comes to foreign and EU policy, Mélenchon is barely distinguishable from Le Pen: a nationalist who believes that France is too small to do anything but close in on itself – and look to Russia for guidance. If the presidential contest comes down to Mélenchon v Le Pen in the final round then Abitbol says he would vote Mélenchon, but “with vomit in my mouth”. Pity him and the others like him who might have to choose between two equally disastrous visions of France in Europe and the world.
- 
  Alexander Hurst writes for Guardian Europe from Paris. His memoir Generation Desperation is out now
