articles.title: War, power games and impunity. I watched the farce that is the UN general assembly: what a tragedy, what a mess | Nesrine Malik
articles.body:
UN general assembly meetings are not usually riveting occasions. But this year’s encapsulated a world in flux and crisis, an international law and organisation structure that is falling apart, and a humanitarian order machine running hot. What unfolded was less a gathering for resolution and resolve than a display of showboating, frustration and fractiousness.
It was a snapshot for the history books of four huge destabilising conflicts for which there seems to be no means of, or interest in, resolution – Ukraine, Iran, Palestine and Sudan. Volodymyr Zelenskyy delivered an account of five years of Russian aggression: the staggering loss of life – hundreds of thousands killed on both sides – the porousness of the sanctions on Russia, the “madness” of it all. Donald Trump once again threatened to “annihilate” Iran if it did not make a deal, a promise that has now been made so many times its restating only reveals its hollowness. Iran’s president, Masoud Pezeshkian, responded in his own speech by saying that Iran has been the victim of US terrorism and aggression, and would defend itself with the “utmost strength”. The sole US delegation representative in the room walked out.
In the middle of this unbridled, unseemly pugnaciousness, pleas to restate facts were trampled over by power-lust. The Israeli government’s sense of impunity “has reached terrifying levels”, said Jordan’s King Abdullah II. “It no longer feels compelled to ask, ‘Can we get away with this?’ It already knows the answer.”
“If international law can be ignored for decades,” he added, “then what exactly is that law worth?” As if to answer that question, Benjamin Netanyahu became the only ICC indicted leader to address the UN general assembly, with a characteristically belligerent speech. Nothing – that law is worth nothing.
And on international law meaning nothing, the assembly was subjected to the farce of the United Arab Emirates, the key player in Sudan’s war, piously preaching about how Sudanese people deserve peace and civilian rule, while the UAE’s leaders are accused of arming and funding the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), itself accused of genocide and ethnic cleansing. A close ally of the US and the UK, the UAE has managed to extend Sudan’s war into a calamitous conflict, without even a breath of censure, or even acknowledgment from its friends. A $500m investment in the Trump family’s cryptocurrency scheme, and multibillion-pound partnerships with the UK, have seemingly captured the two states. Indeed, the silence it has bought is so compliantly observed that the US’s senior adviser on African and Arab affairs (Tiffany Trump’s father-in-law) acknowledged foreign interests but refused to name any of the countries.
Even procedurally, the ground was tilted by those who have the power and shamelessness to do so. The Trump administration invoked its sovereign ability to decide who could attend and who could not, wielding a sort of weaponisation of the visa system that rendered the UN not a neutral body with its own rules and protocols, but a tool to be leveraged for the interests of the US and its allies because it sits in US territory. Palestinian president Mahmoud Abbas (not ICC-indicted) and 80 other Palestinian officials were denied visas to attend for the second time under Trump’s watch. The head of the Sudanese government and Sudanese armed forces, the antagonists to the UAE-backed RSF, was denied a visa, seemingly an indication of successful Emirati manoeuvrings in Washington. The dynamics were an expression of how foreign policy and conflict are managed today, with constant gaming of the system to amplify one side over the other and produce outcomes friendly to regional and global powers.
Amid the collapse there was Tom Fletcher, the UN undersecretary-general for humanitarian affairs, darting energetically from meeting to meeting, with a grittily sunny disposition. He posted a hectic flurry of social media clips talking about what could be done in the middle of the fire, a sort of diplomatic “this is fine” meme. And God bless him. In one, he is on a walk with Alexander De Croo, administrator of the UN development programme, who talks about the problem being “crises piling up on one another”. “The answer,” Fletcher says, “to a lot of what we do is actually diplomacy. Getting those chokepoints open, Bab al-Mandab, the Black Sea, the strait of Hormuz, because otherwise we both have a much bigger development caseload and humanitarian caseload.”
He represents an emerging new model of international and humanitarian worker – navigating funding cuts, a lack of interest in peace and politicised drawdown of international aid to at least maintain some traffic of funds. To make sure some support gets to the millions labouring under war, the climate crisis, disease, poverty, hunger and predation. The wars will carry on, and now the strategy is to negotiate with powers to un-choke and unblock what can be opened to get supplies and relief in, from winter aid in Gaza to containing the Ebola outbreak.
But where we are now isn’t just a matter of earnest diplomats and cynical, irresponsible warring powers. A far more complex problem is upon us: the rapidly changing nature of military conflict itself. Wars are becoming vastly less containable through the spread, sophistication and low cost of AI and drones. They are now conducted remotely, veering between high-intensity and low-grade assaults that render their beginnings and ends less decisive. They are more likely to just suspend normal life with dispensable drones, the sort that have held the Gulf hostage to Iran’s response to US attacks, Sudan’s war without a clear frontline, and the “ceasefire” in Gaza essentially just a lower-grade assault.
The UN general assembly meeting of 2026 was a study in so many things – the degradation of international law, the rickety system it has bequeathed, the acceleration of the demise of international community, and the importance of resolve to somehow attend to the victims. But we are also entering an era in which belligerents themselves are coming to grips with asymmetrical warfare and an elusive status quo. There is much talk of “what comes next”: an equilibrium of middle powers in compact, a rupture with the US and within Nato, a nihilistic free for all? We as humans tend to think in clear-cut scenarios. What is more likely is what was demonstrated last week in New York – a messy prolonged state of constant stress under careless leaders giddy with what they realise they can get away with, no exit plan, and the rest of the system given no option but to work with and around them to somehow alleviate the consequences of their actions. The new world order is one of active resignation.
- 
  Nesrine Malik is a Guardian columnist

articles.title: 'We will defend every inch of NATO territory’: Rutte dismisses Russia’s nuclear threat
articles.body:
Aysu Bicer
30 September 2026•Update: 30 September 2026
NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte on Wednesday dismissed Russian nuclear warnings over Kaliningrad, saying Moscow could not win a confrontation with the alliance.
Speaking at the Euronews Defense and Space Summit in Brussels, Rutte said NATO was prepared to defend its territory.
“We will defend every inch of NATO territory. That threat is not there, and if anything happens, we are ready to counter it,” he said.
His comments followed reports that Russia, in a letter, had warned NATO against any attempt to cut off Kaliningrad, its western exclave between Poland and Lithuania, saying it was prepared to use its entire arsenal, including nuclear weapons.
Rutte declined to confirm the contents of the reported letter but rejected the suggestion of an imminent nuclear threat to the Baltic states.
“We are a defensive alliance. Stop the nuclear threat. This is absolutely not called for and not helpful. And particularly stop the war in Ukraine, which is an unprovoked war of aggression against Ukraine,” he said.
Rutte also said Russian President Vladimir Putin could not defeat NATO. “Everybody knows that he can never win against NATO. I don't take this seriously.”
 
Europe’s defense role
Rutte said Russia was suffering heavy losses in Ukraine and claimed 43,000 troops were being killed or seriously wounded each month.
He said Moscow was trying to divide NATO allies and shift attention away from the battlefield.
“If necessary, of course we will defend ourselves. But the most important thing is this is all happening because the war is not going well for him in Ukraine. He wants to divide us. He wants us to lose attention when it comes to Ukraine,” Rutte said.
The NATO secretary general also said Europe must become more capable of handling security threats without relying so heavily on Washington.
“Why are the Americans doing it, taking out the Iranian nuclear capability? Because we can't. But in the future, we have to make sure that as Europeans, we can do this ourselves,” he said.
Rutte said increased European defense spending should eventually allow the continent to assume greater responsibility while keeping the US engaged in NATO.
“Still, the US being involved not only in the nuclear sense but also in the conventional sense, but the Europeans taking much, much more responsibility for the defense of this part of NATO,” he said.

articles.title: Russia warns NATO of possible nuclear response if Kaliningrad is cut off
articles.body:
Russia warns NATO of possible nuclear response if Kaliningrad is cut off
Moscow claims that NATO is preparing an air and naval blockade in the Baltic Sea.
Russia has warned NATO it is prepared to use its entire arsenal, including nuclear weapons, if the Western alliance attempts to cut off the Baltic exclave of Kaliningrad, according to a diplomatic document sent to member states.
The diplomatic memo sent on Wednesday claimed Moscow has “information that NATO is preparing an air and naval blockade of Kaliningrad”.
NATO’s response came through its Secretary-General Mark Rutte, who said that NATO is a defensive alliance and that Russia should “stop the nuclear threats”, calling the document unhelpful.
Rutte also downplayed the seriousness of the threat, saying that “Putin knows that he can never win” in a direct escalation with NATO.
Bordered by Poland and Lithuania, both NATO members, the Russian territory of Kaliningrad sits on the Baltic Sea. The region serves as a major military outpost, housing Russia’s Baltic fleet and nuclear-ready Iskander missile systems.
The exchange comes more than four and a half years into Russia’s full-scale war in Ukraine, as tensions increasingly spill into neighbouring states.
Poland has heightened its air defence posture following alleged incursions into its airspace in recent weeks, while Danish authorities said a Russian warship fired two flares near a Danish military helicopter over the Baltic Sea two weeks ago.

articles.title: P1-SUN JetKiller Destroys Geran-5 Jet-Powered Drone
articles.body:
The Ukrainian P1-SUN JetKiller interceptor drone, manufactured by SkyFall, destroyed a Russian Geran-5 jet-powered UAV.
SkyFall told Militarnyi about the interception.
Operators of the Lasar’s Group unmanned systems unit of Ukraine’s National Guard intercepted the target.
During the combat mission, the crew also used a remote control system developed by SkyFall that allows operators to control the interceptor over the internet while remaining at a considerable distance from the launch site.
The company previously integrated this system into P1-SUN family interceptors. In particular, in June 2026, at Eurosatory, the company unveiled the P1-SUN Long with an integrated AI module, which also supports remote control from any location with a stable internet connection.
SkyFall presented the JetKiller in July 2026 at the Farnborough International Airshow. The interceptor can reach speeds of up to 370 km/h, has a flight range of up to 30 km, can operate at altitudes of up to 9 km, and can remain airborne for up to 15 minutes. Its warhead weighs 500 grams.
The interceptor can be equipped with day or night cameras, as well as an AI module for automatic target detection, tracking, and acquisition. The guidance system can detect a target up to one kilometer away.
In September, Russian forces began using a new modification of the Geran-5 equipped with an autonomous optical navigation system and a modified fuselage design.
According to official data from Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence, the Geran-5 is about 6.5 meters long, has a 3.2-meter wingspan, and a maximum takeoff weight of up to 850 kilograms. Its warhead weighs about 90 kilograms, while its cruising speed is 450-600 km/h. Its flight range is about 950 km.
In September, the Defense Forces demonstrated several successful interceptions of similar aerial targets using various Ukrainian systems. In particular, on Sept. 28, a crew of the 1020th Anti-Aircraft Missile and Artillery Regiment destroyed a Geran-5 that was traveling at about 425 km/h when it was intercepted.
SkyFall manufactures several Ukrainian unmanned systems, including interceptors, Vampire heavy strike drones, and Shrike FPV drones. In August 2023, more than 270 Vampire strike drones were transferred to the military as part of the Army of Drones project.
The company developed a separate line of specialized interceptor drones in the P1-SUN family. Their use against jet-powered targets was first reported in late 2025, when a P1-SUN destroyed a Russian jet-powered Shahed.
In May, P1-SUN interceptors shot down Russian Gerbera drones carrying FPV drones.

articles.title: Air Force: defense forces down and suppress 87 of 107 enemy UAVs, hits at 11 locations
articles.body:
On Thursday night, air defense forces shot down and suppressed with electronic warfare (EW) equipment 87 out of 107 drones of various types used by Russian occupation forces to attack Ukraine, the Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported on its Telegram channel.
"On the night of October 1 (from 18:00 on September 30), the enemy attacked with 107 Shahed-type strike UAVs (63 of them jet-driven), Gerbera drones, and Parodiya-type decoy drones from the directions of Orel, Millerovo, Bryansk, and Shatalovo in Russia, temporarily occupied Donetsk region, and temporarily occupied Crimea (Hvardiyske)," the statement reads.
According to preliminary military data as of 08:00, 87 Shahed, Gerbera, and other types of drones were shot down and suppressed.
At the same time, hits by air attack weapons were recorded at 11 locations, and falling debris from downed targets was registered at four locations.
The air attack was repelled by aviation, anti-aircraft missile troops, electronic warfare and unmanned systems units, and mobile fire groups of the Defense Forces of Ukraine. As of morning, the attack is ongoing, with enemy UAVs remaining in the airspace.

articles.title: Russian Military Court Orders Senior Training Official Held in Custody
articles.body:
A Moscow military court has ordered a senior Russian general responsible for military training facilities and equipment held in pre-trial detention in a criminal case whose details have not been disclosed, the Kommersant newspaper reported.
The 235th Garrison Military Court issued the ruling against Major General Sergei Nikitushkin on Wednesday evening, the newspaper said. The charges against him were not immediately known.
Nikitushkin heads the department responsible for training facilities and equipment within the Russian Armed Forces’ Main Directorate of Combat Training.
The directorate oversees troop training, develops training infrastructure and supplies equipment used to prepare soldiers for combat.
Nikitushkin, 51, served in Russia’s war on Ukraine and was promoted to major general by President Vladimir Putin in December 2024. The Baza Telegram channel reported that he had worked on modernizing tank training grounds in Russia.
He previously complained of insufficient funding to buy simulators for training troops to operate armored vehicles, communications equipment, drones and night-vision devices. He said the war in Ukraine had demonstrated the importance of such equipment in preparing soldiers for future combat.
The directorate also oversees Patriot Park, a military exhibition complex near Moscow that has been implicated in embezzlement cases involving several senior officers.
Those convicted include former Deputy Defense Minister Pavel Popov, whose prison sentence was reduced to 10 years, and Major General Vladimir Shesterov, a former deputy head of the Defense Ministry’s innovation development directorate, who received six years.
Putin appointed Colonel General Rustam Muradov to lead the Main Directorate of Combat Training in June.

articles.title: Chief of NATO ‘defensive alliance’ advocates war of aggression
articles.body:
NATO chief advocates war of aggression
European NATO members should have been able to attack Iran instead of relying on the US and Israel, according to Secretary-General Mark Rutte, the head of the self-described defensive alliance.
Iran has been attacked twice in two years, both times over allegations that it seeks to develop nuclear weapons, which Tehran rejects as false. Speaking at the Euronews Defence & Space Summit on Friday, Rutte endorsed the idea that European nations should acquire the military capabilities needed to carry out such wars of aggression themselves.
In the future, “the Europeans will be able to take care of their backyard themselves. It should be us doing this, not the Americans,” he said.
“Europe was not able to take out the nuclear capability of Iran. We couldn’t. We didn’t have the capabilities. In 10 years, we can and we should,” he added, referring to multi-billion euro rearmament efforts now underway in European members of the military bloc.
Earlier in the day, the NATO chief dismissed Russian concerns over hostile rhetoric by some members of the bloc regarding the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad Region.
“Basically what we said is, ‘hey, listen, we are a defensive alliance, and stop the nuclear threat’,” he told journalists when asked about a formal warning Moscow had sent to Brussels.
Russia cited remarks by Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski, who proposed in September deploying additional troops near the Russian border so that Moscow would be “uncertain of what we will do.” Moscow said it would use its “entire available arsenal” to defend Russian territory from a possible attack by NATO states.
NATO was created in the early years of the Cold War, ensuring a continued US military presence in Western Europe. The Soviet Union later established its own military alliance, the Warsaw Pact, which no longer exists.
While NATO describes itself as a defensive alliance, it has carried out military attacks against other countries, including the UK- and French-led 2011 intervention in Libya, after which the North African state was balkanized.
Russia considers NATO’s eastward expansion since the end of the Cold War a major national security threat and has cited it as one of the principal causes of the Ukraine conflict.
Rutte’s argument in support of the US-Israeli attacks on Iran echoed remarks by German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, who said in June 2025 that the Israelis were doing “[the] dirty work for us.”

articles.title: Forget ‘superintelligence’: error-prone AI nearly sparked world war three this month | Timnit Gebru and Emily M Bender
articles.body:
Amid a barrage of news stories warning about superintelligent machines rendering humanity extinct, a CNN story describing the opposite scenario – one in which the US military’s reliance on brittle chatbots almost brought the US into war with China – went mostly unnoticed by the public.
The biggest international AI news of the past three weeks was the Anthropic engineer Jacob Coxon’s resignation. According to him, OpenAI and Anthropic are “racing straight towards self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives”. Coxon’s description of a “terminator” scenario, a machine becoming much smarter than humanity and deciding to wipe us out, captured the public’s, journalists’ and politicians’ attention, stirring waves of fear-inducing, credulous reporting, and policy actions.
The California governor, Gavin Newsom, issued a mandate to create an “AI kill-switch”; New York’s governor, Kathy Hochul, is similarly exploring the possibility of having “AI kill-switches”; and Senator Bernie Sanders and Congressman Greg Casar introduced legislation to “ban artificial superintelligence”.
While so many of us were focused on fictional superintelligent machines that we were told could hypothetically cause human extinction, however, there was a more serious story being reported.
A series of events almost got us to armageddon, not caused by “rogue, superintelligent AI”, but by government reliance on error-prone systems that are marketed by their manufacturers as being close to superintelligent.
A CNN report published on 18 September, which hasn’t been verified by other major outlets, describes how the US “almost started a war” with China, based on an intelligence report that claimed a Chinese ship was transporting components of nuclear weapons. Military personnel made plans to intercept the Chinese vessel, complete with aircraft and soldiers ready to board the ship. A military skirmish of this kind between China and the US could quickly escalate and spiral into world war three.
It was only moments before executing on the plan that American officials further investigated the intelligence report and found that it had been generated with the use of a chatbot and contained erroneous information about the vessel’s contents.
Unlike the terminator, “rogue AI”, scenario, this incident didn’t galvanize lawmakers into announcing calls for regulation so as to avoid potential human extinction. Media outlet after media outlet didn’t warn the public that we almost triggered a war against a nuclear superpower because of our military’s reliance on error-prone chatbots.
We describe the large language models (LLMs) powering these chatbots as stochastic parrots, that is, models that are designed to regurgitate the patterns of the data they are trained on. News coverage describing them as “powerful” “rogue” models that could render humanity extinct all on their own, bolsters perceptions of tools based on these models being infallible enough to merit usage in stakes as high as warfare.
Even CNN’s more critical coverage describes the chatbot used by the US military as presenting “profound risks” because it is “powerful, new and relatively poorly understood technology”.
In fact, today’s LLMs and the chatbots they power are not poorly understood, nor are they powerful in the sense of being effective tools for this use case. They are systems for generating plausible-looking text, built out of enormous, haphazardly collected datasets and then “fine-tuned” (that is, further trained) to be especially appealing to their intended users.
CNN wasn’t able to learn which chatbot product was used in this case, but the LLM powering the product was probably fine-tuned to output text with the stylistic hallmarks of intelligence reports. Both the basic functionality and the risks of such a model have been well-understood and well-documented for years, including in our 2021 paper On the Dangers of Stochastic Parrots: Can Language Models Be Too Big?
Claims that system behavior is mysterious arise from deliberate mystification on the part of those selling those systems, and a misapprehension of what their output is by those procuring and using it.
Unlike the unscientific and fantastical claims of OpenAI and Anthropic CEOs and those who uncritically repeat their talking points, the harmful, and well-documented, impacts of these companies’ products have arisen because people believe that the products are superintelligent, not because they actually are.
From “AI” scribes used by hospitals erroneously classifying patients as illicit drug users, to governments killing children after relying on “intelligence analysis” systems which mistake schools for military facilities, we are seeing the predictable harms that come from misplaced faith in unreliable automated software.
Meanwhile, the marketing campaigns from the companies selling this software warn of impending superintelligence, directing our attention away from the real risk to their fantasies of doom.
It is high time for us to regulate usage of systems sold as “AI”, not because they are magical machines, but because they are error-prone products that shouldn’t be used in high-stakes scenarios. Any automation used in military, medical or other life-and-death situations must be thoroughly evaluated within its use case and paired with usage norms that keep accountability with people who have actual power to make decisions.
As the former FTC chair Lina Khan has repeatedly reminded us, there is no exemption from the law when it comes to AI: there are existing laws that federal agencies and other regulators can enforce to protect the public against the AI industry’s unsafe and unscientific practices of pushing unsound products while marketing them as “magic intelligence in the sky”.
Going along with company executives and describing their products as beings with agency allows these executives to evade accountability while deceiving the public. We call on journalists and lawmakers to hold companies accountable rather than parrot their marketing talking points.
- 
  Timnit Gebru is executive director of Dair and author of the forthcoming book Deep Unlearning: The Radicalization of a Tech Idealist, which is available for preorders now and set to publish on 16 February.
- 
  Emily M Bender is professor of linguistics at the University of Washington and co-author of The AI Con.

articles.title: No ‘real proof’ Russia is preparing attack on NATO – Lithuanian PM (VIDEO)
articles.body:
Baltic state’s PM trashes NATO ‘Russian threat’ claim (VIDEO)
Lithuanian Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevicius has said there is no evidence that Russia is preparing an attack on NATO territory, following a meeting with the military bloc’s chief, Mark Rutte, in Brussels.
His remarks came amid heightened tensions between Russia and NATO, as some Western officials and intelligence agencies have warned that Moscow could be preparing operations against member states in Europe.
At a press conference on Tuesday, an AFP reporter asked Sinkevicius, whose Baltic country borders Russia’s Kaliningrad exclave and Moscow’s close ally Belarus, whether the “increasing hysteria and fear of hybrid attacks” could undermine Europe’s confidence and play into Russia’s hands.
“We’re not shaking. We’re not shivering. We are investing hugely in our defense capabilities,” Sinkevicius replied.
“I think it’s a must to say if the threat is there for the society. But you can’t exaggerate and say, ‘Oh, something is happening in the upcoming months or weeks,’” he added.
“I was addressing the secretary general [Rutte, asking] ‘Is there any proof, real proof intelligence services are providing, something on the table, that Russia is getting ready for something?’ And there is actually none,” Sinkevicius said.
“The risk remains but it is not fluctuating, increasing or decreasing. We have to calmly do our work, and we’re doing it,” he added. His comments were also reported contemporaneously by international media.
👀 Lithuanian PM: "I was addressing the secretary general [Mark Rutte asking,] 'Is there any proof, real proof intelligence services are providing, something on the table, that Russia is getting ready for something?' And there is actually none."
In other words, most of the “OMG!… pic.twitter.com/2UdYUWWKPR
Rutte said the bloc should respond to potential threats by strengthening its own defenses and doing “even more for Ukraine, and not less.”
Speaking at the Euronews Defence & Space Summit in Brussels the following day, the NATO chief similarly sought to play down fears of an imminent Russian attack.
“There is no imminent threat to NATO territory. If there is a build-up, we will see it and we will deal with it,” Rutte said.
European officials have increasingly discussed the possibility of a military confrontation with Russia, particularly around Kaliningrad, which is sandwiched between NATO members Poland and Lithuania.
Lithuanian Foreign Minister Kęstutis Budrys argued in May that NATO must demonstrate its ability to “break into” the Russian exclave and destroy its air-defense and missile systems if necessary. Polish Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski said last month that NATO members should closely monitor Russian forces in Kaliningrad and conduct exercises “so aggressively” that Moscow would be forced to divert troops from Ukraine to defend the region.
The Kremlin has described remarks about Kaliningrad as “borderline crazy,” while the Russian Embassy in Belgium condemned what it called “an unprecedented surge” in NATO military activity along Russia’s western borders.
“The Alliance is conducting a large-scale information campaign to propagate the myth of the ‘Russian threat’ and spread false information about Moscow’s alleged ‘intentions’ to attack one of the Baltic states by 2029 at the latest, or even sooner,” the Russian Embassy said on X on Monday.
It warned NATO members that “reckless and irresponsible” actions risked triggering a direct armed conflict.

articles.title: Russia adds new weapon to its jet-powered drones, even more dangerous: 40-kilogram charge made to sever high-voltage pylons and iron bridges
articles.body:
Russia has a new warhead for its drones, and it is built to cut down power lines. For the first time, a jet drone has carried a shaped "cumulative-cutting" charge designed to sever high-voltage pylons and iron bridges, Serhii Beskrestnov, presidential adviser, known as Flash, said, as Russia opened its heaviest assault on Ukraine's power grid since last winter.
On 30 September, Russia launched its massed fall-winter campaign on Ukraine's energy infrastructure since the last heating season, hitting power sites across 11 regions overnight with missiles and drones, Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi said.
The new warhead fits the aim: Flash says it is meant to bring down the high-voltage lines that carry the country's electricity. And Ukraine enters the winter exposed, with its energy resilience plans less than half complete.
A new charge targets the pylons
The device, which Flash calls a cumulative-cutting special load, is designed specifically to bring down high-voltage pylons and iron bridge structures.
"It consists of a main charge weighing 40 kilograms and four strike modules," he says.
In his reading, Russia intends to go after the major transmission lines that move power across the country, the backbone of the grid, rather than the substations it has struck before.
The campaign builds toward November
On 29 September, two senior Ukrainian officials told The Economist that Russia launched a three-part campaign of attacks on Kyiv, combining massive bombardments, sabotage, and the creation of political chaos. These efforts aimed at destabilizing the Ukrainian capital would peak by November, they said.
According to a representative of the Security Service of Ukraine, Russia has "thousands" of drones in its arsenal and is simultaneously expanding its stockpile of ballistic missiles. The plan is to "deploy the entire arsenal over the next two months," given that Ukraine lacks an effective weapon against jet-powered drones.

articles.title: White House Taps Miller to Lead US Space Command
articles.body:
The White House has nominated Lt. Gen. David N. Miller Jr. to lead U.S. Space Command, succeeding Gen. Stephen Whiting, who is expected to retire by January 2027.
A notice of Miller’s nomination for promotion to general appeared in the Congressional Record on Sept. 29, but the notice did not include an assignment. U.S. Space Command and the Space Force both confirmed Sept. 30 that Miller has been tapped for the SPACECOM commander job.
“Congratulations to Lt. Gen. Miller on his nomination to serve as Commander, U.S. Space Command,” Chief of Space Operations Gen. Douglas Schiess said in a statement. “He is an exceptional Guardian who has represented our service with distinction, and we believe he is a strong candidate for this critical joint leadership role.”
Miller, currently the Space Force’s deputy chief of space operations for strategy, plans, programs, and requirements, is a career space operator. He served as commander of Combat Forces Command—then Space Operations Command—from 2024 to 2025, and was director of operations, training, and force development at U.S. Space Command before that. Earlier in his career, he was chief of the Space Control Division within Air Force headquarters, led weapons and tactics development for the 21st Operations Group, and was an intercontinental ballistic missile operator and instructor.
His nomination would make him SPACEOM’s fourth leader since the command was reestablished in 2019, and its third to hail from the Space Force. Charles Galbreath, director of the Mitchell Institute’s Spacepower Advantage Center of Excellence praised Miller as a “straightforward leader” and said he’s glad to see another Guardian in the top SPACECOM job.
“The unique relationship between the space-focused service and combatant command is undeniable,” Galbreath said. “I look forward to seeing that partnership continue to mature under the leadership of Gens. Schiess and Miller.”
If confirmed, Miller would take the reins of the command as the U.S. military’s reliance on space capabilities both in peacetime and in combat takes center stage—and as leaders increasingly emphasize the role of offensive operations in the domain.
Top Pentagon officials have said military space assets and SPACECOM forces played a key role in operations against Iran, providing electronic warfare, navigation, missile warning, and communications capabilities. Speaking at AFA’s Air, Space & Cyber Conference on Sept. 14, Air Force Secretary Troy Meink revealed that the Space Force has “space control weapons”—the Defense Department’s most direct acknowledgement to date that the U.S. operates offensive systems in orbit.
Miller will also oversee construction of SPACECOM’s first purpose-built headquarters at Redstone Arsenal in Huntsville, Ala., and the accompanying relocation of personnel and operations from Peterson Space Force Base, Colo. The new facility is in the midst of a phased transition slated to conclude in 2031.
Whiting, the current SPACECOM commander, has been at the helm since January 2024. During his tenure, he has been a vocal proponent of better space domain awareness capabilities, a stronger space “kill chain,” and more dynamic, maneuverable satellites. In a recent speech at the AMOS Conference in Maui, Hawaii, he advocated for improved space-based target tracking and detection capabilities, which he said are foundational to the military’s ability to effectively perform space control operations.
“To be able to negate threats in space, we must be able to find, fix, track, and target those threats,” Whiting said Sept. 16. “Targeting in the space domain is maturing, but it still has a long way to go.”

articles.title: Ukraine corruption scheme funded by EU taxpayers: SVR statements
articles.body:
MOSCOW, October 1. /TASS/. The scale of corruption in Ukraine is impeding a peaceful settlement, while the new leadership of the Ukrainian Security Service (SBU) has organized a scheme to steal money from pistol supplies originating in European Union countries by tripling the price per unit, the press bureau of Russia’s Foreign Intelligence Service (SVR) said.
TASS has compiled the SVR’s key statements.
Reasons Kiev rejects peaceful settlement
The scale of corruption in Ukraine stands in the way of a peaceful settlement.
The "Ukrainian Gauleiter" Vladimir Zelensky and his inner circle refuse to end the conflict as they continue lining their pockets, "driven mad by the prospect of easy pickings": "They simply cannot stop and continue to line their pockets through a war that is devastating for the people of Ukraine."
Covering budget losses at EU expense
The corruption-driven "gap" in Ukraine’s budget will be covered with money taken from ordinary citizens of European countries: "However, a clue can be found in Vladimir Zelensky’s words about the unexpected $27 billion gap in Ukraine’s military budget. By tradition, Kiev and its European sponsors will cover this deficit using funds seized from ordinary citizens of European states."
Corruption scheme
The new SBU leadership has organized a scheme to steal money from pistol supplies originating in EU countries by tripling the price per unit: "According to information coming to the SVR, the new leadership of the Security Service of Ukraine has orchestrated yet another scheme to embezzle money from European taxpayers, this time by procuring guns from EU states for the agency’s needs. The scheme involves purchasing arms through a network of intermediaries in Eastern Europe, causing the cost per unit to triple from 250 to 750 euros."
Trusted individuals close to the SBU leadership receive 625,000 euros from every batch of 5,000 pistols resold to Ukrainians through third-party European companies, while the Belgian and German defense ministries cover all the costs: "For every batch of 5,000 guns, 625,000 euros are transferred to the accounts of trusted individuals close to the leadership of the Security Service of Ukraine. All expenses related to the specified arms purchase are covered by the defense ministries of Belgium and Germany."
"A key role is played by the Polish company Wytwornia Broni Jacek Popinski, registered in Rogow, Lodz Voivodeship. The company purchases the guns, including from the Panamanian subsidiary of Austrian arms manufacturer Glock, and resells them to the Ukrainians."
"One can only speculate about the scale of theft and corruption involved in Kiev’s procurement of more expensive weaponry, particularly the scarce components for anti-aircraft missile systems."
EU assistance to Ukraine
On September 11, European Commission Spokesman Balazs Ujvari said at a briefing in Brussels that the Commission had allocated all the funds earmarked in the 2026 budget for military assistance to Ukraine.
EU countries agreed to provide Ukraine with 6.6 billion euros from the European Peace Facility, EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said on September 25.
She stated that 900 million euros would be allocated to the EU military assistance mission in support of Ukraine, 1 billion euros would finance new joint equipment purchases, and 4.7 billion euros would reimburse member states for their expenses.
The growing integration of the Ukrainian and Western defense industries shows that Europe is unwilling to pursue de-escalation in the conflict with Russia, Yulia Zhdanova, head of the Russian delegation to the Vienna Negotiations on Military Security and Arms Control, said on September 23.
EU budget
Six EU countries led by Germany have warned Brussels that they will reject the bloc’s proposed seven-year budget for 2028-2034 unless spending is cut by "hundreds of billions" of euros, the Financial Times (FT) reported on September 29, citing a letter also signed by the leaders of the Netherlands, Sweden, Denmark, Austria and Finland.
The EU budget, which could reach almost 2 trillion euros under the European Commission’s proposal, "must be fundamentally reformed," the letter said.
The budget requires unanimous approval from all 27 EU member states.

articles.title: CAR: More Than Half of Identified Components in North Korean Missiles Counterfeit
articles.body:
Researchers have identified counterfeit electronic components in Russian, Iranian, and North Korean weapons seized in Ukraine.
The findings are detailed in a report by the international organization Conflict Armament Research (CAR).
The highest share of counterfeit components was found in North Korean Hwasong-11 (KN-23) ballistic missiles, with more than half of the identified components found to be counterfeit.
Since January 2024, CAR specialists have examined the debris of 11 North Korean missiles, recovering hundreds of microchips, voltage converters and memory components.
CAR sent 147 requests to manufacturers to identify components. Ten companies confirmed that markings on components were likely or definitively counterfeit.
Of the 81 North Korean missile components CAR traced, 42, or 51.9%, were identified as counterfeit or suspected counterfeits.
By comparison, counterfeit components accounted for 16% of those identified in Iranian weapons and about 20% in Russian weapons.
Among the counterfeit components were metal-oxide-semiconductor field-effect transistors (MOSFETs) from a U.S. brand, found in a Hwasong-11 missile after a strike on the Poltava region in December 2024.
The U.S. manufacturer confirmed the components were counterfeit, citing discrepancies in casing shape, marking placement, and serial numbers.
Manufacturers identify counterfeit components by errors in logos, incorrect fonts, or date codes indicating periods when the company did not yet exist at the time.
The widespread use of counterfeit components indicates the effectiveness of international sanctions, which are forcing North Korea, Iran, and Russia to procure components on the black market.
The use of uncertified components directly affects missile reliability and accuracy, which helps explain the high rate of deviations among North Korean missiles in early 2024.

articles.body:
Exclusives
Intelligence and technology
Russia is now wiring its attack drones into one network in flight, so a single drone can scout, strike, and relay for the rest. Chains of Russian drones keep crossing near the Belarus border, Ukraine's Air Force says.
Ukrainian combat simulator, used to train more than 500,000 troops, can now be ordered from NATO’s supply catalogs by single code. Each trainer assigned a 13-digit NATO Stock Number.
Russia adds new weapon to its jet-powered drones, even more dangerous: 40-kilogram charge made to sever high-voltage pylons and iron bridges. Russia opens a massed assault on the grid.
Ukraine’s new ground robot switches from land to water in seconds. It just ran its first supply mission, 40 kilometers to positions others can’t reach. A Ukrainian robot drives to the front, then swims.
Most drone interceptors ram or explode. This Ukrainian one just throws a net—six shots to a module. The Mangal launcher carries two cameras, picks out drones on its own, and mounts on a vehicle or a fixed post.
The EU sanctioned Russia’s Starlink rival but not the company that builds it. Experts call that the gap that matters. Ukraine can jam Russian drones into drifting off course—a satellite relay overhead would let them fly straight through the jamming and strike.
International
EU wants reforms before more money. Kyiv wants Europe to touch Russia’s frozen billions. The push comes as Ukraine seeks access to €210 billion in immobilized Russian central-bank assets to help cover its needs.
Humanitarian and social impact
Ukraine brings 14 more children home from Russian-occupied Kherson Oblast. One of them was being forced onto Russia’s military rolls. This year's returns from the occupied south now reach 204.
Russia struck a school in Sumy with a 250-kilogram bomb while children in grades 1–4 were studying there. The bomb hit as about 40 children sheltered inside, one of many Russian strikes on Ukrainian cities and villages over the past 24 hours.
Kyiv’s supermarkets are the new front line as Russia hunts civilian life before winter. Officials say the Kremlin is blending drone strikes, sabotage, and bot-farm propaganda to break the capital before the cold arrives.
Russian troops seize drone-dropped food in occupied Oleshky, accusing recipients of cooperating with Ukraine. Some people go missing, a local official says. One family in Oleshky was taken "to the basement" and has since disappeared without a trace, an Oleshky official says.

- Category

Over Half the Components in North Korean Missiles Fired at Ukraine Are Counterfeit
More than 50% of the identified electronic components in North Korean Hwasong-11 (KN-23) ballistic missiles recovered in Ukraine were found to be fake, according to a report by Conflict Armament Research (CAR).
Since January 2024, CAR investigators examined the wreckage of 11 North Korean missiles and recovered hundreds of microchips, voltage converters, and memory modules.

Out of 147 inquiries sent to global component manufacturers, 10 firms confirmed that branding on their parts was either likely or definitely forged.
In total, of the 81 tracked components recovered from North Korean missiles, 42 parts—or 51.9%—were identified as counterfeit or suspected fake. By comparison, counterfeit parts account for 16% of components in Iranian weapons and about 20% in Russian military hardware.
Among the discovered fake parts were metal-oxide-semiconductor field-effect transistors (MOSFETs) bearing the mark of an American company, which were recovered from a Hwasong-11 missile following a strike in the Poltava region in December 2024.
The US-based manufacturer confirmed the components were counterfeit, citing discrepancies in body casing, logo placement, and serial numbers. Manufacturers typically spot fake parts by identifying logo errors, incorrect fonts, or date codes that reference periods before the company even existed.
The widespread use of knockoff components indicates that international sanctions are working, forcing North Korea, Iran, and Russia to source critical electronics on the black market.
Utilizing uncertified components directly harms the reliability and accuracy of these systems, which explains why North Korean missiles experienced such high failure rates in early 2024.
Previously, it was reported that North Korea secretly supplied Russia with between 8 million and 11 million artillery shells over a two-and-a-half-year period to support its full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Operating through a covert maritime supply chain, four Russian cargo ships completed at least 112 voyages between North Korea and the Russian Far East to bypass international sanctions.
These deliveries provided Moscow with up to 350,000 shells per month—accounting for as much as half of Russia’s artillery fire in some combat zones—before maritime shipments slowed significantly in early 2026 due to rising Russian domestic production and depleted North Korean stockpiles.

articles.title: Iran hails US withdrawal from Iraq as ‘historic victory’
articles.body:
Iran hails US withdrawal from Iraq as ‘historic victory’
Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) has welcomed the US withdrawal from Iraq, adding that the Americans should also leave all other countries in the region.
On Wednesday, the Pentagon announced that the last American troops had departed from Iraq after being there for 23 years.
In its statement yesterday dedicated to the US pullout, the IRGC said that it “congratulates the proud nation of Iraq… and the revolutionary fighters of the Islamic world on this historic victory.”
The US lost a total of 4,419 troops in Iraq, according to the Pentagon. The Watson Institute at Brown University has estimated that the invasion cost American taxpayers some $2.8 trillion dollars. “These figures show America’s heavy and disgraceful defeat,” the IRGC statement read.
The Guard insisted that “America’s presence not only brought no security, but was itself the source of insecurity, terrorism and instability in West Asia.”
The US invaded Iraq in 2003, toppling the country’s longtime leader Saddam Hussein, and than carried out smaller-scale operations against Islamic State (IS, formerly ISIS), which emerged in 2014 out of the chaos created by the American interference. According to some estimates, over a million Iraqi civilians lost their lives during the period, with millions more displaced.
“It can be firmly said that America’s expulsion from Iraq is the prelude to its expulsion from all of West Asia… America must leave the region and leave security management to the peoples themselves,” it said.
Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi said on Wednesday that the US withdrawal signaled the beginning of a “new phase, one defined by Iraq’s sovereignty, the strength of its institutions, the readiness of its forces, the unity of its decision-making, and balanced partnerships with its friends.”
In a post on his Truth Social platform on the same day, US President Donald Trump described the American involvement in Iraq as “a very expensive excursion into Hell.” Its conclusion is a win for both Washington and Baghdad, he claimed.
It was “very bad decision-making that got us involved in this quagmire in the first place,” Trump said.
The invasion of Iraq was launched under the administration of then President George W. Bush over accusations the country’s longtime leader Saddam Hussein possessed weapons of mass destruction, which were never substantiated by Washington.
Trump himself initiated a conflict with Iran in late February on the pretext of preventing it from obtaining a nuclear bomb, despite claiming the previous June that the Islamic Republic’s nuclear program had been “obliterated” by US-Israeli strikes. Tehran has repeatedly insisted that it is not working on a weapon.
Washington’s position in the Middle East has been dealt a blow during the Iran war, as Tehran has damaged or outright destroyed key US radar, communications, and other military infrastructure at bases in Gulf nations, including the UAE, Saudi Arabia, Bahrain, Jordan, Kuwait and others.
The Pentagon is now considering whether to reduce the US military footprint in the region after the Iran war ends, the Washington Post reported in August, citing anonymous officials. Diplomatic efforts to settle the crisis currently remain in a stalemate.

articles.title: Russia nuclear warning to NATO not confrontational: Kremlin
articles.body:
The Kremlin on Thursday defended a letter outlining Russia’s readiness to use nuclear weapons if NATO cuts off Kaliningrad, saying the warning was meant to secure the Baltic exclave rather than provoke confrontation.
Earlier Wednesday, Moscow sent a document to NATO, accusing the alliance of a "dangerous and reckless course" that entailed "high risks of the outbreak of a direct armed conflict."
The document said this included the possibility of "Russian strikes against decision-making centers in the alliance's member states right from the outset."
"Russia will be ready to use the entire arsenal of forces and capabilities at its disposal, including nuclear weapons, in order to defend its territory should NATO countries undertake any attempt aimed at isolating the Kaliningrad Region from the rest of the country," the diplomatic note said.
The warning highlighted Moscow's urgent concern at what it has presented as a growing NATO threat to Kaliningrad, a heavily militarized Russian territory that is wedged between Poland and Lithuania and is slightly bigger than the U.S. state of Connecticut.
Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova, in a commentary on the ministry's website, cited statements by dignitaries from NATO states which she said demonstrated "Russophobia" and a readiness to wage war with Moscow.
These figures, Zakharova wrote, "need to be brought back down to earth. We hope that our warnings will be heard by those to whom they are addressed."
"If Europe attacks Russia, it will be a completely different sort of war – a very short war."
NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte said the alliance had responded to Russia's message by declaring: "We are a defensive alliance. And stop the nuclear threats. This is absolutely not called for and not helpful."
In its response to the Russian document, seen by Reuters, NATO also said that none of its "exercises or activities pose a threat to the territory of the Russian Federation."
"We call upon the Russian Federation to end its unprovoked full-scale invasion of Ukraine. We urge the Russian Federation to refrain from increasingly reckless behaviour towards the Allies and to cease its irresponsible nuclear rhetoric," it said.
Asked if the risk of nuclear weapons being used against the Baltics was now real, Rutte told a defense conference in Brussels hosted by broadcaster Euronews: "No, it's not. Putin knows that he can never win (against) NATO, so I don't take this that seriously."

articles.title: Pentagon wants a hypersonic cruise missile for jets, ships and bombers
articles.body:
- DARPA issued a request for information on Sept. 30 for a Next Generation Hypersonic Cruise Missile demonstrator, with responses now due Nov. 6.
- The agency wants an air-breathing missile that leaps ahead in range, speed or altitude and can be built affordably at high rates.
The Pentagon’s research agency DARPA is asking industry how to build a new hypersonic cruise missile that would fly much farther, faster or higher than current designs and could still be produced cheaply in large numbers.
DARPA’s Tactical Technology Office posted a request for information for the Next Generation Hypersonic Cruise Missile on Sept. 30 and later pushed the response deadline back a month, from Oct. 6 to Nov. 6. The agency says the answers will shape the requirements and acquisition plan for a possible competitive program whose goal is to design, build and flight-test a complete hypersonic cruise missile demonstrator. The notice is not a solicitation, and DARPA has not said how much the program could cost or when a first flight might take place.
A hypersonic cruise missile flies at more than five times the speed of sound using an air-breathing engine, usually a scramjet, that draws oxygen from the atmosphere instead of carrying it on board. DARPA says earlier demonstration programs have already proven that scramjet-powered flight works, but that existing concepts deliver only incremental gains and that legacy manufacturing makes them too expensive and complex to build at the scale a war with a major power would demand.
The agency wants a “revolutionary leap” in at least one of three areas, range, cruise speed or altitude, so the missile can strike targets defended by advanced air defense networks. It also wants the design built for easy manufacturing and assembly from the start, with a realistic path from a demonstrator to affordable, high-rate production.
DARPA is open to very different sizes of missile. The notice lists four broad classes: a weapon carried inside or under a fighter jet for quick response, one sized for a bomber’s internal bay, cargo-aircraft pallets or a ship’s vertical launch tubes, a larger missile carried under a heavy bomber, and a large ground-launched version for strategic missions that would make the most of an air-breathing engine’s range at bigger scales.
The request covers three areas for industry. One asks for overall missile concepts and a fast plan for reaching a first flight. Another seeks high-risk technologies such as new engines, high-energy fuels, boosters, heat-resistant materials and cooling systems, and DARPA says it is not interested in modernization or incremental improvements. A third asks for new ways to test hypersonic weapons, which is one of the slowest and most expensive parts of any program. DARPA is running its own studies on the missile’s operational use in parallel.
The testing section stands out. DARPA wants flight test methods that can cover distances of 250 to 2,000 nautical miles (460 to 3,700 km), reduce reliance on traditional test ranges so programs can test on demand, and give off fewer signs that a test is about to happen. It asks for autonomous telemetry, tracking and data systems that could be based on the surface, underwater, in the air or in space.
DARPA is encouraging companies outside the traditional defense industry to respond, particularly on the technology and testing questions, and to form teams with established contractors. The agency’s earlier Hypersonic Air-breathing Weapon Concept program flight-tested scramjet-powered designs from Raytheon, Northrop Grumman and Lockheed Martin and fed into the U.S. Air Force’s Hypersonic Attack Cruise Missile program.

articles.title: Russia Strikes Kyiv Nuclear Institute Housing Reactor
articles.body:
On Wednesday, a Russian drone struck the grounds of Kyiv’s Institute for Nuclear Research, where a research nuclear reactor is located, Ukraine’s nuclear regulator said.
The State Nuclear Regulatory Inspectorate of Ukraine said the drone hit the institute’s grounds at 6:18 p.m. local time, citing information provided by the research facility.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
A fire caused by the attack was quickly extinguished, with no casualties reported. Investigators and specialists continued assessing the damage.
Reactor undamaged and radiation levels normal
The VVR-M research reactor and systems essential to its safety were not damaged, according to the regulator.
Radiation monitoring recorded no changes following the strike. Radiation levels remained within the natural background range of 0.16 to 0.20 microsieverts per hour.
The reactor has been shut down since February 2022 as a precaution against wartime nuclear risks. Its active zone has been completely unloaded, meaning it currently contains no nuclear fuel.
Operations at the facility have since been limited to scheduled maintenance of systems important for nuclear and radiation safety.
“An attack by a [unmanned aerial vehicle] UAV on the grounds of the Institute for Nuclear Research is an attack on a peaceful nuclear facility that performs exclusively scientific and research functions,” the regulator said.
It described the strike as another violation of internationally recognized nuclear and radiation safety principles, characterizing it as a war crime.
UAE Government Used Sanctioned Russian ‘Shadow’ Airline
Institute conducts peaceful nuclear research
The Institute for Nuclear Research of Ukraine’s National Academy of Sciences is one of the country’s leading research institutions in nuclear physics, nuclear energy, and radioecology.
Its VVR-M reactor serves as a neutron source for fundamental and applied nuclear physics research.
The institute also operates particle accelerators and laboratories used for research in radiation physics, nuclear technologies, and reactor materials.
Russia continues attacks on Kyiv
The strike on the institute occurred during an extended series of Russian attacks on Kyiv and other Ukrainian regions.
On Wednesday, Russia launched its first mass combined attack on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure since the end of the previous heating season, using missiles and drones against facilities in Kyiv, the surrounding region and elsewhere. The assault affected 11 regions, killing five people, including a child, and injuring 14.
Russian attacks on the capital continued into Thursday. A drone struck a school in Kyiv’s Solomianskyi district while children were sheltering during an air raid alert, damaging the third floor and causing a fire. The children were not injured, and firefighters extinguished the blaze. Russian forces also struck warehouse facilities in the same district.
Later on Thursday, two Russian drone strikes hit near the supports of Kyiv’s Pivdennyi (South) Bridge, forcing authorities to suspend metro and surface public transport across the bridge. Municipal specialists began inspecting the structure, while social media claims that a drone struck as a metro train was crossing, blowing out windows in one of its cars.
Previously, Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi said that Russia has launched a renewed campaign of mass assaults against Ukraine’s energy infrastructure ahead of the winter.
“Since the summer, there has effectively not been a single day when the enemy did not attack energy infrastructure. But such a massive and combined attack took place for the first time since the end of the previous heating season,” he said.
The strikes damaged and destroyed energy equipment, although Koretskyi did not disclose which facilities were hit or the extent of the damage. He said he was awaiting a detailed report on the condition of the equipment and the expected timeframe for repairs.
The attacks also disrupted electricity supplies in the capital and the surrounding Kyiv region. DTEK said emergency power cuts were introduced in Kyiv on Ukrenergo’s instructions, meaning regular schedules temporarily did not apply. The capital was later returned to scheduled stabilization outages, while planned power-cut schedules were also introduced across the Kyiv region on Wednesday.
