articles.title: Ukraine scrambles as Russia’s jet drones breach Kyiv’s defences
articles.body:
Ukraine scrambles as Russia’s jet drones breach Kyiv’s defences
Daily strikes turn the Ukrainian capital into frontline city as Moscow deploys high-speed drones
Russia’s new class of jet-powered drones rip across the night sky in Kyiv at hundreds of kilometres per hour, leaving Ukrainian air-defence units only moments to intercept them. It’s rarely enough time.
With many of the drones getting through to the capital, defence manufacturers are scrambling to develop a new generation of interceptors to counter the deadly threat. They are building their own jet propulsion systems and training artificial intelligence to help guide the chase.
They need to move fast because the Russian drones are driving a new tactic, ramped up in recent weeks, to hit the infrastructure keeping Ukraine’s war-battered economy afloat. Recent targets have included energy systems, key industries, railways, post offices, shopping centres, telecom networks, petrol stations and grain exports.
Russia also has an advantage with its ballistic missile arsenal, which poses another challenge as Ukraine runs low on interceptor missiles.

articles.title: Pentagon taps Musk and Luckey to map the future of war
articles.body:
- Secretary of War Pete Hegseth announced Project Meridian on Sept. 30, co-led by Elon Musk, Palmer Luckey and Newt Gingrich.
- The 120-day study will identify future battlefields and the technologies U.S. forces need, with findings due in a public report.
Secretary of War Pete Hegseth has put Elon Musk, Anduril co-founder Palmer Luckey and former House Speaker Newt Gingrich in charge of Project Meridian, a 120-day Pentagon study of where future wars will be fought and what weapons the U.S. military will need to win them.
Hegseth announced the project on Sept. 30 during his “State of the Force” address at Marine Corps Base Quantico, Virginia, after Pirate Wires first reported the plan. The three co-leads will work under Emil Michael, the Department of War’s chief technology officer, alongside a wider team drawn from industry, academia and the policy world, though the Pentagon has not said how many people will take part or whether the co-leads will be paid.
“Project Meridian will provide the transformative vision to secure American dominance across every future warfighting domain,” the Department of War’s chief technology office wrote on X.
In a letter launching the effort, Hegseth directed Michael to study the battlefields of the future, identify the weapons and technologies troops will need there, and propose concrete steps to start developing, testing and fielding them. The findings are due within 120 days, which puts the deadline in late January 2027, and are expected to be released in an unclassified report with a classified annex. Hegseth said the Joint Staff and all the military services should be ready to connect their own future-warfare research to the project.
Hegseth framed the effort as a look decades ahead, saying it would consider the wars the United States cannot afford to fight in 2030, 2050 and 2100. He also said the project was deliberately futuristic and was not meant to produce new strategies or policies, The Hill reported, and that the three co-leads would hold their first meeting immediately after the speech in a secure facility at the base.
The choice of leaders has drawn attention because two of them run companies that sell to the Pentagon. Musk’s SpaceX holds billions of dollars in U.S. military contracts for rocket launches and satellites, and Luckey’s Anduril builds drones, counter-drone systems and other autonomous weapons for the U.S. Army, U.S. Navy and other services, the kinds of technologies a study of future warfare is likely to examine. The Pentagon has not said how it will handle potential conflicts of interest.
The appointment is also Musk’s first official advisory role in the Trump administration since he left the Department of Government Efficiency and fell out publicly with President Donald Trump last year, Axios reported. Gingrich, who led the House from 1995 to 1999, has long written and spoken about defense reform and space policy.
Project Meridian was one of several changes Hegseth announced in the same speech, which also included a new Autonomous Warfare Command focused on robotic, drone and artificial intelligence warfare, and a plan to cut 20% of general and admiral positions by January.

articles.title: Trump’s surrender fantasy: The knot in talks
articles.body:
Trump’s surrender fantasy: The knot in talks
TEHRAN — Iran has received Washington’s response to its latest initiative aimed at ending the seven-month-long conflict that began with unprovoked, joint US-Israeli strikes on February 28, as President Donald Trump remains stubbornly wedded to the delusion that military pressure and economic warfare can force the Islamic Republic into submission.
The US response was submitted to President Masoud Pezeshkian during a Cabinet session on Wednesday by Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, government spokesperson Fatemeh Mohajerani confirmed.
Addressing the Cabinet, President Pezeshkian reaffirmed Tehran’s principled position on resolving the crisis through diplomacy without compromising fundamental rights.
“We will make every effort to bring the agreement to fruition and will firmly stand up for the rights of the Iranian people,” Pezeshkian said, emphasizing: “The agreement must now be based on a win-win strategy.”
The development follows Araghchi’s return from the 81st Session of the United Nations General Assembly in New York, where Iranian diplomats engaged in indirect exchanges with American representatives while holding intensive consultations on the sidelines with Qatari and Pakistani mediators. Mohajerani noted that Araghchi briefed the Cabinet on these diplomatic engagements, which detailed Iran’s framework for reopening the strategic Strait of Hormuz.
Last week, Araghchi presented a comprehensive seven-point proposal to reopen the waterway within seven days, contingent upon Washington lifting its naval blockade of Iranian ports, unfreezing national assets, and removing illegal sanctions on Iranian oil exports. While Trump hastily dismissed the initiative—claiming Iran was “losing so badly” and that Tehran’s terms “would not be acceptable”—regional mediators have persisted in their efforts to forge a diplomatic resolution based on the reality on the ground.
Paralyzed by strategic deadlock
Tehran views Washington’s mixed signals not as strength, but as profound strategic disorientation. Speaking on Tuesday during a meeting in Tehran with Shahin Mustafayev, Azerbaijan’s Deputy Prime Minister, Major General Mohsen Rezaei, Secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council (SNSC), characterized the US president as trapped in a state of absolute paralysis.
“Trump is caught in a quagmire where he can neither negotiate nor fight,” Rezaei stated. “Iran’s conditions have been conveyed to the United States, but Trump is unable to make a decision, and the United States, out of desperation, has resorted to an air siege in the military war.”
Denouncing the initial February 28 aggression as a blatant violation of international law, Rezaei noted that Iran “powerfully defended itself,” citing the hundreds of precise drone and missile retaliatory strikes conducted by the Iranian Armed Forces against US and Israeli military installations across the region. Tehran has repeatedly cautioned Washington that it will never leave any act of aggression unanswered, demonstrating through seven months of sustained resistance that its deterrence remains fully intact.
This is not the first time Washington has squandered diplomatic off-ramps. Following the collapse of the fragile April 8 ceasefire and the subsequent Islamabad memorandum of understanding (MoU) brokered on June 17, Tehran has demonstrated a readiness to engage in serious diplomacy if national sovereignty is respected. President Pezeshkian reiterated his commitment to seeing the Islamabad MoU come to fruition while safeguarding vital national interests, rejecting US bullying: “We will never bow our head or bend at the knee.”
From military failure to psychological warfare
Having failed to break Iran’s defensive capabilities, the US and Israel have shifted their tactics toward internal disruption. Addressing mayors of major metropolitan centers and provincial capitals on Tuesday, President Pezeshkian pointed out that Washington and Tel Aviv have pivoted toward hybrid subversion after suffering strategic setbacks on the battlefield.
“After failing to force the Iranian people to surrender through military war, enemies have focused their entire plan on creating and intensifying internal divisions,” Pezeshkian cautioned.
Despite this dual track of subversion and rhetoric, the White House continues to escalate coercive measures. On Tuesday, the US Treasury Department unveiled fresh sanctions under its so-called “Operation Economic Outcast,” blacklisting ten individuals and entities across Iran, Hong Kong, and Pakistan over alleged roles in Iran’s defense procurement.
Trump’s search for an off-ramp
However, the coercive campaign has boomeranged disastrously onto the US domestic arena. With US legislative elections just five weeks away, polls indicate that Trump’s war against Iran has been overwhelmingly unpopular from its inception. The disruption of Persian Gulf transit corridors and the subsequent spike in global crude prices have placed immense strain on American households, threatening Republican control of both chambers of Congress.
In a stark illustration of the domestic fallout, California Governor Gavin Newsom suspended the state’s seasonal summer-blend gasoline requirement, directing regulatory bodies to immediately permit the distribution of cheaper winter-blend fuel. In just seven months, Trump’s war has drained over $120 billion in extra fuel expenses from American consumers—imposing an estimated $428 burden on every California household and eroding US economic stability.
With domestic outrage mounting, the Islamic Revolution Guards Corps (IRGC) directly addressed the American public on Tuesday in an unprecedented 26-page open letter, calling on voters to reject the architects of the conflict.
“Remove from power the evil, deceitful, and violent politicians who are responsible for America’s current state,” the IRGC stated, adding: “Make sure your politicians understand that the world has changed.”
While Donald Trump is desperately seeking an off-ramp before voters head to the polls, analysts emphasize that any genuine breakthrough will remain elusive until Washington completely discards the Israeli-instigated illusion that Iran can be coerced into capitulation. Until the White House frees itself from Tel Aviv’s maximalist adventurism and faces strategic realities, its policies will remain locked in the very quagmire of its own making.

articles.title: Iran warns regional states against hosting Israeli officials after Netanyahu’s UAE visit
articles.body:
Iran warns regional states against hosting Israeli officials after Netanyahu’s UAE visit
TEHRAN – Iran has warned regional countries about the consequences of the presence of destabilizing actors such as Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on their soils, warning about Tel Aviv’s efforts to sow regional tensions.
Iran’s Foreign Ministry issued the remarks in a statement on Tuesday, reacting to reports of Netanyahu’s presence in the UAE at the official invitation of Emirati ruler Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan.
It strongly condemned the “child-killing and war-mongering prime minister of the Israeli regime’s provocative presence” in the region and warned of the “extremely dangerous consequences.”
The ministry noted that “regional security is a collective and indivisible matter,” warning that facilitating the entry of destabilizing actors could lead to “greater division, insecurity, and instability in West Asia.”
It called on regional governments to “refrain from facilitating the Israeli regime’s destabilizing presence” and to prevent their territories from becoming “a platform for destabilizing actions against other countries in the region.”
The statement reminded that the region was experiencing “one of the most fragile and sensitive periods in its history,” citing the regime’s “proven hostility and animosity towards Iran and other countries in the region” and its “repeated threats” against the Islamic Republic.
“All countries in the region must be vigilant about the consequences and repercussions of such a presence, which threatens regional peace and collective security,” the ministry said.
The strong rebuke followed reports by Israeli media and statements from senior Israeli officials to Reuters confirming that Netanyahu paid a visit to Abu Dhabi on Sunday, holding closed-door consultations with UAE President Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan for most of the day before returning to Tel Aviv.
The trip was initially kept under wraps. Late on Monday, the United Arab Emirates officially confirmed that Netanyahu had met with Sheikh Mohamed over the weekend. Israeli broadcaster Channel 12 was the first to break news of the visit, prompting Israel’s internal security agency, Shin Bet, to file an immediate complaint with the military censor over alleged breaches of operational secrecy.
According to Reuters, the weekend trip was not Netanyahu’s first covert foray into Abu Dhabi; the Israeli premier had also traveled secretly to the Persian Gulf state on March 26 for closed-door discussions with the Emirati leadership.
Normalization as an instrument of destabilization
Ties between Abu Dhabi and Tel Aviv were formalized in 2020 through the controversial, US-brokered Abraham Accords. While marketed by Washington and Abu Dhabi as an engine for regional “peace and prosperity,” the normalization drive has systematically functioned as a mechanism to fracture Islamic and regional unity, undermine the Palestinian liberation struggle, and embed the Zionist regime directly along the strategic waterways of the Persian Gulf.
Over the past four years, the UAE has evolved into Israel’s primary operational, logistical, and commercial bridgehead in the immediate neighborhood. Rather than fostering regional coexistence, Abu Dhabi’s entente with Tel Aviv has exacerbated regional fault lines.
Strategic and military integration between the two sides has deepened rapidly. In May, United States Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee stated that Israel had deployed Iron Dome air defense batteries and operational personnel directly to the UAE. The presence of Israeli military hardware and intelligence operatives on Emirati soil represents a direct violation of regional security arrangements and a blatant concession of Persian Gulf sovereign territory to an expansionist entity actively carrying out genocidal aggression against the Palestinian people in Gaza and escalating confrontations across the regional front.
Political observers have repeatedly warned that the UAE’s willingness to outsource its defense architecture to Tel Aviv compromises the collective security of all littoral states. By permitting Israeli intelligence agencies and military hardware to establish footprints just kilometers away from Iranian shores, Abu Dhabi is transforming the Persian Gulf from a zone of peaceful commerce and sovereign cooperation into a theater of Zionist espionage and provocation.
A pattern of malign regional intervention
The welcoming of Netanyahu into the Emirati capital is seen by analysts as part of a wider, destructive pattern defining Abu Dhabi’s regional foreign policy over the past decade.
Across West Asia and North Africa, the UAE has repeatedly operated as a destabilizing force, pursuing interventionist agendas that have fueled sectarian friction, funded mercenary proxy networks, and undermined sovereign central governments.
From its active participation in the devastating, years-long war of aggression against Yemen—which created one of the worst humanitarian catastrophes of the modern era—to its illegal occupation of strategic Yemeni islands such as Socotra and Mayyun, Abu Dhabi has sought to unilaterally dominate maritime chokepoints along the Red Sea and the Bab al-Mandab Strait. Extensive reports have revealed that the UAE has facilitated Israeli intelligence installations on Socotra, leveraging occupied Yemeni territories to project joint Israeli-Emirati influence over vital international shipping corridors.
Beyond the Arabian Peninsula, Abu Dhabi’s footprint has proven equally destructive in the Horn of Africa and North Africa. In Sudan, the UAE has drawn fierce international condemnation for arming and financing the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), whose campaign has pushed the country into devastating civil war and famine. In Libya, Emirati financial and military backing for renegade military factions severely derailed United Nations peace efforts for years.
By tying its regional ambitions to Tel Aviv’s geopolitical objectives, the UAE is effectively functioning as a sub-imperial vector for Western and Zionist interests, attempting to displace the organic, sovereign mechanisms of indigenous regional diplomacy in favor of imported, militarized alliances.
The secretive summit in Abu Dhabi also underscores Netanyahu’s desperate drive to manufacture diplomatic breakthroughs abroad to stave off mounting domestic collapse at home.
Facing intense internal turmoil and trailing sharply in domestic polls ahead of Knesset elections, the beleaguered Israeli prime minister is confronting fierce political challenges.
Facing persistent corruption trials and widespread public outrage over his regime’s strategic failures in Gaza and the North, Netanyahu is exploiting ties with Abu Dhabi as a political lifeline. By rolling out the red carpet for a war criminal wanted for crimes against humanity, Abu Dhabi is not only shielding Netanyahu from international isolation but actively facilitating his political survival.

articles.title: Russia is now wiring its attack drones into one network in flight, so a single drone can scout, strike, and relay for the rest
articles.body:
Russia is wiring its long-range attack drones together by a mesh network in flight and buying pricier, higher-resolution cameras for them, Ukraine's Air Force reported on 29 September. Its spokesperson said one drone could serve as a scout, strike drone, and relay for the rest, which is why they often fly one behind another over long distances. Chains of them keep crossing near the Belarus border, UkrInform reports.
For Ukraine, the danger in each such upgrade is arithmetic: the more Russia networks cheap, once-disposable drones and pushes its control links away from the front, the harder they become to jam or shoot down, and the more of them reach the cities they are aimed at.
Sharper, pricier eyes
Ihnat said on a national broadcast that Russia is sourcing higher-quality materials and raising the resolution of its drone cameras. The cameras it buys are increasingly expensive and higher-quality, he said, which lets its operators study the ground in fine detail and use each drone for a specific purpose.
On a mesh network, he said, the drones talk to each other and hand the control signal back toward the operator, so no single link has to carry it alone.
Russia is mapping everyday targets across Kyiv, from trolleybus depots to Zhuliany airport, top monitoring channel says, ahead of next ballistic strike
Chains along the Belarus border
Asked about relays operating out of Belarus and about Russia's guidance of jet-powered Shaheds, the exploding drones it fires in swarms, Ihnat said Moscow had already claimed its satellite network was ready. He confirmed mesh networks are in use and said their use was quite dangerous. Ukraine has no information yet on whether Russia is using towers, he said.
It often sees drones crossing long distances in chains along the Ukrainian-Belarusian border, so nothing can be ruled out, but intelligence would have to confirm whether such relays exist. Asked whether Russia is preparing a fresh ballistic strike, he said intelligence would warn when extra vigilance is needed.
Ukraine's countermeasures
Ihnat has also said Russia launched more attack drones in September than in August, counting 3,177 jet-powered drones so far this month against 2,850 in August. To knock them down, Ukraine leans mainly on tactical aviation, including F-16 fighters, and on ground-based air defense when missiles are available, he said, with shoulder-fired man-portable air-defense systems (MANPADS) working well against jet drones inside their range. He said Ukraine needs more missiles for both Patriot systems and ground-based launchers, plus faster domestic solutions it can scale up.

articles.title: Moscow’s message to European business: your Russian assets are now leverage against your governments
articles.body:
The Kremlin is signaling that it will hold the Russian assets of European companies hostage to pressure Europe into rethinking its sanctions, the Institute for the Study of War (ISW) wrote on 30 September. Moscow has already put well-known European retailers and food makers under Russian "temporary management." A senior Russian official has now hinted that European banks could be next.
As Russia continues its invasion of Ukraine, it has long turned hostages and threats into weapons. Its record includes nuclear threats against Europe from its Oreshnik missile launch sites and a fresh warning over Kaliningrad. It has played games with Europe's largest nuclear plant that it occupied in 2022, applied gas and water pressure on its neighbors, and Kyiv accuses it of blackmailing the families of Ukrainian prisoners of war. Europe's companies are now one more lever in that kit.
"Let them be scared"
Russia is taking "asymmetric measures" to make Europe rethink its sanctions, a senior Russian government source with direct knowledge of the seizures claimed, Reuters reported. "Let them think about what measures they are taking and what sanctions they are introducing," the source said.
Asked whether the Russian units of Italy's UniCredit and Austria's Raiffeisen could be placed under temporary management, the source answered: "Let them be scared."
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov claimed the decisions were driven by "the increasing level of involvement of these unfriendly countries in direct battlefield hostilities" against Russia. He suggested the moves were "reversible," but added: "For now, we do not see any grounds for a reversal."
EU lawmakers renew push to seize frozen Russian assets as Ukraine faces its toughest winter yet with a €23 billion defense funding gap
Nestlé, Auchan, and Metro under "temporary management"
Putin's decree of 17 September placed 16 companies under the "temporary management" of a firm called L.E.V. Management, with no end date. They include the Russian units of France's Auchan and Lemana PRO, formerly Leroy Merlin, and of Switzerland's Nestlé. A second decree, on 28 September, handed the Russian assets of German wholesaler Metro AG to UK Torg Rus.
Both decrees amend Putin's April 2023 decree No. 302, which lets Moscow take over the property of firms tied to countries it labels "unfriendly." Because the "temporary" management has no expiry date, ISW considers it effectively nationalization. Independent outlet Novaya Gazeta Europe identified L.E.V. Management's director as retired Russian Major General Andrei Krayushkin.
European companies as corporate hostages
The Kremlin likely wants to use the seizures to take European companies as corporate hostages, ISW assessed. It also likely expects a temporary fiscal boost from the revenues of the seized businesses.
The strategy assumes that European firms will judge the benefits of staying in Russia to outweigh the risk of losing their assets, the think tank said. Whether a company is seized depends entirely on Moscow's relations with the country where it is headquartered, ISW added.
Seizing others' property is an old Moscow habit
Since the start of the full-scale war, Russia has introduced temporary administration at 135 foreign-linked firms, mostly from EU countries, according to TASS data cited by Reuters. Earlier targets included French food group Danone and Danish brewer Carlsberg.
The method was tested on Ukraine first. Russia's proxies in occupied Donetsk and Luhansk oblasts stole most Ukrainian assets there in 2014 and 2015. In March 2017, after Ukrainian activists blocked rail trade with the occupied areas, they placed the remaining Ukrainian-registered firms under "temporary administrations," a label close to the one Moscow uses today. The published Donetsk list alone ran to 43 assets, from coal mines and ironworks to the Donbas Arena stadium. Much of the coal and steel business later ended up with firms tied to Serhii Kurchenko, a fugitive oligarch from Yanukovych's era.

articles.title: Zelenskyy orders review of agreements on F-16 ammunition, air defense missile supplies
articles.body:
The Ministry of Foreign Affairs, the Ministry of Defense, and the team at the Office of the President of Ukraine will conduct an urgent review of agreements with partners regarding the supply of ammunition for F-16 fighter jets and air defense missiles, and must prepare an updated delivery schedule by Friday, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy announced.
“First, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, the Ministry of Defense, and the Office team will conduct an immediate review of the agreements reached with our partners on providing F-16s with the necessary ammunition. The same applies to the supply of air defense missiles – country by country, agreement by agreement, and package by package – with an updated schedule of deliveries for Ukraine to be presented by tomorrow,” Zelenskyy said on X Thursday.
He emphasized the importance of delivering additional missiles to Ukraine this October.
“As of today, some of our agreements already approved by national leaders have still not been implemented at the command level,” the President noted.
He thanked Germany, Norway, Finland, and all other partners ready to work as quickly as possible. The head of state added that he had been in contact with leaders on Wednesday and Thursday, noting that "it is important to spur the teams into action."

articles.title: A useful ritual: Why authoritarian regimes still need elections — and why Russia’s model is weakening
articles.body:
From Sept. 18 to 20, Russia held its first State Duma elections since the start of the full-scale invasion of Ukraine. The official results — nearly 58% in favor of the Kremlin’s ruling United Russia party — appear to have been inflated by upwards of 23%. Over Vladimir Putin’s 26 years in power, the country’s electoral system has evolved from one that was at least somewhat competitive into one that is tightly controlled. At first glance, it might seem like a government this authoritarian would be able to dispense with elections entirely, simply appointing officials directly rather than putting them through an electoral process that is almost entirely manipulated. Yet Putin’s Russia, like most autocracies, prefers to preserve elections as an instrument of political legitimization. Elections allow governments — even authoritarian ones — to safely co-opt opponents and refresh its cadre of elites, reducing the likelihood of internal conflict while gathering information about officials’ performance and the strength of potential rivals. Russia’s electoral system, however, has now reached such a high level of restriction that these stabilizing functions are becoming less effective. Voting is ceasing to serve as a feedback channel and instead risks becoming a problem for the system itself.
Allowed to run, then banned when the authorities got nervous
On Aug. 10, Russia’s Supreme Court barred the anti-war Yabloko party from running in the September parliamentary election. The traditional “liberal” party entered the campaign in an extremely weakened state: it no longer had the necessary financial resources to run a major campaign, nor did it boast a line-up of candidates with sufficient charisma and name-recognition to attract voters on their own. Some of its most prominent figures, including Lev Shlosberg in Pskov and Maxim Kruglov in Moscow, were being held in pretrial detention. Others were barred from running because of new legal restrictions.
Most Russians had not heard much about Yabloko in recent years, and its support had hovered around 1% for over a decade, receiving an official 1.34% of the vote in the 2021 Duma election as opposition-minded Russians cast their ballots en masse for the Communist Party as part of the late Alexei Navalny’s “smart voting” campaign. In other words, Yabloko’s participation in the fall election initially appeared to pose little threat to Russia’s political system.
Then Yabloko’s anti-war platform unexpectedly began attracting widespread attention, including among young people on TikTok. Videos supporting the party went viral, mentions of Yabloko on social media began approaching those of the Communist Party, and even previously apolitical bloggers joined the trend.
After being added to the ballot, Yabloko’s polling numbers rose sharply with even Kremlin-friendly pollsters recording the change. According to the Public Opinion Foundation (FOM), support for the party rose from 1% in July to 4% in early August.
Within days of appearing on the ballot, Yabloko’s poll numbers surged
Data published by the state-run Russian Public Opinion Research Center (VTsIOM) is even more revealing. VTsIOM does not publish separate results for parties that did not clear the 5% threshold in the 2021 election, instead combining them into a single category. In mid-July, that group was polling at around 4%. However, by Aug. 2, it had reached 10.3%, and by Aug. 9, it stood at 12.7%. After Yabloko was removed from the slate of available options, the figure fell back to 4.1%.
The difference — 8.6 percentage points — was almost certainly attributable to Yabloko, and the figure roughly matched leaked data from unpublished polling. At that level of support, the party would have comfortably cleared the 5% barrier necessary for representation in the State Duma. Even more importantly, that support appeared to still be in the early stages of growth.
presidential administration sets the basic parameters in advance — deciding which parties and candidates will compete, where they will run, and roughly how many votes they will receive. Vladimir Putin’s ruling United Russia party had already reached agreements with its nominal opponents over the division of single-member districts in order to avoid competition even at that level. The expectation was that the so-called “systemic opposition” — officially registered parties that operate within the Kremlin-controlled political system — would be allowed to win in the 16 districts where no United Russia nominees appeared on the ballot. Unsurprisingly, candidates from United Russia won elections in 208 out of the country’s 224 single-mandate districts, leaving precisely 16 such seats to politicians from the Kremlin-approved “opposition,”
Meanwhile, activist networks and genuinely anti-Kremlin politicians were, as usual, neutralized through repression long before voting began. Parties with representation in the Duma frequently decline to nominate strong candidates so as not to lose the Kremlin’s approval for participation, and unwanted independent contenders are prevented from collecting signatures or are denied registration even after seeming to have met all of the bureaucratic obstacles to inclusion. And of course, election results themselves can be falsified or adjusted through opaque electronic voting systems.
By 2026, opportunities for independent election monitoring had been reduced to almost zero. Organizations that previously took on that task, including the independent group Golos, have been subjected to repression, with the movement’s co-chair Grigory Melkonyants handed five years in prison in May 2025. Candidates have also lost the right to appoint commission members with advisory voting rights, a mechanism that had remained an important tool for monitoring during the previous election campaign.
That raises an obvious question: if Russia’s presidential administration already controls the election process almost entirely, why hold elections at all? Why not simply appoint officials instead of putting them through a nominal electoral process that runs the risk of producing evidence of falsification potentially serious enough to threaten a loss of control?
What elections do for autocracies
According to calculations by Danish researcher Merete Bech Seeberg, before the end of the Cold War 65% of authoritarian regimes worldwide qualified as “electoral autocracies” — systems that held elections in some form — but in only 15% of these cases were alternative options permitted to appear on the ballot.
A major shift came during the so-called “third wave” of democratization from 1974 to 1991, which culminated in the collapse of the Soviet bloc. As the overall number of authoritarian regimes fell, the way those regimes were structured also changed.
During the Cold War, only about 15% of the autocracies mentioned above held actual multiparty elections. Afterward, however, that share rose to 55%. This did not simply reflect the disappearance of other regime types. Hegemonic authoritarian regimes — systems built around a dominant ruling party such as United Russia — increased their share of all political regimes worldwide from 10% to 27%.
During the Cold War, only about 15% of autocracies held multiparty elections. Afterward, the figure rose to 55%
Today, even highly authoritarian countries such as China and Iran hold elections in which voters are formally offered more than one party or candidate. Iran has no single dominant party, and elections can be relatively competitive among approved candidates. The main filtering takes place before voting, when the Guardian Council excludes office-seekers deemed insufficiently loyal.
In China, the Communist Party holds more than 80% of seats in the National People’s Congress, and its leading role is enshrined in the constitution. However, eight other parties are represented, along with independent candidates. Notably though, none describe themselves as being opposed to the Communist Party.
Since 2023, even North Korea has formally allowed voters to cast ballots against candidates proposed by the authorities, although only about one-tenth of 1% of voters reportedly dared to do so.
Research shows that while elections can pose short-term risks to authoritarian governments, allowing opposition forces to mobilize supporters and coordinate protests, over the longer term, elections tend to strengthen such regimes. In both democracies and autocracies, elections perform several important functions beyond simply deciding who takes office.
Co-opting elites
Elections determine who gets access to political office. In an autocracy, the regime controls the limits of acceptable choice and can use elections to bring people with their own independent resources into the system. A businessperson, regional politician or other influential figure receives an office and the benefits that come with it, but at the same time becomes integrated into institutions controlled by the state.
Elections can similarly co-opt part of the opposition. A potential rival is offered limited political influence within the system in exchange for giving up efforts to overthrow it.
In Russia, for example, businesspeople are more likely to enter politics in poorer regions and in places where parties spend less money building their own networks. That allows businesses to protect their lobbying investments and increase profits, while parties gain access to private resources in parts of the country where their own organizations are weak.
Researchers note that business-linked candidates are less likely to run in wealthy regions, less likely to compete simultaneously in both single-member districts and party lists — which would insure them against defeat — and less likely to receive paid political positions. Most importantly, they are less likely to run again after serving one term, even though incumbents usually have an advantage when it comes to reelection.
Gathering information
Election campaigns reveal which candidates can independently mobilize voters, which groups possess their own political resources and which issues attract public attention. For an autocrat, information about potential rivals is particularly valuable. An unexpectedly strong result by a candidate or party can reveal that they have a larger political network than authorities had assumed.
Past campaigns have helped Russian authorities identify where opposition groups are strongest and then target activists and prominent lawmakers in those areas. For example, the government may bar popular Communist Party lawmakers such as Nikolai Bondarenko from running or refuse to register lists of Yabloko’s candidates precisely in those places where the party has a realistic chance of winning seats.
Managing conflicts inside the political system and rotating elites
Political coalitions are constantly changing. Some groups become stronger, others lose influence. Governors are replaced along with the patronage networks surrounding them, and new categories of potentially loyal personnel emerge.
Election cycles allow these shifts to be translated into formal changes in representation without abandoning the rules through which offices are distributed. Russian political scientist Grigory Golosov, studying three electoral cycles between 2003 and 2014, showed that changes in regional governors were usually accompanied by unusually high turnover among regional lawmakers.
The same pattern was visible in the current campaign. Many lawmakers who did not seek reelection were either associated with governors who had left office, had fallen into conflict with sitting governors, or were tied to politicians and organizations that had lost influence (such as followers of the late nationalist politician Vladimir Zhirinovsky or some of the remaining figures associated with the All-Russia People’s Front, a Kremlin-created political coalition).
Legitimacy
Authoritarian regimes use the fact that voting takes place — and the officially declared support of a majority — to portray themselves as expressions of the popular will. The electoral process preserves the appearance of a public mandate, while high turnout and electoral victories allow regimes to demonstrate to loyal elites, society, and outside observers that they still command support.
Eliminating elections entirely can be risky for authoritarian governments. Studies show that democracies are considerably more stable and less likely to descend into civil war than multiparty autocracies. Multiparty autocracies, in turn, are somewhat more stable than one-party regimes that hold elections without genuine competition. The difference between those two authoritarian models is relatively small: when dominant-party autocracies become one-party states, intraparty competition often survives and replaces competition between parties meaning that even if United Russia were to ban every other party, internal primaries would still ensure some minimal form of political competition. Still, the bigger picture shows that such a regime would be less stable than Russia’s current multiparty authoritarian system.
A striking Russian example is the abolition of direct mayoral elections. Researchers analyzed more than 400,000 responses to Russian public-opinion surveys over the past 25 years and found that abolishing mayoral elections had reduced support for Vladimir Putin. The effect was strongest in places where elections had previously been more competitive. Citizens who had experienced a genuine choice reacted more strongly when that choice was taken away.
From one-party systems to dominant parties
After the collapse of the Eastern bloc in 1989 and the fall of the Soviet Union in 1991, the states that became independent of Moscow’s influence faced a situation in which the ruling party that had previously bound the system together lost control. The European Union exerted significant influence on these countries, demanding political reforms in exchange for the provision of aid and the establishment of closer economic ties.
Even so, dominant-party regimes still emerged in a number of countries (including Ukraine, Georgia, and Croatia) before the democratisation truly began. Transnational networks of nongovernmental organizations and democracy-supporting institutions contributed to those transitions.
Central Asia, by contrast, lacked such an institutional anchor. The Soviet Union was often viewed there as a broadly progressive project, and local elites had little incentive to break sharply with the past, particularly because they hoped to preserve their privileges. As a result, many of the same power structures that had existed before the Soviet collapse survived.
In most Central Asian states, the Communist Party of the Soviet Union effectively changed its name and was replaced by local dominant parties led by former first secretaries of Communist Party organizations — a common model for one-party regimes. Between 1950 and 2006, only 19.3% of transitions from one-party regimes ended in democracy, while about one-third transformed into dominant-party systems. Another 38.6% became military regimes. Dominant-party regimes, by comparison, had roughly equal chances of becoming either one-party systems (28.6%) or democracies (30.2%).
Between 1950 and 2006, only 19.3% of transitions from one-party regimes ended in democracy
Russia stood at a crossroads. Boris Yeltsin was in a confrontation with the Communist Party and its central apparatus. He therefore could not simply transform the old Soviet nomenklatura into a new ruling party capable of controlling the state apparatus and regulating the distribution of offices and resources.
Ora John Reuter, in his book on the rise of United Russia, also argues that Yeltsin was unable to create a dominant party due to the fact the federal government was too weak to offer governors sufficient incentives to join a nationwide party project. Governors possessed their own political machines and resources and were unwilling to invest them in such a party. As a result, the Kremlin itself had little reason to commit substantial resources to building one.
That changed in the early 2000s. As Reuter notes, rising oil revenues after Putin came to power gave governors an incentive to trade loyalty and their ability to deliver votes in the regions for resources from the federal center. The Kremlin, meanwhile, needed their support in order to carry out reforms and govern the country. Both sides therefore gained from investing in a party that could regulate that exchange. The governors who resisted joining United Russia for the longest tended to oversee wealthier regions with more developed economies and to enjoy high personal popularity, or to lead ethnic republics where politics relied heavily on personal networks.
How a dominant-party regime can change
As long as the state has sufficient resources at its command, a dominant party can maintain its advantage. Comparative research on dominant-party regimes shows that their edge comes less from popularity than from their ability to provide supporters with jobs and state benefits and maintain a larger organizational network than the opposition.
As long as that resource base remains intact, even elections free of direct ballot-rigging do not necessarily create equal competition. However, when the state begins losing control over economic resources, such as through privatization or a shrinking public sector, the ruling party’s advantages weaken, giving the opposition a chance to build an organization of comparable strength.
Since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February of 2022, the space for political competition has narrowed dramatically. In recent years, laws and enforcement practices have tightened to the point that the authorities can remove a candidate from an election — or even strip an already elected lawmaker of office — at virtually any time. Holding office no longer provides protection or meaningful lobbying opportunities. Instead, it can attract unwanted attention from Russia’s security services or expose the officeholder to international sanctions. As a result, the number of people willing to run for office has dropped significantly, especially among businesspeople.
Holding office no longer provides protection or meaningful lobbying opportunities. Instead, it can attract unwanted attention from Russia’s security agencies or expose the officeholder to international sanctions
These changes mean elections are becoming less effective at stabilizing the political system. The regime’s ability to co-opt strong opponents is declining, forcing it to refresh elites increasingly from within the state bureaucracy. At the same time, the amount of money available for election campaigns is shrinking, as is candidates’ ability to reflect voters’ actual concerns and preferences and, as a result, mobilize supporters of the regime.
As often happens in authoritarian systems, the mechanisms used to gather information about citizens and public sentiment also become distorted. Over time, that leads to accumulated errors and growing public dissatisfaction. Paradoxically, the more tightly the government controls the electoral process, the greater the chance that, over the long term, that control will gradually weaken and the political system will become increasingly difficult to manage.
That reality did not lead to anything resembling a seismic event after the Russian Central Election Commission declared United Russia the winner of a flagrantly inflated 58% of the vote earlier this week. It remains to be seen what effect it may have on the country’s next presidential election in 2030.

articles.body:

Bulgaria not only has a long-standing history in space exploration, science, and technology, but also has a well-deserved place in today’s joint efforts to develop European space capabilities, said Prime Minister Rumen Radev at the Euronews Defense and Space Summit in Brussels, according to the government press service.
The Prime Minister highlighted the country’s strong traditions in this field, as well as its recent achievements, with the Bulgarian company EnduroSat standing out as a prime example. He recalled that Bulgaria was the sixth country in the world to send a representative into Earth’s orbit. Radev also noted that just two decades ago, space was the exclusive domain for countries with enormous financial resources and industrial capacity. Advances in new technologies and artificial intelligence, however, had greatly expanded the available opportunities, the Bulgarian Prime Minister concluded.
“When Putin feels strong, he does not talk about nuclear weapons, but when Russia feels weak, talk of nuclear weapons start again. We need to have this into account. We cannot close our eyes (to the fact) that there are nuclear weapons on our continent, there are nuclear weapons in the arsenal of Russia. And this is part of the game calculation”, Radev said in an interview with “Euronews.”

articles.title: Latvia could host nuclear weapons if NATO chooses to deploy them, president says
articles.body:
Nuclear weapons could be stationed in Latvia if NATO decides to do so and the need arises, Latvian President Edgars Rinkēvičs said.
“Our laws pose no legal obstacles to stationing nuclear weapons in Latvia,” he said.
No specific talks on stationing nuclear weapons in Latvia are currently underway, however, Rinkēvičs said.
On September 29, Britain proposed extending its nuclear umbrella to the Baltic and Nordic countries. The proposal calls for an additional deterrent that would operate independently of NATO. British nuclear submarines would play a key role in providing that deterrent.
In mid-September, Lithuania’s parliament backed a bill to lift the constitutional ban on stationing nuclear weapons in the country. Amid debate over the bill, the Kremlin said Lithuania would be “in the crosshairs” of Russian nuclear weapons if it hosted a nuclear arsenal.
It emerged on September 30 that Russia had sent NATO a document warning that it could use nuclear weapons if there were an attempt to “isolate the Kaliningrad region from the rest of the country.”

articles.title: Pezeshkian: US, Israel resort to sowing internal division after military failure
articles.body:
Pezeshkian: US, Israel resort to sowing internal division after military failure
TEHRAN — President Masoud Pezeshkian has warned that the United States and Israel are aggressively pursuing a campaign to foment internal discord in Iran, having failed to break the nation’s resolve through direct military confrontation.
Speaking during a meeting with mayors of major metropolitan centers and provincial capitals on Tuesday, President Pezeshkian emphasized that Iran’s adversaries have pivoted to psychological and political warfare following strategic setbacks on the battlefield.
“After failing to force the Iranian people to surrender through military war, enemies have focused their entire plan on creating and intensifying internal divisions,” Pezeshkian stated.
Underscoring the critical necessity of national unity, the president warned against political monopolism, noting: “A group must not weaken the country under the illusion that they are ‘all-knowing’; public participation by all citizens is the most important way to overcome conspiracies.”
Pezeshkian’s remarks come in the wake of the major military confrontation that erupted on February 28, during which joint US-Israeli strikes and regional escalations were met with comprehensive retaliatory missile and drone operations by Iranian armed forces. Iran has established operational deterrence and retained the upper hand during the conflict, demonstrating advanced air defense capabilities and the capacity to project precision firepower against critical adversary infrastructure across the region.
The military deadlock and subsequent failure to achieve operational objectives—such as neutralizing Iran’s strategic assets—have forced Washington and Tel Aviv to recalibrate their posture. Facing domestic political fallout and strategic exhaustion following the February clashes, the US-Israeli alliance has increasingly shifted focus toward hybrid warfare, economic pressure, and psychological operations aimed at fracturing domestic consensus in Iran.
Iranian leadership across both civilian and military branches has consistently maintained that internal cohesion remains the primary pillar underpinning the country’s defense doctrine. In his address, Pezeshkian called on local administrators and municipal leaders to actively engage local populations, address socioeconomic challenges transparently, and reinforce public trust to neutralize covert foreign destabilization efforts designed to compensate for adversary defeats on the conventional battlefield.

articles.title: Ukraine Working on Large-Scale Purchase of 20mm Ammunition for F-16s
articles.body:
Ukraine is negotiating with several European countries and manufacturers to obtain tens of thousands of rounds of 20mm ammunition for F-16 fighter jets, sources told Bloomberg.
Ukraine is increasingly using the M61A1 Vulcan cannon on its F-16 fighters to destroy Russian drones.
According to Bloomberg’s sources, using the cannon to intercept drones is currently the most cost-effective and operationally effective solution.
Due to shortages of AIM-120 and AIM-9 air-to-air missiles, Ukrainian F-16 pilots are increasingly using the 20mm cannon against drones.
According to the news agency’s sources, about 150 rounds are required to intercept a single target, or approximately 10,000 rounds per day.
As of the end of September, Ukrainian F-16 pilots had already shot down more than 3,150 aerial targets.
The destroyed targets included 666 cruise missiles and 2,500 drones of various types.
The M61A1 Vulcan is a U.S. six-barrel 20mm aircraft cannon with a rotating barrel assembly.
It uses an electric drive to rotate the barrels and provides a very high rate of fire.
The cannon was developed by General Electric for use on various aircraft, including F-15 and F-16 fighter jets.
It has primarily been used against aerial targets, as well as to engage lightly armored and ground targets.

articles.title: American troops are coming back to Lithuania. Will they stay?
articles.body:
After a six-month break, US troops are set to return to Lithuania, with about 1,000 soldiers expected to deploy under a new rotation. Lithuanian officials and defence experts say the return sends a strong deterrence message to Russia, while Vilnius is also seeking a permanent US military presence.
The Americans are familiar with the forests around Pabradė, where their presence in Lithuania grew steadily over the past decade – from several hundred troops to more than 1,000 following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.
But the continuous US mission ended in June as Washington reassessed its military role in Europe. A newly built facility in Lithuania stood empty for six months. Within a month, however, it is expected to house American troops again.
The new rotation will include a heavy battalion equipped with Abrams tanks, as before, while an artillery battalion will be replaced by an engineering unit, President Gitanas Nausėda said.
Defence Minister Robertas Kaunas said the deployment would contribute significantly to the development of Lithuania’s national division and strengthen the protection of defensive lines along the border.
The engineering capability is particularly important because Lithuania’s own engineering regiment in Kaunas is still being developed and lacks much of the equipment needed for heavy units, said retired Col. Gintaras Ažubalis.
Former military commanders said Lithuania is developing its own artillery capabilities, making the US engineering deployment a useful complement to the country’s existing forces.
“The artillery unit means fire support; now we have an engineering unit, which means logistical support, so that the tank battalion can operate effectively,” said Lt. Gen. Jonas Vytautas Žukas, who served as Lithuania’s military chief from 2014 to 2019.
The Americans will also bring specialised equipment and machinery that Lithuania does not have, said Lt. Gen. Arvydas Pocius, who served as military chief from 2009 to 2014.
The number of US troops is expected to remain around 1,000, although it is not yet clear whether the rotation will continue without another break after nine months.
“I doubt this nine-month rotation would have happened if there were no plan to continue the rotation afterward,” Žukas said.
Pocius agreed, saying there had been no indication that the deployment would be a one-time arrangement.
A regional deterrence message
Estonia has also secured the temporary return of US troops.
“That is good news, because American troops on the eastern flank are very important for our security, and it is a very clear message to President Putin: There is no point even thinking about aggression against NATO’s eastern flank,” Estonian Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna said.
It is not yet clear where the US troops returning to Lithuania will come from.
They could be drawn from US units already stationed in Poland, Ažubalis said, arguing that the source of the troops would not change the strategic significance of the deployment.
Former MP, security and defence expert Giedrimas Jeglinskas said the deployment was linked to US forces in Poland and Washington’s plans for a permanent base there.
US President Donald Trump has said progress has been made toward establishing a permanent American base in Poland, where negotiations have been underway for about six months.
Experts say such a move would fit into a broader strengthening of NATO’s eastern flank.
The precise form of the US presence in Poland remains unclear. It could involve a permanent deployment sought by Warsaw, potentially involving about 5,000 additional troops, or strengthened rotational forces numbering around 10,000, said Gerlinde Niehus, a former deputy director of NATO’s defence policy and planning division.
“Whatever form it takes, the overall direction is clear – strengthening the eastern flank,” she said.
Lithuania is also seeking a permanent US base.
“Since we are compensating for the presence of US troops in Lithuania, I proposed establishing a permanent US military base,” Kaunas said.
Whether Lithuania’s existing military infrastructure will be enough to persuade Washington to establish permanent bases in both Poland and Lithuania remains uncertain.
Retired officers say NATO and the United States view Poland and the Baltic states as part of a single strategic region.
“All of this is part of the security of our common region. I have no doubt that these groups will not be separated,” Žukas said.
He nevertheless argued that Lithuania should first focus on completing the establishment of the German brigade.
Germany’s brigade remains Lithuania’s priority
By the end of next year, Lithuania expects the German brigade to number about 5,000 troops – roughly five times the planned US deployment.
But Germany has faced difficulties recruiting enough personnel, particularly specialists.
“Our commitment to transfer a full-capability brigade to Lithuania no later than the end of 2027 is carved in stone,” German Ambassador to Lithuania Cornelius Zimmermann said. “We are particularly looking for specialists in information technology and other fields, and they are not so easy to find.”
Fausta Šimaitytė, head of the Konrad Adenauer Foundation in Lithuania, said the brigade should be viewed as a military commitment rather than a voluntary project.
Germany’s domestic politics could also affect the broader environment in which the brigade is established, with the Alternative for Germany party continuing to gain support.
“Germans keep their word, especially the military. Of course, much will depend on political decisions and who comes to power,” Pocius said.
Nausėda sought to reassure those concerned about the German commitment.
“I see that various messages are being spread again. Rest assured, the German brigade will be in Lithuania at full strength,” he said.
While Germany is building up its presence in Lithuania, Canada plays the leading role in NATO’s forward presence in Latvia, with France also increasing its contribution.
French President Emmanuel Macron has committed to strengthening French forces in Latvia, particularly in air defence, Latvian Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs said.
NATO is also moving toward transforming its Baltic air-policing mission into an air-defence mission, although for now that remains a political decision rather than a fully implemented capability.
“Of course, we would always like to have more, but what we have is a sufficient basis for deterrence,” Žukas said. “The message being sent to a potential adversary is that NATO countries will act together, and perhaps the Americans will act together with NATO.”
Pocius said the presence of US forces itself carries particular weight.
“It is sufficient deterrence. For Russia, the American flag is the main bogeyman,” he said.
The United States is expected to present its plans for its military forces in Europe in December. US forces are widely expected to decline in western Europe as Washington urges European allies to take greater responsibility for their own security.
At the same time, Lithuania and other countries on NATO’s eastern flank hope that any reduction in the US presence in Western Europe will be accompanied by a stronger American role farther east, stretching from Romania to Finland.

articles.title: ‘No way they can beat us’: Rutte rebuffs Russian nuclear threats to NATO
articles.body:
BRUSSELS — NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte on Wednesday issued a strong rebuke to Russia after Moscow sent a letter to the alliance threatening nuclear escalation over NATO activity near its border.
"We had to reply and make clear to [Russia] that NATO is a defensive alliance ... and stop the war in Ukraine and stop the nuclear threats because it's not helpful," Rutte said at a security summit in Brussels. "NATO is so much stronger than Russia is, so there's no way they can ever beat us."
"The best way to deal with this is to have a little bit of calm," he added. "That's the message: calm, carry on, keep the support for Ukraine going — that's how we deal with it."
Advertisement
Rutte's unusually strong remarks underscore the growing tensions between Moscow and NATO countries as hybrid attacks and Russian-linked sabotage proliferate across Europe.
In recent days, Russia's embassy in Belgium sent NATO a note alleging the alliance was displaying "reckless and irresponsible" behavior near its Kaliningrad exclave, following alliance exercises involving several reconnaissance planes, ground forces and fighter jets near the region, which is between Poland and Lithuania, last month.
"We have emphasised that Russia possesses the necessary means to repel any potential aggression and is prepared to deploy its entire arsenal to defend its territory should NATO countries attempt to isolate the Kaliningrad region from the rest of our country," the embassy wrote on social media.
In its letter to NATO, Moscow explicitly mentions the use of its nuclear arsenal and issues specific threats to hit allied territory, according to one NATO diplomat briefed on the letter, who was granted anonymity to speak freely.
NATO has sent a note back to Russian officials in response, the alliance's spokesperson Allison Hart confirmed.
"We have sent a response, noting that NATO is a defensive Alliance and none of our activities or exercises pose a risk to any part of Russia," she said in a statement. "We strongly denounce the threat of force, including any irresponsible nuclear rhetoric."
Advertisement
Inside NATO, some allies are dismissing the threat. "Our reading is that they want to intimidate allied public opinion so that allies stop supporting [Ukraine], while, at the same time, presenting NATO as the one that would be responsible for an eventual escalation," said the same NATO diplomat cited above. "Textbook Russian propaganda."
"Russia always accelerates when it's the most guilty or when [it] loses," said a second alliance diplomat. "So they are cornered now and they transfer the blame on NATO."
The Russian embassy to Belgium referred POLITICO to its statement on social media.
This article was updated with comment from the Russian embassy.

articles.title: Russia Threatens NATO With Nuclear Weapons if Kaliningrad Is Isolated
articles.body:
Russia has warned NATO that it could use nuclear weapons if the Alliance attempts to isolate the Kaliningrad region.
The warning was contained in a diplomatic document delivered by Russia to NATO and reviewed by Reuters.
In the document, Moscow accused the Alliance of pursuing a “dangerous and reckless course” that, according to Moscow, creates a high risk of direct armed conflict.
Russia claimed that if NATO attempts to isolate the Kaliningrad region, it is ready to use its entire arsenal, “including nuclear weapons.”
The document also mentions Russian strikes on “decision-making centers” in NATO member states at the initial stage of a potential conflict.
The document has not been made public. Reuters reported its contents based on a copy of the diplomatic note reviewed by its journalists.
On September 28, the Russian Embassy in Belgium said that NATO activity near Russia’s borders was increasing. It accused the Alliance of modeling scenarios for isolating the Kaliningrad region and said such actions increased the risk of direct confrontation. The embassy also said Russia was ready to use its “entire arsenal.”
The embassy said this position had been conveyed to NATO headquarters and Belgium’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs.
The following day, Russian diplomatic missions in the United Kingdom and Ireland directly mentioned nuclear weapons.
NATO confirmed that it had received the document and said it had provided a written response. The Alliance emphasized that it is defensive and that its exercises and activities do not pose a threat to Russia.
NATO called on Moscow to end its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, refrain from risky actions toward NATO member states and stop its “irresponsible nuclear rhetoric.”
An unnamed NATO diplomat shared with Reuters that the Russian letter was another attempt by Russia to intimidate Europeans and that NATO’s response was resolute and responsible. The diplomat added that the response again confirmed NATO would not be deterred from supporting Ukraine.
Moscow has linked the statements to increased NATO activity in the Baltic Sea.
The Russian Embassy in Belgium mentioned the Baltic Sentry operation, which NATO launched in January 2025 after damage to critical underwater infrastructure in the Baltic Sea.

articles.title: Bristling with steel spikes and guarded by a bomber drone, two Ukrainian tanks charged Russian infiltrators and lived to tell the tale
articles.body:
- The 475th Assault Regiment found a new way to protect its tanks from Russian drones
- It surrounded its up-armored tanks with drones of its own
- During a recent counter-infiltration mission, two 475th Assault Regiment tanks were shepherded into battle by three different drone types
Russian infiltrators have been slipping into villages and towns along Ukraine's northeastern border with Russia, likely aiming to draw Ukrainian troops away from the bigger fights farther south around the cities of Sloviansk and Kramatorsk.
Desperate to clear out the infiltrators without dedicating too many precious infantry to the task, the Ukrainian 475th Assault Regiment formed a unique team: two heavily up-armored tanks plus three different types of drone. The drones scouted ahead of the tanks and protected them as they trundled through Russia's own drone kill zone on their way to a point-blank clash with Russian troops.
In this mission, the blend of mechanized and unmanned forces worked: the tanks accomplished their mission and survived to fight another day. If the tank-drone pairing keeps working, expect it to become more common all along the 1,200-km gray zone as Ukraine struggles with a deepening shortage of manpower.
It's unclear what kinds of tanks the 475th Assault Regiment operates. It is clear how the regiment protects the tanks from ever-present Russian drones. The unit wraps the tanks in metal cages and then welds hundreds of metal spines on the cages. The spines trigger incoming explosive drones at a safe distance from the tank's hull. The cage supports the spines and catches any drones the spines may miss.
We call these kinds of tanks "hedgehog tanks." The Russians developed the hedgehog application but, seeing that it worked, deflecting potentially dozens of drones at a time, the Ukrainians copied it.
Hedgehog helpers
But even the best-protected hedgehog tank might struggle to get through the enemy's kill zone when that kill zone may include bomber and one-way attack drones in the air and loitering ambush drones waiting on the ground as well as mines and other threats.
Sometimes the best defense against a drone is another drone, and the 475th Assault Regiment put that truism into practice. To shepherd those two hedgehog tanks into battle with Russian infiltrators in the village of Vilkhuvatka, in Kharkiv Oblast 9 km from the border with Russia, the regiment deployed a Vampire heavy bomber drone, at least one explosive first-person-view (FPV) quadcopter, and at least one surveillance quadcopter.
Trending Now
The surveillance drones could scout ahead. The bomber drone could blast mines and loitering ambush drones. The FPVs could intercept incoming enemy FPVs. The layered protection was effective. As evident in the 475th Assault Regiment's video depicting the two-tank counter-assault, the tanks took multiple hits from Russian drones and mines, but not enough hits to slow them down.
Both tanks reached an intersection inside Vilkhuvatka, fired their cannons at nearby Russian infiltrators, and then withdrew.
It should come as no surprise that the 475th Assault Regiment is pioneering mixed formations of drones and tanks. The regiment recently partnered with the 1st Assault Regiment to develop new "multi-domain" tactics combining ground, air, and cyber forces. "We came to the conclusion that fighting in only one domain makes no sense," said "Perun," the 1st Assault Regiment commander. "We'd simply lose because the enemy would bring another domain into play."
The key takeaway is that, despite the serious threat that drones and mines pose to tanks in the fifth year of Russia's wider war on Ukraine, tanks can still fight, win, and survive—if they have plenty of support from the same kinds of drones that, in enemy hands, vex them along every kilometer of disputed terrain. The tank isn't dead yet. It just needs a little help.

articles.title: Ukrainian Air Force: 285 attack drones detected over Ukraine on Wed, 254 shot down
articles.body:
The Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine (AFU) reported that as of 18:30, 285 enemy strike drones of various types were detected in Ukrainian airspace, and 254 were shot down or neutralized.
"Throughout the day on September 30 (from 06:30 to 18:30), the enemy attacked Ukraine with 285 attack UAVs (174 of which were jet-powered), Gerber drones, and other types of drones," according to a statement by the Ukrainian Air Force on Telegram on Wednesday.
Air defense forces managed to shoot down or neutralize 254 UAVs (146 of them jet-powered).
In addition, according to the Air Force, the enemy launched a strike in the eastern sector using a ballistic missile and several Banderole/Dan-T drones. The information is being verified.
As of 18:30, there were about 10 attack drones in the airspace.
"Do not ignore the air raid alert," the Ukrainian Air Force said in the statement.

articles.title: Putin envoy praises Lithuanian PM for toning down ‘Russian attack’ warnings
articles.body:
Russian President Vladimir Putin’s special envoy Kirill Dmitriev on Thursday praised Lithuanian Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius’ comments that there is no evidence Russia is preparing an attack on NATO, calling the remarks “unusually wise”.
“The unusually wise words from a Lithuanian PM who openly says that the ‘scare with Russia’ EU hysteria is not based on ANY facts,” Dmitriev wrote on X. He said EU officials were using Russia as a “bogeyman” to divert attention from what he described as failures over migration, the economy, “woke” policies and what he called warmongering.
The unusually wise words from a Lithuanian PM who openly says that the “scare with Russia” EU hysteria is not based on ANY facts. The EU BU bureaucrats need Russia as a bogeyman to distract from their terrible failures on migration, the economy, woke policies and warmongering. https://t.co/MyYgRgY88Q
— Kirill Dmitriev (@kadmitriev) September 30, 2026
Dmitriev was responding to comments Sinkevičius made Tuesday at a joint news conference with NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte. The Lithuanian prime minister said there was no intelligence indicating that Russia was preparing an attack against NATO.
“I think it is necessary to tell the public if there is a threat, but we cannot exaggerate it and say that something will happen in the coming months or weeks,” Sinkevičius said.
He said he had asked Rutte whether there was evidence or intelligence showing that Russia was preparing for such an action.
“In fact, there is no such data,” Sinkevičius said. “The risk remains, but it is not changing, neither increasing nor decreasing. Therefore, I think we need to calmly do our work, and that is what we are doing.”
The comments came amid heightened tensions between Russia and NATO. NATO has said there is no immediate threat to alliance territory from Russia, while warning that Moscow continues to pose a long-term security challenge.
Dmitriev is Putin’s special presidential envoy for investment and economic cooperation with foreign countries and heads the Russian Direct Investment Fund. He has emerged as one of Moscow’s key interlocutors with the United States over efforts to end the war in Ukraine. He has also advocated easing US sanctions and expanding business ties between Washington and Moscow.
‘Propaganda’
Meanwhile, Sinkevičius’s team, asked to comment on Dmitriev’s comments, dismissed them as “propaganda”.
“Commenting on propaganda would not be a meaningful exercise,” the prime minister’s spokesman Gedas Salyga said on Thursday.

articles.title: With nuclear threats, the Kremlin is trying to distract the world from Russia's failures in Ukraine — Rutte
articles.body:
With nuclear threats, the Kremlin is trying to distract the world from Russia's failures in Ukraine — Rutte
Kyiv • UNN
NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte said that Russia currently does not pose a threat to the Alliance. He called the Kremlin's nuclear threats an attempt to divert attention from its failures in Ukraine.
There is currently no direct threat to NATO from Russia, while the Kremlin’s nuclear threats are a diversionary tactic to distract from its failures in Ukraine. NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte said this, reports UNN, citing Euronews.
Details
According to Rutte, he does not take Russia’s nuclear threats seriously, as Moscow cannot defeat NATO.
We are ready for this, we anticipated it, and this applies to all of NATO. We will defend every inch of NATO territory. There is no such threat at present, and if something happens, we are ready to confront it
He called on Moscow to stop its nuclear blackmail, as "there is absolutely no need for it; it helps in no way."
"If necessary, of course, we will defend ourselves. But the main point is that all of this is happening because the war in Ukraine is going badly for him (Russian dictator Putin — ed.). He wants to divide us and divert our attention from Ukraine," the NATO chief added.
Context
The day before, in a letter sent to NATO, Russia stated that it was ready to use nuclear weapons to defend its Baltic exclave — the Kaliningrad region.
In response, NATO "strongly condemned" Russia’s nuclear threat and called on the Kremlin to end its unprovoked war in Ukraine.

articles.title: Russian Drone Hits Kyiv Nuclear Research Institute Housing VVR-M Reactor
articles.body:
- Category
- War in Ukraine
Russian Drone Hits Kyiv Nuclear Research Institute Housing VVR-M Reactor
A Russian drone struck the grounds of Ukraine’s Institute for Nuclear Research in Kyiv, where the VVR-M research reactor is located, Ukraine’s State Nuclear Regulatory Inspectorate reported on October 1.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to the regulator, citing the Institute for Nuclear Research of the National Academy of Sciences of Ukraine, the strike occurred at 6:18 p.m. local time on September 30. A fire broke out following the attack but was quickly extinguished, with no casualties reported.
The reactor itself and systems important to its safety were not damaged. Authorities recorded no changes in radiation levels, which remained within the natural background range of 0.16 to 0.20 microsieverts per hour.
An investigation into the incident is ongoing, while specialists continue to assess the extent of the damage caused by the strike.
The VVR-M reactor has remained shut down since February 2022 as a precaution aimed at reducing radiation risks. Its core has been fully unloaded, and operations at the facility are currently limited to routine maintenance of systems important to nuclear safety.
“Thus, the drone strike on the territory of the Institute for Nuclear Research constitutes an attack on a peaceful nuclear facility used exclusively for scientific and research purposes. It is yet another cynical disregard by Russia for internationally recognized principles and standards of nuclear and radiation safety and constitutes a war crime,” the regulator concluded.
The incident follows another recent Russian strike on a facility belonging to Ukraine’s National Academy of Sciences. On September 28, a Russian drone hit an academy building in central Kyiv, sparking a fire in the capital’s Shevchenkivskyi district.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said emergency crews were deployed to extinguish the blaze and search for people who may have been inside the building.
