articles.title: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth Announces More Sweeping Cuts to the Military's Top Ranks
articles.body:
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced on Wednesday that he had directed the U.S. military to cut 20% of the number of general roles.
The new reduction, which Hegseth revealed during an address at the Marine Corps Base Quantico in Virginia on Wednesday afternoon, doubles the already 10% cuts to general and flag officer positions that Hegseth instructed the military to make last year.
According to Fox News, which previously reported Hegseth's intention to announce the cuts, military services are being ordered to finish making the reductions by Jan. 1, 2027. The network reported that some of the affected roles are expected to be downgraded, rather than cut entirely.
During his speech on Wednesday, Hegseth did not specify a timeline for the cuts, but said that “the number crunchers say we’ve fired 10% of the generals and admirals across the force, and that number sounds about right.”
“And I know—because I directed it—that we’ve also reduced the overall number of general officer slots by an additional 10%,” Hegseth said. “So yes, 20% reduction across the board.”
“Now, the media calls that a purge,” he continued. “I call it accountability, and long overdue, and frankly, the bare minimum. As usual, what the media levels as an accusation, I wear as an accomplishment. You see, you can’t change a culture with the same people who enabled it.”
Peter Feaver, a professor of political science at Duke University and a specialist in civil-military relations, says that many experts agree “that there probably could be a trimming of the general and flag officer ranks, that they had grown perhaps unnecessarily large in recent years, and that some rebalancing would be prudent if it was done carefully and managed carefully.”
“In the abstract, could the U.S. military absorb a 20% cut in general flag officer ranks if properly managed? I’d say yes, and I think most experts would say yes,” Feaver says.
He notes, though, that the 20% reduction also comes after additional cuts to the military’s top ranks, and on a relatively fast timeline.
“The burden will be on Secretary Hegseth and his team to demonstrate that they are making these cuts wisely and consolidating wisely and not recklessly,” Feaver says. “The faster they do it, and the less explanation that they give, and the more that really good officers are cut, the more doubt there will be.”
Upheaval in military leadership
During his speech, Hegseth referenced an address he gave in Quantico, Virginia last year, in which he outlined his vision for the Department of Defense. Last year’s speech, he said on Wednesday, “reestablished a singular mission for this department: warfighting. Preparing to fight and preparing to win. Unrelenting, unapologetic, and uncompromising in that single pursuit.”
“Now, I think the generals heard the message,” he continued. “Those who responded positively, which is most of them, are leading newly focused and newly empowered and disciplined formations. Those generals who did not, who clung to the ‘woke’ department or seemed to think civilian control of the military is simply a suggestion—well, they no longer work here.”
Hegseth’s speech comes at a time of turmoil within the military’s leadership: At least 20 military and civilian leaders have been pushed out or resigned since Hegseth was sworn in as Defense Secretary. In 2025, Hegseth told the active duty military to cut 20% of its four-star general officers and the National Guard to cut 20% of its top officials. It is not known if all of those reductions have been completed.
Hegseth said in a memo at the time that the reduction plan would eliminate “redundant force structure to optimize and streamline leadership” and that the goal was to prevent “unnecessary bureaucratic layers” within the military, The Associated Press reported.
“This is not a slash-and-burn exercise meant to punish high-ranking officers,” Hegseth said in May 2025. “This has been a deliberative process, working with the Joint Chiefs of Staff with one goal: maximizing strategic readiness and operational effectiveness by making prudent reductions in the general and flag officer ranks.”
Hegseth has faced a wave of backlash from Democrats and some Republicans over his management of the Department of Defense, in addition to his handling of other issues, such as the war in Iran. Republican Rep. Thomas Massie, who has clashed with the Trump Administration on multiple occasions since President Donald Trump returned to the Oval Office, introduced articles of impeachment against Hegseth earlier this month, including allegations regarding the Iran war.
Before that, Republican Sen. Thom Tillis of North Carolina publicly criticized Hegseth’s management of the agency, after Dan Driscoll resigned as Army Secretary amid reports of tension between him and Hegseth.
“I have never witnessed more inept management of the brave men and women who serve our country,” Tillis said in a social media post. “I urge the President to find a new leader at the Pentagon who will retain and empower our military talent rather than diminish it.”
Hegseth announces future plans
The Defense Secretary also unveiled a slew of new initiatives on Wednesday, including something called “Project Meridian,” which he said would be “an effort led by America’s best minds to study the future of warfare,” including “discovering, developing, and fielding the weapons and systems that our children and our grandchildren will need in their lifetimes … on any future battlefield, from under the Earth to beyond the Moon.” Hegseth said that Elon Musk, who previously served as one of President Donald Trump’s top advisers before their very public feud last year, along with former Republican House Speaker Newt Gingrich and Anduril co-founder Palmer Luckey, will co-lead the initiative.
Hegseth also announced that the Department of Defense plans to build “the next great American base.” He lamented that a new military base hadn’t been constructed within the U.S. in decades, and called on governors to “bring us their best sales pitch.”
“If your state wants the honor of hosting 15 to 25,000 of America’s great troops, show us why and how you’re going to do it,” he said.
A shift in military culture
During his speech, Hegseth applauded his efforts to eliminate what he called “woke” culture within the American military, such as rolling back diversity, equity, and inclusion initiatives.
“The only focus, as you know, in your formations should be training, readiness, accountability, discipline, and lethality. And when you pursue those things, you don’t have to walk on eggshells,” Hegseth said. “The complainers, the ideologues, and the poor performers are no longer in the driver’s seat. No more silly PowerPoint trainings or drag queen shows. No more diversity quotas. No more gender pronouns. No more identity months. Only the warrior ethos.”
“We are no longer the ‘woke’ department or the weak department,” he said. He went on to use derogatory terms to refer to people who are overweight and people who are transgender.
“No wimps, no radicals,” he said. “Just warriors. Just tough, ready, committed troops.”

articles.title: Latvia is ready to deploy nuclear weapons by NATO decision - president

Latvia is ready to deploy nuclear weapons by NATO decision - president
Kyiv • UNN
Edgars Rinkēvičs said that Latvian laws do not prohibit the deployment of nuclear weapons in the country. No negotiations are currently underway, but if NATO makes such a decision, it will be carried out.
If NATO adopts a collective decision and such a need arises, nuclear weapons could be stationed in Latvia. This was stated by the country's president, Edgars Rinkēvičs, reports UNN, citing Delfi.
Details
The publication states that, in its first reading, the Seimas of Lithuania supported the repeal of the constitutional ban on stationing nuclear weapons in the country's territory. Currently, Article 137 of the constitution of Latvia's neighboring country stipulates that weapons of mass destruction or foreign military bases may not be located in Lithuania. Rinkēvičs emphasized that Latvia has no such ban.
There are no legal obstacles in our laws to stationing nuclear weapons in Latvia
He said that in 2003, when Latvia was preparing to join NATO, each member country assured that it would have no restrictions on implementing the full mechanism of NATO's collective security, including participation in the nuclear deterrence system.
If such a need arises and NATO adopts such a collective decision, nuclear weapons will be stationed in Latvia
At the same time, he emphasized that no specific negotiations on stationing nuclear weapons in Latvia are currently under way.
We remind you
Latvia imposed national sanctions on Russian oligarchs Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman after the announcement that the European Union's restrictions had been lifted.

articles.title: Ukrainian air defense neutralizes 87 of 107 Russian drones launched overnight
articles.body:
Ukrainian air defense neutralizes 87 of 107 Russian drones launched overnight
The Ukrainian Air Force reported this in a Telegram post, according to Ukrinform.
Beginning at 18:00 on September 30, the enemy attacked Ukraine with 107 strike UAVs, including Shahed-type drones (63 of them jet-powered), Gerbera drones and Parodiya-type decoy drones, launched from Oryol, Millerovo, Bryansk and Shatalovo in Russia, as well as from the temporarily occupied territories of the Donetsk region and the Autonomous Republic of Crimea, from the area of Hvardiiske.
The aerial attack was repelled by aircraft, anti-aircraft missile forces, electronic warfare units, unmanned systems units and mobile fire groups of the Ukrainian Defense Forces.

Hits by enemy air attack weapons were recorded at 11 locations, while debris from downed drones fell at four locations.
The attack is ongoing, with several enemy UAVs still in Ukrainian airspace.

articles.title: Ukraine’s training facilities get boost: EU is funding centers where its army prepares soldiers, with Denmark putting in €33 million
articles.body:
The EU is putting money into the places inside Ukraine where the army trains its soldiers. The bloc will fund the modernization of several military training centers in Ukraine, upgrading facilities, housing, and equipment, with Denmark administering the funds and the Come Back Alive charity carrying out the work, the Defense Ministry said.
The Ministries of Defense of Ukraine and Denmark previously signed a Letter of Intent to implement a project to modernize one of the Armed Forces of Ukraine's training centers. Under this agreement, Denmark allocated about €33 million to training infrastructure, living and sanitary conditions, equipment, and drones for training defenders.
The money goes into the centers
The support will pay to modernize several training sites: better living quarters for the troops who cycle through them, upgraded facilities, and improved infrastructure, the ministry says.
The project runs under the EU's diplomatic and military-planning bodies, the European External Action Service, the Military Planning and Conduct Capability, and the bloc's military-assistance mission for Ukraine, with the Come Back Alive foundation carrying it out alongside the Defense Ministry.
Halan calls training a foundation
The aim is a modern environment for preparing soldiers.
"Modernized centers let us train the military on real combat experience," Deputy Defense Minister Liubov Halan says, thanking the EU and every partner country.
Training inside Ukraine, she says, is as fundamental to defense as ammunition and equipment, because weapons do not work without people trained to use them. The modernized sites, the ministry says, are meant to let Ukraine prepare its own forces to a higher standard, faster, and closer to the front.
Denmark administers the funds
The project is an EU initiative, open to any partner willing to contribute, with Denmark as the fund administrator. The ministry thanked the EU, Denmark, and Come Back Alive for support it says raises the quality of Ukraine's training.

articles.title: Gaza documentary NAZA tops Italian box office, beats Avengers
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Gaza documentary NAZA tops Italian box office ahead of 'Avengers Endgame: Encore'
Award-winning Gaza documentary NAZA, directed by Israeli filmmakers Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, has beaten Avengers Endgame: Encore to top the Italian box office at number one.
The documentary, which examines the mass killing of Palestinian civilians in Gaza through testimonies from Israeli military and intelligence personnel, topped the Italian box office during its first two days in cinemas.
Its debut marked its first theatrical release following its premiere at the Venice Film Festival, with ticket sales reaching nearly €1.1 million ($1.24 million) by Tuesday, according to Italian box office tracker Cinetel.
Meanwhile, Avengers Endgame: Encore, an extended re-release of the 2019 Marvel film, grossed €356,000 ($404,000) over the same period in Italy.
NAZA was initially released as a three-day cinema event across 515 cinemas in Italy, with many screenings selling out.
However, strong demand has led to screenings continuing beyond the initial run.
More than 150 cinemas have extended the film’s programming, according to The Guardian, which produced the documentary, with further extensions expected.
Interest in Italy was already high ahead of the film’s release after it won the Special Jury Prize at the Venice Film Festival earlier this month, with a premiere that was followed by a 25-minute standing ovation, a festival record.
NAZA features testimony from 24 Israeli military and intelligence personnel whose identities, voices and appearances were digitally altered for allegedly for their protection.
The interviews were conducted over three years and focus on the use of AI-powered surveillance and targeting systems in Gaza, including how targets were identified and struck despite expected civilian casualties.
According to reports about the documentary, some of those interviewed describe witnessing Palestinian civilians being killed and residential areas used as shelters being set ablaze.
The film’s title is derived from an acronym used by Israel’s intelligence service to indicate the number of civilians expected to die in an airstrike, according to The Guardian.
The documentary has faced significant backlash from senior Israeli officials since its Venice win.
Israeli Culture Minister Miki Zohar called for Abraham and Szor to have their citizenship revoked, accusing them of “treason against the state”.
“I will act immediately to revoke the Israeli citizenship of these despicable creators for treason against the state,” Zohar posted on X.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu subsequently said he would pursue legislation allowing citizenship to be revoked in cases involving people who "defame" Israeli soldiers abroad.
Netanyahu also proposed a second bill that would increase damages in defamation cases involving the Israeli military or state.
Simiarly, Israeli military chief Eyal Zamir said the military was examining possible legal measures over the film.
Israeli media subsequently reported that the military was considering a leak investigation and seeking assistance from the Shin Bet.
Abraham and Szor were among the co-directors of the 2025 Oscar-winning documentary No Other Land, which focused on Israeli settler violence and the destruction of Palestinian villages in the occupied West Bank.

articles.title: Poland implements new response rules for air defence amid Russian attacks on Ukraine
articles.body:
Poland implements new response rules for air defence amid Russian attacks on Ukraine
Poland enacts simplified procedures for detecting and shooting down foreign aerial assets starting 1 October. The rules are being changed to protect Polish airspace during Russian attacks on Ukraine.
Source: European Pravda, citing Polish media outlet Gazeta Prawna
Details: Defence Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz announced the full readiness of the new, simplified rules for detecting and shooting down foreign objects in Polish airspace, which take effect on 1 October.
"First of October is always a good time to implement these procedures," Kosiniak-Kamysz noted.
On 28 September, Cezary Tomczyk, Deputy Minister of National Defence, spoke about the planned changes to the rules for Polish pilots participating in missions to protect Polish airspace during Russian airstrikes in Ukraine.
Tomczyk explained that these changes primarily concern modifying the rules for identifying foreign aerial assets. Peacetime procedures requiring visual identification of a target before shooting it down are to be replaced by dynamic sensor-based identification.
Following the procedural changes, a pilot or their commander will be able to make the decision to shoot down an unidentified object based on information gathered by radars and other systems or on information provided by the Ukrainian side, which regularly faces attacks from Russian drones and missiles.
Background:
- On 28 September Cezary Tomczyk reported that Poland would change the rules for shooting down aerial assets that violate its airspace.
- Earlier, it was reported that starting Friday 25 September, the Polish government will begin to distribute guidance on how to respond to air attacks which explains the basic rules for finding a safe place – indoor or outdoor – in the event of threats from the air.

articles.title: Hegseth military cuts fuel fears of Trump loyalty purge
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Hegseth military cuts fuel fears of Trump loyalty purge
US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has announced a 20 percent cut to the number of generals and admirals in the US military, intensifying concerns that the Trump administration is reshaping the armed forces around its political and ideological agenda.
Hegseth portrayed the cuts as an exercise in "accountability", suggesting that officers who failed to embrace his drive to purge what he calls "woke" policies from the military had been removed.
"The number-crunchers say we fired 10 percent of the generals and admirals across the force," Hegseth told troops at the Quantico military base on Wednesday.
"We've also reduced the overall number of general officer slots by an additional 10 percent."
"So yes, 20 percent reduction across the board," he added. "The media calls that a purge. I call it accountability, and long overdue."
The announcement comes amid mounting concerns among Democratic lawmakers and some current and former military officials that the Trump administration is eroding the traditionally non-partisan character of the US armed forces and making adherence to its political agenda increasingly important for senior officers.
Since returning to office last year, President Donald Trump and Hegseth have removed a succession of senior military leaders, often without publicly explaining the reasons for their dismissal.
They include former chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff General Charles "CQ" Brown, who Trump fired without explanation in February 2025, as well as the heads of the US Army, Navy and Coast Guard, the general who headed the National Security Agency, the vice chief of staff of the US Air Force, a Navy admiral assigned to NATO and three senior military lawyers.
Hegseth has also fired or blocked the promotions of scores of generals and admirals during his tenure, according to US media reports.
The upheaval has prompted warnings from some former senior officers about the potential creation of a loyalty culture within the military.
H.R. McMaster, a retired Army general who served as Trump's national security adviser during his first term, recently warned against creating "a climate in which everything's a loyalty test".
Hegseth rejects accusations that the changes amount to a political purge, insisting that Trump is entitled to select the military leadership he wants and that his reforms are intended to restore an apolitical force focused on combat effectiveness.
In Wednesday's address, however, he explicitly linked the fate of senior officers to their response to his previous efforts to reshape military culture.
Hegseth said officers who "responded positively" to a speech he delivered to senior commanders last year were now "leading newly focused and newly empowered and disciplined formations", while those who did not "no longer work here".
"We are no longer the woke department, or the weak department," Hegseth said.
"Simple translation of that: no fatties, no trannies, no beardos, no weirdos, no wimps, no radicals. Just warriors -- just tough, ready, committed troops."
Hegseth ordered major cuts to the military leadership in May 2025, including a 10-percent reduction in the overall number of generals and admirals and a 20-percent cut to the highest four-star ranks.
During his confirmation hearing in January 2025, Hegseth argued that the Pentagon bureaucracy was top-heavy and that resources should instead be directed towards combat capabilities.
"It's going to be my job, working with those that we hire and those inside the administration, to identify those places where fat can be cut, so it can go toward lethality," he told lawmakers.
His campaign has extended beyond the military's senior ranks. The Pentagon has dismantled diversity programmes and Hegseth this week moved to end tenure for future civilian faculty at US military academies, saying the institutions should refocus on their "warfighting" mission.
Critics argue that the combination of ideological changes and unexplained dismissals risks encouraging officers to tailor their conduct to the political preferences of the administration.
Hegseth, meanwhile, has cast the changes as necessary to reverse what he regards as years of misplaced priorities at the Pentagon.
"The media calls that a purge," he said on Wednesday. "I call it accountability."

articles.title: UK may reverse Brexit – Burnham
articles.body:
UK may reverse Brexit – Burnham
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said the UK could eventually rejoin the European Union as his government considers options for reshaping relations with the bloc a decade after the Brexit referendum. 
In an interview with the BBC on Wednesday, Burnham said Brexit had done “more harm than good,” arguing that the current settlement was holding back economic growth and had failed to deliver the promised control over immigration. 
He said the government would examine alternatives ranging from maintaining the status quo to joining a customs union or the single market, or even potentially going “all the way” and returning to the EU. 
Talk of reversing Brexit has grown recently, with several prominent British politicians floating the idea. Burnham’s comments are the clearest indication yet that rejoining the EU could be on the table, although any such move would reopen questions over sovereignty, immigration, and regulatory control that drove much of the Leave vote.
Why did Britain leave the EU in the first place?
Britons voted 52% to 48% to leave the EU in June 2016, triggering years of negotiations over the terms of Brexit. The UK formally left the bloc in January 2020 and exited the single market and customs union at the end of that year. 
For many Leave voters, Brexit was primarily about sovereignty and immigration rather than economics. An Ashcroft poll conducted immediately after the referendum found that 49% of Leave voters said their main reason was wanting decisions about the UK to be made in Britain, while 33% pointed to regaining control over immigration and borders. Only 6% primarily cited expected benefits from leaving the EU for trade and the economy. By contrast, 43% of Remain voters said their main concern was the risk Brexit posed to the economy, jobs, and prices.
What did Brexit achieve?
Brexit ended EU free movement and gave London control over who could move to Britain from the bloc. That did not, however, translate into lower overall immigration. Net migration instead surged as arrivals from outside the EU increased, reaching a record 944,000 in the year to March 2023 before falling sharply following tighter visa rules. Non-EU nationals continue to account for most immigration. 
The change also worked both ways. British citizens lost EU freedom-of-movement rights and are now subject to the entry requirements that apply to non-EU travelers in the Schengen area.
Brexit also gave Britain an independent trade policy, allowing it to negotiate agreements without the approval of EU members. The UK has since struck deals with Australia, New Zealand, and India and joined the CPTPP, a major Indo-Pacific trade bloc. However, the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) estimates that the long-term economic gains from post-Brexit trade agreements are small compared with the impact it expects from higher trade barriers with the EU. 
The bloc nevertheless remains Britain’s largest trading partner, accounting for about 41% of UK exports and roughly half of imports in 2025.
Why is the issue being reopened now?
Critics contend that the economic costs of Brexit have overshadowed its benefits. The OBR estimates that Brexit will ultimately reduce the trade intensity of the British economy by around 15% and productivity by about 4% relative to remaining in the EU. These are long-term modeling assumptions rather than directly observed losses, while Britain’s economic performance since Brexit has also been affected by the Covid-19 pandemic, the Ukraine conflict, and wider disruptions to global trade. 
Leaving the EU single market and customs union also created new barriers to trade with Britain’s largest trading partner. Businesses face customs declarations, rules-of-origin requirements, and additional checks that did not apply when Britain was an EU member. 
While Brexit gave Britain greater control over legal migration, Burnham has argued that it weakened the country’s ability to tackle irregular migration by reducing cooperation with European countries, particularly over Channel crossings.
Is preserving the UK part of the calculation?
Burnham has not explicitly linked his EU rethink to preserving the United Kingdom. But it comes as pro-independence and Irish nationalist parties in Scotland, Wales, and Northern Ireland push for independence or Irish reunification while presenting closer integration with the EU as part of their preferred future. 
This month, the pro-independence SNP and Plaid Cymru, together with the pro-Irish-unification Sinn Fein, jointly asserted their nations’ right to self-determination and called on London to facilitate a constitutional change, declaring that their future “belongs in the European Union.” 
Burnham, meanwhile, has made preserving the UK an explicit priority. Responding on Tuesday to Scottish First Minister John Swinney’s prediction that he would be the UK’s last prime minister, he vowed to “fight with everything I’ve got to keep it together.”
Haven’t Britain and the EU already been moving closer?
In security policy, Britain and the EU have already moved significantly closer despite Brexit. The UK remains one of NATO’s leading European military powers, while the 2025 UK-EU Security and Defense Partnership established regular strategic consultations and expanded cooperation on Ukraine, sanctions against Russia, military mobility, and arms production. It also opened the way for greater British involvement in EU defense initiatives.
Much of the alignment has centered on Russia and Ukraine. London and its European partners have coordinated weapons supplies and training for Kiev, sanctions against Moscow, and efforts to expand European arms production. 
In July, Britain secured participation in the EU’s €90 billion Ukraine Support Loan, allowing British defense companies to compete for procurement contracts financed through the scheme. The UK agreed to make a contribution proportionate to the value of contracts awarded to British companies.
Could Britain simply rejoin the EU?
Any return would be neither automatic nor a restoration of Britain’s previous membership terms. The UK would have to formally reapply and go through the EU accession process, requiring unanimous approval from member states and the consent of the European Parliament. Nor would Britain be guaranteed the opt-outs and special arrangements it enjoyed before Brexit; the terms of any renewed membership would have to be negotiated. 
Immediately after the 2016 referendum, EU leaders said they regretted Britain’s decision but respected the result. During the subsequent withdrawal negotiations, Brussels took a firm line, insisting that Britain could not retain the benefits of EU membership from outside the bloc and rejecting “cherry picking” from the single market. 
A decade later, however, Brussels is not ruling out London’s return. In July, EU Commissioner Maros Sefcovic said applying for membership was “entirely a prerogative” of the UK. Former EU Brexit negotiator Michel Barnier said in June that the EU’s “door is open,” while stressing that Britain could not simply choose which EU rules to follow.
